queries.name: above_top_solid
queries.summary: y just above the highest solid block of the column at (x, z); world gen only
queries.hover:
`q.above_top_solid(x, z)` - y of the first position above the highest solid block in that column.
Leaves never count as solid; in dimensions without sky (Nether) the roof is skipped first.
World-generation Molang only; wrong argument count returns 0 without an error.
queries.description: Scans the world column at the given x and z from the top down and returns the y just above the first solid block it finds. Available only in world-generation expressions.
queries.long:
Returns the y coordinate one above the highest *solid* block in the column at `x`, `z` - the position where something standing on the surface would go.

Both coordinates are rounded to the nearest whole block (halves away from zero), and the result is a whole number in world coordinates.

**What counts as solid.** A block counts when its material blocks movement. Leaves never count, so on a forest the scan passes through the canopy to the ground below it. Water and lava do not count either, so over an ocean the result is the sea floor + 1, not the water surface. Plants, flowers, grass and other materials that do not block movement are skipped the same way. Glass does count.

**Where the scan starts.** Normally it starts just above the highest section of the column that contains any block. In a dimension without a sky - the Nether - it first walks down through the solid roof and only then looks for the next solid block, so the result is the cave floor under the bedrock ceiling, not the top of the ceiling.

**No solid block.** If the whole column is non-solid the result is the dimension's lowest y. If the column's chunk is not available the result is the top of the dimension instead (`320` in the Overworld, `128` in the Nether, `256` in the End); a chunk that is present but not filled in yet can read like an empty column (the lowest y).

Compare `query.heightmap`, which reads the stored height of the column: it counts leaves and water as terrain but skips glass, so the two queries can disagree in either direction.

args.name: x
args.description: World X
accepts: number; rounded to nearest, halves away from zero

args.name: z
args.description: World Z
accepts: number; rounded to nearest, halves away from zero

queries.formula: y(top solid block) + 1

whenUnavailable.when: no world access in the context
no solid block in the column

pitfalls: Leaves are not solid here: under a tree the result is the ground, not the canopy top.
Over water or lava the result is the floor + 1, not the liquid surface; `query.heightmap` gives the surface.
In the Nether the bedrock roof is skipped; the result is the floor beneath it.
A wrong argument count is silent: `q.above_top_solid(v.worldx)` is 0.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: actor_count
queries.summary: How many entities the client is drawing this frame (client only)
queries.hover:
`q.actor_count` - number of entities the client is rendering in the current frame.
Client-side rendering only; in behavior packs / on the server it is expected to be 0 (not yet verified).
Arguments are ignored.
queries.description: Returns how many entities the client is drawing in the current frame. Only meaningful while the client renders; elsewhere it is 0.
queries.long:
Returns a count of entities that the client is rendering in the current frame. It is a scene-wide number, the same for every entity that asks during one frame, and is typically used to scale back costly visuals when many entities are on screen.

The value comes from the client's render state, so it only exists while something is being drawn. Evaluated without a render context it returns `0` without an error; on the server, in behavior-pack Molang, it is expected to do the same (not yet verified in game).

The count is taken when the client starts drawing entities for a frame, so every expression evaluated during that frame sees the same number. Whether entities culled as off-screen are included is not yet verified in game.

The query takes no arguments; extra arguments are ignored.

appliesTo.entities: any; the value is the same for the whole scene

whenUnavailable.when: no render context (server side expected, not yet verified)

pitfalls: In behavior-pack Molang it is always 0, not an error.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: all
queries.summary: 1 if every argument after the first is identical to the first, else 0
queries.hover:
`q.all(value, a, b, ...)` - 1 if every later argument is identical to `value`, else 0.
Needs at least 3 arguments; fewer logs an error and returns 0.
Numbers must match bit for bit (`0` and `-0` differ); stops at the first mismatch.
queries.description: Takes a reference value and two or more candidates; the result is 1 only if every candidate is identical to the reference, and 0 at the first one that is not.
queries.long:
Evaluates `value` once, then walks through the remaining arguments in order. Each one must have the same kind as `value` (number vs. string) and the same value; the first one that differs ends the scan and the result is `0`. If every argument matches, the result is `1`.

**How values are compared.** Numbers are compared bit for bit, which is stricter than `==`: `0` and `-0` are different, and `NaN` equals an identical `NaN`. Strings are compared by name (case matters). A string never equals a number, even when the text looks like one.

**Evaluation.** The arguments after the first are evaluated only until the answer is known, so an expression placed after the first mismatch never runs.

**Argument count.** At least three arguments are required - the value and two or more candidates. With fewer the query logs an error and returns `0`; for a single comparison write `a == b`.

`query.any` is the counterpart that returns `1` when *at least one* candidate matches.

args.name: value
args.description: Reference value, evaluated once

args.name: candidate
args.description: Values that must all be identical to `value` (two or more)

appliesTo.entities: no entity needed

pitfalls: `q.all(v.x, 1)` is an error (needs 3 arguments), not a comparison.
`q.all(0, -0, 0)` is 0 because numbers are compared bit for bit; `0 == -0` is 1.
A string and a number never match: `q.all('1', 1, 1)` is 0.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: all_animations_finished
queries.summary: In a controller: 1 once every animation of the current state reached its end
queries.hover:
`q.all_animations_finished` - 1 once every animation in the active controller state has reached its end.
Only answers while an animation controller is being evaluated; anywhere else it is 0.
A state with no animations counts as finished (1). Looping animations count once they reach the end.
queries.description: While an animation controller evaluates its current state, returns 1 when each animation listed in that state has reached its end at least once, else 0.
queries.long:
Meant for the `transitions` of an animation-controller state: it becomes `1` once every animation the active state plays has run to its end at least once, which is the usual way to leave a one-shot state.

An animation counts as having reached its end when its animation time becomes greater than or equal to its length. That mark is kept afterwards, so a looping animation counts as finished after its first full cycle, and a `hold_on_last_frame` animation counts as soon as it reaches the last frame.

A state that plays no animations at all returns `1` immediately (nothing is left unfinished).

**Where it works.** The controller marks its active state only while it is being evaluated. Outside an animation controller - in an animation, a render controller, entity scripts - the query returns `0` without an error. Contexts that have no animation data (world particles, blocks) also return `0`.

`query.any_animation_finished` returns `1` as soon as one animation of the state has finished.

appliesTo.entities: entities with animation controllers
fields: animation controller state transitions and other state expressions

whenUnavailable.when: not evaluated inside an animation controller

queries.side: both (server-side animation controllers not yet verified)
pitfalls: Outside an animation controller it is 0, never an error - a render controller condition using it never fires.
A state with no `animations` list makes it 1 at once, so a transition on it fires on the first evaluation.
It does not wait for blending into the next state; it only looks at the animations' own times.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: all_tags
queries.summary: 1 if the item or block being matched carries every one of the given tags
queries.hover:
`q.all_tags('tag', ...)` - 1 if the item or block being tested has every listed tag, else 0.
Tag names must match exactly, including the namespace (`'minecraft:is_sword'` is not `'is_sword'`).
Only in `tags` fields of item and block descriptors; with nothing to test it returns 1.
queries.description: Tests the item or block that a descriptor is matching against a list of tag names and returns 1 when it has all of them.
queries.long:
Used in the `tags` field of item and block descriptors (recipe ingredients, item filters, block lists in entity components). Returns `1` when the item or block being tested carries **every** tag you list, and `0` as soon as one is missing.

Each argument is a tag name as a string. Names are compared exactly: `'minecraft:planks'` and `'planks'` are different tags, and so are names that differ in case.

**Checking stops early.** Tags are checked in order and the query returns `0` at the first missing one; later arguments are not looked at.

**Wrong arguments.** Written as `q.all_tags` with no argument list, the query logs an error and returns `0`; written with empty parentheses, `q.all_tags()`, the expression does not parse at all. A number where a tag name is expected logs an error and is then treated as a tag that nothing has, so the result is `0`.

**Nothing to test.** If the expression is evaluated with neither an item nor a block, the result is `1` - an empty match succeeds. The arguments are not examined in that case, so even a number gives `1` without an error.

`query.any_tag` needs only one of the tags.

args.name: tag
args.description: Tag name, e.g. 'minecraft:is_pickaxe' (one or more)
accepts: string tag name, exact (namespace and case matter)
args.onInvalid: non-string: content-log error, treated as a missing tag

whenUnavailable.when: an argument is not a string
neither an item nor a block to test

pitfalls: Namespaces matter: vanilla item tags are `minecraft:`-prefixed, so `q.all_tags('is_sword')` is 0 for a sword.
Not available in entity, animation or world-generation Molang - only in descriptor `tags` fields.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: anger_level
queries.summary: Anger of the entity toward its current target (warden-style anger), server only
queries.hover:
`q.anger_level` - anger toward the current target, else the general anger value; whole number, 0 and up.
Server-side only: evaluated on the client it logs an error and returns 0.
Entities without anger tracking return 0 silently; arguments are ignored.
queries.description: Returns how angry the entity is, for entities that track anger per suspect (the warden). Only works in server-side Molang.
queries.long:
For entities that keep a per-suspect anger table (the warden's `minecraft:anger_level` component), returns the anger value as a whole number.

**Which anger.** If the entity currently has a target and that target is in its anger table, the value is the anger toward that target. Otherwise - no target, or a target it holds no anger toward - the entity's general anger value is returned instead (believed to be the anger toward its primary suspect; not yet verified in game).

Vanilla compares it with the warden's thresholds (`>= 40` agitated, `>= 80` angry) and uses it to speed up the heartbeat.

**Where it works.** Only on the server: behavior-pack Molang such as entity events, environment sensors and component intervals. On the client (resource packs, render controllers, client animations) it logs an error and returns `0` for every entity, warden or not. Without an entity it logs an error and returns `0`. On the server, entities without anger tracking return `0` without an error.

The query takes no arguments; vanilla writes `query.anger_level(this)`, and any arguments are ignored.

appliesTo.entities: entities with an anger table (warden); others always 0

pitfalls: Resource-pack Molang cannot read it: on the client it is 0 plus a content-log error.
With a target the warden is not angry at, the value is its general anger, not 0.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: anim_time
queries.summary: Current playback time of the animation, in seconds
queries.hover:
Playback time of the animation being evaluated, in seconds (after looping/clamping).
Inside `anim_time_update` it is the previous frame's time.
Only meaningful in entity/attachable animations; 0 in particles, blocks and server Molang.
queries.description: The current playback position, in seconds, of the animation whose expressions are being evaluated.
queries.long:
The animation's own clock, in seconds.

On every update the animation first evaluates its `anim_time_update` expression - by default the previous time plus `query.delta_time` - and then applies its loop mode:

| `loop` | when the time passes `animation_length` |
|---|---|
| `true` | wraps around (`time mod animation_length`) |
| `"hold_on_last_frame"` | stays at `animation_length` |
| `false` | the animation finishes |

The result is what `q.anim_time` returns to the animation's bone and effect expressions.

**Inside `anim_time_update`** `q.anim_time` holds the time from the previous update, which is what makes `"query.anim_time + query.delta_time * 2"` play the animation at double speed.

Outside animations (render controllers, particles, blocks, behavior packs) there is no animation clock. Read on an entity outside any animation on the client, it has returned the same value as `query.life_time`; do not rely on that. Particles, blocks and server-side Molang read `0`.
queries.formula: `t = anim_time_update(t_prev)`, then loop: `t mod length` / hold: `min(t, length)`
queries.range: 0 .. animation_length for looping or held animations
pitfalls: With a custom `anim_time_update` the value is whatever that expression produces - not necessarily seconds.
In animation controllers and render controllers the value is not tied to any one animation; use `query.life_time` or a variable for a clock there.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: any
queries.summary: 1 if at least one argument after the first is identical to the first, else 0
queries.hover:
`q.any(value, a, b, ...)` - 1 if at least one later argument is identical to `value`, else 0.
Needs at least 3 arguments; fewer logs an error and returns 0.
Numbers must match bit for bit (`0` and `-0` differ); stops at the first match.
queries.description: Takes a reference value and two or more candidates; the result is 1 at the first candidate identical to the reference, and 0 if none is.
queries.long:
Evaluates `value` once, then walks through the remaining arguments in order and returns `1` at the first one that has the same kind (number vs. string) and the same value. If none matches, the result is `0`.

**How values are compared.** Numbers are compared bit for bit, which is stricter than `==`: `0` and `-0` are different. Strings are compared by name (case matters). A string never equals a number; a candidate of the other kind is simply skipped.

**Evaluation.** Candidates after the first match are not evaluated.

**Argument count.** At least three arguments are required - the value and two or more candidates. With fewer the query logs an error and returns `0`; for a single candidate write `a == b`.

`query.all` requires *every* candidate to match.

args.name: value
args.description: Value to look for, evaluated once

args.name: candidate
args.description: Values to compare with (two or more)

appliesTo.entities: no entity needed

pitfalls: `q.any(v.x, 1)` is an error (needs 3 arguments); use `v.x == 1`.
`q.any(-0, 0, 1)` is 0: numbers are compared bit for bit.

queries.hover:
`q.any_animation_finished` - 1 once at least one animation in the active controller state has reached its end.
Only answers while an animation controller is being evaluated; anywhere else it is 0.
A state with no animations gives 0.
queries.description: While an animation controller evaluates its current state, returns 1 when at least one animation listed in that state has reached its end, else 0.
queries.long:

An animation counts as having reached its end when its animation time becomes greater than or equal to its length, and it stays counted afterwards, so a looping animation counts after its first cycle.

A state that plays no animations returns `0`.

**Where it works.** The controller marks its active state only while it is being evaluated. Outside an animation controller - in an animation, a render controller - the query returns `0` without an error. Contexts without animation data (world particles, blocks) also return `0`.

`query.all_animations_finished` waits for every animation of the state.

appliesTo.entities: entities with animation controllers
fields: animation controller state transitions and other state expressions

queries.summary: 1 if the item or block being matched carries at least one of the given tags
queries.hover:
`q.any_tag('tag', ...)` - 1 if the item or block being tested has at least one listed tag, else 0.
Tag names must match exactly, including the namespace.
Only in `tags` fields of item and block descriptors; with nothing to test it returns 0.

queries.long:

Each argument is a tag name as a string, compared exactly (namespace and case matter).

queries.name: approx_eq
queries.summary: 1 if all arguments are numerically equal; currently an exact float comparison
queries.hover:
`q.approx_eq(a, b, ...)` - 1 if every argument equals the first, else 0.
Despite the name, this version compares exactly: no tolerance is applied (`q.approx_eq(0.6 + 0.1, 0.7)` is 0).
Needs at least 2 arguments; fewer logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Compares every argument after the first with the first one and returns 1 when all are equal. In this game version the comparison is exact, with no tolerance.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when every argument is equal to the first one and `0` as soon as one differs.

**No tolerance.** The name suggests a comparison within a small margin, but in this version the numbers are compared exactly as 32-bit floats - the same test as `==`. Results that only differ by rounding are *not* considered equal: `q.approx_eq(0.6 + 0.1, 0.7)` returns `0`. If you need a margin, write it out: `math.abs(v.a - v.b) < 0.0001`.

Because it is a numeric comparison, `0` and `-0` count as equal (unlike `query.all`), and `NaN` is never equal to anything.

**Arguments.** At least two numbers are required; with fewer the query logs an error and returns `0`. Arguments after the first mismatch are not evaluated. Strings are not meant to be passed here; they are not rejected, but the result is not meaningful.

args.name: value
args.description: Numbers to compare (two or more)
accepts: number; compared exactly as a 32-bit float

queries.formula: a == b == c ... (exact)

appliesTo.entities: no entity needed

pitfalls: It does not absorb rounding error in this version: `q.approx_eq(0.6 + 0.1, 0.7)` is 0.
Use `math.abs(v.a - v.b) < 0.0001` when you really need a tolerance.

queries.name: armor_color_slot
queries.summary: One color channel (0..1) of the dyeable armor in an armor slot
queries.hover:
`q.armor_color_slot(slot, channel)` - red/green/blue/alpha (channel 0..3) of the armor in that slot, 0 to 1.
Slot 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet, 4 body. Anything not dyeable, an empty slot or a bad channel gives 1.0.
Errors (wrong argument count, no entity) also return 1, with a content-log line.
queries.description: Returns one channel of the color of the dyeable armor worn in a slot, as a fraction from 0 to 1. Used to tint leather-style armor.
queries.long:
Returns a single channel of the color of the armor piece in the given slot, in the range `0` to `1`.

| slot | | channel | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0` | head | `0` | red |
| `1` | chest | `1` | green |
| `2` | legs | `2` | blue |
| `3` | feet | `3` | alpha |
| `4` | body | | |

Only dyeable items have a color. For everything else - an empty slot, iron armor, a pumpkin - every channel reads `1.0`, which leaves a tint unchanged when you multiply by it. Undyed leather (armor and leather horse armor alike) reports its default brown, `160, 101, 64` out of 255 - about `0.627`, `0.396`, `0.251`, alpha `1`.

**Arguments.** Both numbers are truncated toward zero, so `-0.5` and `0.9` act as `0`. Neither is range-checked: a slot above 4, a negative slot such as `-1`, or a channel outside 0-3 simply returns `1.0` without an error (on Windows; see the platform note in the pitfalls).

**Errors return 1, not 0.** With anything other than exactly two arguments, or without an entity, the query logs an error and returns `1`. Entities that are not mobs always return `1.0`.

args.name: slot
args.description: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet, 4 body
args.onInvalid: above 4 or negative whole number: returns 1.0, no log

args.name: channel
args.description: 0 red, 1 green, 2 blue, 3 alpha
args.onInvalid: outside 0..3: returns 1.0, no log

appliesTo.entities: mobs; other entities always 1.0

whenUnavailable.when: slot empty or item not dyeable

pitfalls: The failure value is 1.0, not 0 - a check like `q.armor_color_slot(0, 0) > 0` is true for bare heads.
Only dyeable items report a color; all other armor reads 1.0 on every channel. Undyed leather is not 1.0 - it reads its brown default.
Negative slots are not the head: `(-1, 0)` reads 1.0 on Windows. Whole negative numbers may convert differently on other platforms, so do not rely on them.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: armor_damage_slot
queries.summary: Durability used so far by the item in an armor slot
queries.hover:
`q.armor_damage_slot(slot)` - damage (durability used) of the item in that slot: 0 head .. 3 feet, 4 body.
A new item and an empty slot both read 0; the value counts up as the piece wears.
Needs exactly one argument and an entity, otherwise logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Returns how much durability the item in the given armor slot has used up. Slots: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet, 4 body.
queries.long:
Returns the damage value of the item in an armor slot: `0` for a fresh piece, growing as the item loses durability, up to the item's maximum durability. It is *used* durability, not what is left; for a fraction, divide it by the item's maximum durability yourself (the query does not report the maximum).

| slot | |
|---|---|
| `0` | head |
| `1` | chest |
| `2` | legs |
| `3` | feet |
| `4` | body (horse, wolf armor) |

Any item in the slot is read, armor or not; an empty slot reads `0`.

**Argument.** The slot is truncated toward zero (`1.9` reads the chest). There is no range check: `-1` and slots above 4 read `0` like an empty slot, without an error.

Without an entity, or with a number of arguments other than one, the query logs an error and returns `0`.

args.name: slot
args.description: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet, 4 body

appliesTo.entities: entities with an armor inventory (mobs)

pitfalls: It is durability used, not remaining: a brand-new piece and an empty slot both give 0.
Use `query.has_armor_slot` to tell an empty slot from an undamaged piece.

queries.name: armor_material_slot
queries.summary: Armor render kind in a slot: -1 none, 0 plain, 1 glint, 2 dyed, 3 dyed+glint
queries.hover:
`q.armor_material_slot(slot)` - how the armor in that slot is drawn: -1 none, 0 plain, 1 enchanted, 2 dyeable, 3 dyeable+enchanted.
It does not tell iron from diamond; use `query.armor_texture_slot` for that.
Only humanoid armor counts (so horse/wolf armor in slot 4 is -1); non-mobs -1. Errors log and return 0.
queries.description: Returns a small code telling which kind of armor rendering the humanoid armor piece in a slot needs: none, plain, enchanted, dyeable or dyeable and enchanted.
queries.long:
Returns a code that describes how the humanoid armor piece in the slot has to be drawn - the choice between a plain, an enchanted-glint and a dyeable armor material in a render controller. It does **not** identify the armor's tier or metal.

| value | meaning |
|---|---|
| `-1` | no humanoid armor in the slot |
| `0` | plain armor |
| `1` | plain armor with enchantment glint |
| `2` | dyeable (leather-style) armor |
| `3` | dyeable armor with enchantment glint |

Slots are `0` head, `1` chest, `2` legs, `3` feet. Only humanoid armor items count: a carved pumpkin or mob head reads `-1`, and so does the body slot (`4`), which holds horse or wolf armor. Custom armor items count only when they declare themselves as armor; they report `2`/`3` when they are dyeable.

Every non-dyeable armor type reads `0` when not enchanted: chainmail, iron, gold, diamond, netherite, copper, the turtle shell and even elytra.

**Argument.** The slot is truncated toward zero, so `-0.5` and `0.9` read the head. There is no range check; slots above 3 and negative whole numbers such as `-1` return `-1` (on Windows).

Entities that are not mobs always return `-1`. With no entity, or a number of arguments other than one, the query logs an error and returns `0` - which is also a valid answer (plain armor), so check the argument count carefully.

args.name: slot
args.description: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet
args.onInvalid: 4 or more, or a negative whole number: -1, no log

appliesTo.entities: mobs (players, armor stands included); others always -1

whenUnavailable.when: slot has no humanoid armor (incl. slot 4 and above)

pitfalls: It is not a tier: iron, gold and diamond armor all read 0 (1 when enchanted).
Error paths return 0, the same as plain armor.
Slot 4 is accepted but always -1 (horse and wolf armor are not humanoid armor).
`-1` is not the head slot: it reads -1 on Windows. Keep slot numbers in 0..3.

queries.name: armor_texture_slot
queries.summary: Texture index of the armor in a slot (armor type, or horse/nautilus armor tier)
queries.hover:
`q.armor_texture_slot(slot)` - index of the texture set for the armor in that slot; -1 when nothing applies.
Humanoid armor gives its armor type; on horses and nautiluses the body slot gives the armor tier.
Needs exactly one argument (else logs, 0); without an entity it returns 0 silently.
queries.description: Returns a number that selects the texture set for the armor worn in a slot - the armor type for humanoid armor, the armor tier for horse and nautilus armor.
queries.long:
Returns a number a render controller can use to pick the texture for the armor in a slot (`0` head, `1` chest, `2` legs, `3` feet, `4` body).

What the number means depends on the item and the wearer:

| situation | result |
|---|---|
| built-in humanoid armor piece | the armor type index (table below) |
| horse-family entity | tier of the horse armor in the slot, `0` if the slot holds no horse armor |
| nautilus-type entity | tier of the nautilus armor in the slot, `0` if none |
| anything else (empty slot on a player, custom armor, other mobs) | `-1` |

| humanoid armor | index | | horse / nautilus armor | index |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| leather | `0` | | none | `0` |
| chainmail | `1` | | leather (horse) | `1` |
| iron | `2` | | iron | `2` |
| diamond | `3` | | gold | `3` |
| gold | `4` | | diamond | `4` |
| elytra | `5` | | netherite (nautilus) | `5` |
| turtle shell | `6` | | | |
| netherite | `7` | | | |
| copper | `8` | | | |

Horse-family and nautilus-type entities answer the tier for every slot number, so their head, chest, legs and feet slots read `0`, not `-1`. A carved pumpkin or other non-armor item reads `-1`.

Custom armor items defined with components do not report a type here; on players and other mobs they read `-1`.

**Argument.** The slot is truncated toward zero, so `-0.5` reads the head; there is no range check. A negative whole number such as `-1` reads `-1` on an armor stand or player (on Windows).

With a number of arguments other than one the query logs an error and returns `0`. Without an entity it returns `0` **without** an error. Entities that are not mobs return `-1`.

args.description: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet, 4 body
args.onInvalid: negative whole number: -1 on humanoid wearers (Windows), no log

appliesTo.entities: mobs; other entities always -1

whenUnavailable.when: no matching armor for this wearer

Missing entity is silent here (0), unlike the other armor queries.
Component-based custom armor reads -1 on players (not yet verified in game).
Horse-family and nautilus entities read 0 in every slot, never -1.

queries.name: average_frame_time
queries.summary: Client frame time in seconds, averaged over the last n+1 frames (n up to 29)
queries.hover:
`q.average_frame_time(n)` - average length in seconds of the last n+1 frames; no argument means n = 0.
At most 30 frames are kept: n above 29 acts as 29, negative n acts as 0.
Client rendering only; without a render context it is 0 (server side not yet verified).
queries.description: Returns how long frames took, in seconds: the most recent frame with no argument, or the average of the last n + 1 frames. Only available while the client renders.
queries.long:
Returns a frame time in seconds, taken from the client's record of recent frames.

| call | result |
|---|---|
| `q.average_frame_time` or `(0)` | length of the most recently recorded frame |
| `(n)` | average of the last `n + 1` recorded frames |
| `(29)` and above | average of the last 30 frames |

The client keeps a history of 30 frames, so `n` is capped at 29. The argument has its fractional part dropped; negative values act as `0`. Only the first argument is read.

Divide `1` by it for frames per second: `1 / q.average_frame_time(29)`.

The value only exists while the client renders. Without a render context it returns `0` without an error; on the server, in behavior-pack Molang, it is expected to do the same (not yet verified in game).

args.name: frames
args.description: How many earlier frames to include in the average

appliesTo.entities: any; the value is the same for the whole scene

whenUnavailable.when: no render context (server side expected, not yet verified)

pitfalls: `q.average_frame_time(100)` silently averages only 30 frames.
Always 0 in behavior-pack Molang.

queries.name: base_swing_duration
queries.summary: Swing time in seconds set by the main-hand item (default 0.3 s), before effects
queries.hover:
`q.base_swing_duration` - swing/attack animation length in seconds for the item in the main hand.
Default 0.3 (6 ticks); an item's `minecraft:swing_duration` changes it, rounded down to whole ticks.
Mobs only; other entities and no entity give 0. Haste and mining fatigue are not applied.
queries.description: Length of a swing in seconds as set by the main-hand item (0.3 s when the item sets nothing). Haste and mining fatigue are not included.
queries.long:
Returns the base length of a swing in seconds, taken from the item the mob holds in its main hand:

| main-hand item | result |
|---|---|
| nothing, or an item without a swing duration | `0.3` (6 ticks) |
| item with `minecraft:swing_duration` | that duration, rounded **down** to whole ticks |

The duration is converted to ticks (20 per second) and truncated before it is turned back into seconds, so the result is always a multiple of `0.05`: a component value of `0.33` reads `0.3`.

Status effects that speed up or slow down swinging (haste, mining fatigue) are **not** included.

For players the main hand is the selected hotbar slot. Entities that are not mobs, and calls without an entity, return `0` without an error. Arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: floor(swing_duration_seconds * 20) * 0.05, default 6 * 0.05

appliesTo.entities: mobs (players included); others always 0

pitfalls: Swing durations are truncated to whole ticks: 0.33 reads 0.3, 0.07 reads 0.05.
Haste and mining fatigue do not change it.

queries.name: block_face
queries.summary: Face of the block that an old-style block/item event trigger reports
queries.hover:
`q.block_face` - face number set by an old-style event trigger: 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
Only has a value while such a trigger runs (block placing/interaction events, item use-on event).
Anywhere else it logs an error and returns 6.
queries.description: Returns the face number that an old-style event trigger stored for the expression it is running: 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east. Outside such a trigger it logs an error and returns 6.
queries.long:
Returns the block face involved in the event that is currently being processed, as a number:

| value | face |
|---|---|
| `0` | down |
| `1` | up |
| `2` | north |
| `3` | south |
| `4` | west |
| `5` | east |
| `6` | no face information |

The face is not read from the world. It is a value that three older, event-based triggers put into the evaluation while they run their condition and event: the block triggers fired when a player places the block (`minecraft:on_player_placing`) or interacts with it (`minecraft:on_interact`), and the older item trigger fired when an item is used on a block (`minecraft:on_use_on`). The same triggers also fill in the older `query.cardinal_block_face_placed_on`.

Any other expression - entity animations, render controllers, block permutation conditions, custom component scripts - has no face to read: the query writes an error to the content log and returns `6`.

It takes no arguments.
queries.range: 0..5, or 6 when there is no face

fields: conditions and events of the older block triggers on_player_placing / on_interact

whenUnavailable.when: not running inside one of those triggers

pitfalls: It does not describe a block in the world; outside the event triggers it is always 6 plus a content-log error.
Block permutation conditions and custom components do not supply a face - use the placement traits (`minecraft:placement_position` / `minecraft:placement_direction`) and block states instead.

queries.name: block_has_all_tags
queries.summary: 1 if the block at world x, y, z has all listed tags
queries.hover:
`q.block_has_all_tags(x, y, z, 'tag', ...)` - 1 if the block at world position x, y, z has every of the tags, else 0.
Coordinates are cut to whole numbers toward zero, not floored: -0.5 reads block 0, not -1.
Needs at least one tag; fewer than 4 arguments or a non-string tag logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Looks up the block at absolute world coordinates x, y, z and returns 1 if it carries every of the listed tags, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Looks up the block at the absolute world position `x`, `y`, `z` in the entity's dimension and checks its tags. The result is `1` when the block has every of the tags you list, otherwise `0`.

**Coordinates.** Each coordinate is converted to a whole number by dropping the fractional part (truncation toward zero). That matches the block grid for positive values, but not for negative ones: `-0.5` becomes `0` and `-1.7` becomes `-1`, one block off from the block that contains the point. When you pass an entity position, wrap each coordinate in `math.floor(...)`.

**Tags.** Every argument after the third is a tag name string. Checking stops at the first tag the block lacks and returns `0`; the remaining arguments are not looked at, so a wrong argument after that point goes unnoticed. A non-string tag reached during the check writes a content-log error and the result is `0`.

**Where it works.** It needs access to the world, which entity expressions have. Fewer than four arguments, or no world access (for example world particles), write a content-log error and return `0`. Unloaded positions and positions above or below the world are not reported separately - they read `0`, like a block without the tags, with no error.

For a position relative to the block being evaluated use `query.block_neighbor_has_all_tags`; `query.block_has_any_tag` is the any-of variant.

args.description: World X
accepts: number; truncated toward zero (negative fractions move one block toward 0)

args.name: y
args.description: World Y

args.name: z
args.description: World Z
accepts: number; truncated toward zero (negative fractions move one block toward 0)

args.name: tag
args.description: Block tag name; one or more
args.onInvalid: non-string tag reached during the check: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: any entity (used only to reach the world)

whenUnavailable.when: no world access in the context
a non-string tag is reached during the check

pitfalls: `q.position(0)` of -3.4 selects block -3, not -4: floor negative coordinates yourself.
Tag arguments after the deciding tag are never checked, so a typo there produces no error.
Coordinates are absolute world positions, not offsets from the entity.

queries.name: block_neighbor_has_all_tags
queries.summary: 1 if the block at an offset from this block has all listed tags
queries.hover:
`q.block_neighbor_has_all_tags(dx, dy, dz, 'tag', ...)` - 1 if the block at this block + (dx, dy, dz) has every of the tags.
Block Molang only. Offsets are cut to whole numbers toward zero (0.9 means 0).
A non-number offset logs an error but counts as 0 and the check still runs.
queries.description: Checks the block at the given offset from the block being evaluated and returns 1 if it carries every of the listed tags, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Adds the offset `dx`, `dy`, `dz` to the position of the block the expression belongs to, looks up the block there and returns `1` when it has every of the listed tags, otherwise `0`.

```
q.block_neighbor_has_any_tag(0, -1, 0, 'dirt', 'stone')   // block below
```

**Offsets.** Each offset is converted to a whole number by dropping the fractional part, so `0.9` is `0` and `-0.9` is also `0`. An offset that is not a number writes a content-log error, is treated as `0`, and evaluation continues - so the query still answers, for the wrong block.

**Tags.** Every argument after the third is a tag name string. Checking stops at the first tag the neighbour lacks and returns `0`; later arguments are not looked at. A non-string tag reached during the check writes a content-log error and the result is `0`.

**Where it works.** It is meant for block Molang, where the evaluated block has a position. Fewer than four arguments, or no world access, write a content-log error and return `0`. In entity expressions the "current block" position is not the entity's position: on the client it is the world origin `0, 0, 0`, so the offsets act as absolute world coordinates and no error is written. Use `query.block_has_all_tags` with world coordinates there instead.

queries.name: block_property
queries.summary: Old name of query.block_state; only resolves in files older than 1.20.40
queries.hover:
`q.block_property('name')` - same result as `q.block_state('name')` (number, 0/1 or string).
Only recognised when the file's format version is below 1.20.40; newer files fail to resolve it.
Block contexts only; unknown names log an error and return 0.
queries.description: The older name of `query.block_state`: returns the value of a state of the block being evaluated. Files with a format version of 1.20.40 or newer no longer recognise it.
queries.long:
Returns the value of one state of the block the expression belongs to. It behaves exactly like `query.block_state` - same argument, same result types and the same errors; only the name in the error text differs:

| state type | result |
|---|---|
| integer | the number |
| boolean | `1` or `0` |
| string | a string; compare it with `==` / `!=` |

**Version limit.** The name is only available to Molang from files whose format version is below `1.20.40`. In newer files the expression fails to resolve as an unknown query. Replace it with `query.block_state`, which takes the same argument.

Every failure writes an error to the content log and returns `0`: no argument or more than one, a non-string argument, no block in the context, a block without states, or a state the block does not have.

args.description: Block state name, exactly as registered
args.onInvalid: non-string or unknown name: content-log error, returns 0

fields: block Molang in files with format version below 1.20.40

whenUnavailable.when: block has no state with that name

queries.name: block_state
queries.summary: Current value of one of the block's states (number, 0/1 or string)
queries.hover:
`q.block_state('name')` - value of the named state on the block being evaluated.
Integer states give a number, boolean states 0/1, string states a string to compare with ==.
Only blocks defined in block JSON (custom blocks) answer; built-in blocks and unknown names log an error, 0.
queries.description: Returns the current value of a block state on the block the expression belongs to. The result keeps the state's type: integers as numbers, booleans as 0/1, strings as strings.
queries.long:
Reads one block state from the block the expression is attached to.

```
q.block_state('minecraft:cardinal_direction') == 'north'
q.block_state('my:stage') >= 2
```

The type of the result follows the state:

| state type | result |
|---|---|
| integer | the number |
| boolean | `1` or `0` |
| string | a string; compare it with `==` / `!=` |

The name must be exactly the state's registered name - custom and trait states carry their namespace (`'minecraft:cardinal_direction'`, `'my:stage'`), while states of the few vanilla blocks defined in block JSON may have none (`'growth'`).

**Which blocks answer.** Only blocks defined through a block definition file - custom blocks, and the few vanilla blocks defined the same way - have states this query can read. Built-in blocks such as stairs, logs or furnaces log an error and return `0`, even though they have states.

It is the only query allowed in a block's `permutations[].condition` and in geometry `bone_visibility` expressions.

Every failure writes an error to the content log and returns `0`: no argument or more than one, a non-string argument, no block in the context, a built-in block, or a state the block does not have.

args.description: Block state name, exactly as registered
args.onInvalid: non-string or unknown name: content-log error, returns 0

block has no state with that name
built-in block not defined in block JSON (stairs, logs, furnaces, ...)

pitfalls: String states return strings: `q.block_state('minecraft:cardinal_direction') == 0` is never true.

An unknown state returns 0, which may look like a valid value; watch the content log.

queries.name: blocking
queries.summary: 1 while the player's blocking flag is set - also while sneaking without a shield
queries.hover:
`q.blocking` - 1 while the entity's blocking flag is set, else 0.
The flag follows sneaking even with no shield anywhere; pair it with a shield check, as vanilla does.
A shield on cooldown or swimming clears it; riding not yet verified. No entity: 0.
queries.description: Returns the player's blocking flag: 1 while a shield is held up - and, in practice, whenever the player sneaks, shield or not - otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Reads the entity's blocking flag and returns `1` when it is set, `0` otherwise.

The game recalculates this flag for players on every tick from several inputs: the shield the player is actively using, whether that shield is on cooldown (for example after an axe hit disables it), swimming, riding and other player state. A shield on cooldown or swimming always leaves it at `0`.

**Sneaking sets it without a shield.** Holding sneak turns the flag on even when the player has no shield in either hand, in creative and in survival; releasing sneak turns it off. With a shield in the off hand, sneaking raises the shield and the flag follows the same way, one or two ticks behind the sneak state. So `q.blocking` alone does not mean "a shield is up": combine it with an item check, e.g. `q.blocking && q.is_item_name_any('slot.weapon.offhand', 'minecraft:shield')`.

No code path sets the flag for non-player mobs, so other entities read `0`: a zombie holding a shield in its off hand reads `0`.

The value comes from the flag alone; it does not check which item is held. Without an entity the result is `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players (flag set while a shield is raised or while sneaking); others 0

pitfalls: A sneaking player reads 1 even with empty hands - check the held item too.
A shield on cooldown gives 0 even while the use button is held.
Mobs holding shields are not reported as blocking: a zombie with an off-hand shield reads 0.

queries.name: body_x_rotation
queries.summary: Entity's pitch (up/down look angle) in degrees, smoothed per frame
queries.hover:
`q.body_x_rotation` - the entity's pitch in degrees, smoothed between ticks.
This is the look pitch shared by head and body, not a separate body tilt.
No entity: 0.
queries.description: Returns the entity's pitch - how far it is rotated up or down - in degrees, interpolated between the last two ticks. It is the same pitch the entity looks with; there is no separate body pitch.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's rotation around the X axis (pitch) in degrees.

The value is blended between the previous and the current tick using the frame's position between ticks, so it moves smoothly in resource-pack animations. The blend goes the short way around, so crossing from `179` to `-179` does not sweep through zero.

Entities store a single pitch, used for looking; the name suggests a body angle, but for a mob this is its head/look pitch. It is negative when looking up and positive when looking down; for the player it equals `query.head_x_rotation(0)` and `query.target_x_rotation`, and teleporting the player to a pitch of `-90` / `90` reads back about `-89` / `89`. Limits for other entity types are not verified.

Without an entity the result is `0`.
queries.formula: `prev + t * wrap180(cur - prev)`, where `t` is the frame's position between ticks
queries.range: about [-89, 89] for the player; about [-90, 90] expected for mobs

appliesTo.entities: any entity

pitfalls: It is the look pitch, not a separate body lean: a mob looking up reports a negative value here too.
Without an entity it silently returns 0, which is also a valid pitch.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: body_y_rotation
queries.summary: Body yaw of the entity in degrees, smoothed per frame
queries.hover:
`q.body_y_rotation` - body yaw in degrees, smoothed between ticks.
Mobs and players: the body's own yaw, which trails the head. Other entities: their only yaw.
Not wrapped to -180..180 by the query. No entity: 0.
queries.description: Returns the yaw (rotation around the vertical axis) of the entity's body in degrees, interpolated between the last two ticks. For mobs this is the body angle that lags behind the head; for other entities it is the entity's yaw.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's body yaw in degrees.

| entity | value |
|---|---|
| mobs and players | the body's yaw, which turns separately from (and follows) the head |
| other entities (boats, minecarts, projectiles, ...) | the entity's only yaw, the same one it faces |

The value is blended between the previous and the current tick using the frame's position between ticks, taking the short way around. The query itself does not wrap the result into `[-180, 180)`: it continues from the previous tick's value, so whether it can grow past `180` after several turns depends on how the entity stores its body yaw. For a player turned by teleports it stayed inside `[-180, 180)`, trailing the head yaw by up to 50 degrees while standing; continuous turning with the mouse is not yet verified.Take differences through `math.mod` or compare against `query.head_y_rotation` rather than testing absolute ranges.

Without an entity the result is `0`.
queries.formula: `prev + t * wrap180(cur - prev)`, where `t` is the frame's position between ticks
queries.range: not clamped by the query (see text)

appliesTo.entities: mobs: body yaw; others: entity yaw

pitfalls: For mobs it lags the head: a standing mob that turns its head does not change this value right away.
Do not assume the value stays in -180..180; subtract and wrap before comparing.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: bone_aabb
queries.summary: Bounding box of a bone's own cubes as {min, max} structs
queries.hover:
`q.bone_aabb('bone')` - struct `.min` / `.max`, each with `.x .y .z`: box around the bone's own cubes in the model.
Child bones are not included; the box comes from the geometry, not from the animated pose.
Client only; read it once in `scripts.initialize`. Unknown bone or no model: content-log error, all zeros.
queries.description: Gives the smallest axis-aligned box that encloses the cubes belonging directly to the named bone; read its corners through `.min` and `.max`. Child bones do not count.
queries.long:
Looks up the bone by name and returns the axis-aligned box that encloses its cubes:

```
v.box = q.bone_aabb('body');
v.height = v.box.max.y - v.box.min.y;
```

The result is a struct, so store it in a variable and read its members; it cannot be used in arithmetic directly.

**What the box covers.** Only the cubes that belong directly to that bone - cubes of child bones are ignored, and a bone without cubes gives a zero-size box. The box is built from the model's geometry as loaded, not from the pose after animation. It is in the model's own units (pixels of the geometry file); whether the box always includes the point `(0, 0, 0)` of the model is not yet verified.

The bone is looked up by name in the entity's model on the client. Because the value never changes, the usual pattern (the one vanilla horses use) is to read it once in the client entity's `scripts.initialize` and keep it in a variable. Where no model is attached - behaviour-pack expressions on the server, and possibly some other client evaluations (not yet verified) - it writes a content-log error and returns the default.

**Arguments.** Exactly one argument, a string. A wrong count or a non-string argument writes a content-log error; so does a bone name the model does not have. In every failure case the result is a box with all members `0`.

args.name: bone
args.description: Bone name in the geometry
args.onInvalid: non-string or unknown bone: content-log error, all-zero box

appliesTo.entities: client entities with geometry

whenUnavailable.when: no model attached to the evaluation (server; other cases not yet verified)
bone name not in the model

pitfalls: Cubes of child bones are not part of the box.
Animation does not move or resize the box.
A struct result: `q.bone_aabb('x') > 0` is not a valid use.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: bone_orientation_matrix
queries.summary: Current animated transform of a bone as a 4x4 matrix
queries.hover:
`q.bone_orientation_matrix('bone')` - the bone's current transform (after animation) as a matrix value.
Bone must be in the entity's queryable geometry; a second argument is accepted and ignored.
Missing bone, no argument or server side: content-log error and a default matrix.
queries.description: Returns the named bone's current transform, after animation, as a matrix. The bone has to be part of the entity's queryable geometry; otherwise it logs an error and returns a default matrix.
queries.long:
Returns the transform of a bone as a 4x4 matrix value, as it stands after the entity's animations have been applied:

```
v.m = q.bone_orientation_matrix('head');
```

The result is a matrix, not a number: store it in a variable. To get readable parts use `query.bone_orientation_trs`, which splits the same transform into translation, rotation and scale.

The bone must exist in the entity's queryable geometry (the geometry the client entity names for bone queries). Its transform is refreshed on the client after animations are applied; on the server there is no such data.

**Arguments.** The first argument is the bone name. A second argument is accepted by the parser but not used. With no argument, when the bone is not found, or when the entity has no animation data to ask (for example on the server), the query writes a content-log error and returns a default matrix (expected to be the identity matrix; not yet verified).

The translation part is in model units; its origin and the direction of the vertical axis are not yet verified.

args.name: bone
args.description: Bone name in the queryable geometry
args.onInvalid: unknown bone: content-log error, default matrix

args.name: unused
args.description: Accepted and ignored

appliesTo.entities: client entities that declare queryable geometry

whenUnavailable.when: no animation data in the context
bone not found (including every server-side evaluation)

timing.updates: after animation, when the client refreshes the queryable pose

pitfalls: Only bones of the queryable geometry are found, not bones of whatever model is drawn.
Behaviour-pack (server) evaluation always fails with a content-log error.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: bone_orientation_trs
queries.summary: Current bone transform as {t, r, s}: translation, rotation (deg), scale
queries.hover:
`q.bone_orientation_trs('bone')` - struct `.t` translation, `.r` rotation in degrees, `.s` scale, each `.x .y .z`.
Taken from the bone's current (animated) transform; bone must be in the queryable geometry.
Missing bone or server side: content-log error; result t = 0, r = 0, s = 1.
queries.description: Returns the named bone's current transform split into translation (`.t`), rotation in degrees (`.r`) and scale (`.s`), each with `.x`, `.y` and `.z`.
queries.long:
Takes the same transform as `query.bone_orientation_matrix` and splits it into three parts:

| member | meaning | how it is obtained |
|---|---|---|
| `.t` | translation | the matrix's translation part |
| `.r` | rotation, degrees | Euler angles of the matrix's rotation, converted from radians |
| `.s` | scale | length of each of the three axis vectors of the matrix |

```
v.head = q.bone_orientation_trs('head');
return v.head.t.y;
```

Scale is always positive (a mirrored bone shows up as a rotation instead). The Euler angle order and sign convention may differ from what you author in animation files - check the values before relying on them (not yet verified).

The bone must exist in the entity's queryable geometry (the geometry the client entity names for bone queries). Its transform is refreshed on the client after animations are applied; on the server there is no such data.

**Arguments.** The first argument is the bone name; a second argument is accepted and ignored. With no argument, an unknown bone, or no animation data (server), it writes a content-log error and returns translation `(0, 0, 0)`, rotation `(0, 0, 0)` and scale `(1, 1, 1)`.

args.name: bone
args.description: Bone name in the queryable geometry
args.onInvalid: unknown bone: content-log error, t=0 r=0 s=1

args.name: unused
args.description: Accepted and ignored

queries.formula: `r = eulerAngles(rotation) * 180/pi`; `s = |axis vectors|`
queries.units: t: model units; r: degrees; s: factor

appliesTo.entities: client entities that declare queryable geometry

whenUnavailable.when: no animation data in the context
bone not found (including every server-side evaluation)

timing.updates: after animation, when the client refreshes the queryable pose

pitfalls: Rotation comes back from a matrix: the angles can differ from the ones you keyed (equivalent Euler triples).
Negative scale in an animation reads back as positive scale plus a rotation.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: bone_origin
queries.summary: Pivot of a bone as loaded from the geometry, as an {x, y, z} struct
queries.hover:
`q.bone_origin('bone')` - struct `.x .y .z`: the bone's pivot as loaded from the geometry file.
Animation does not change it. Client only; read it once in `scripts.initialize`.
Unknown bone, wrong argument or no model: content-log error, (0, 0, 0).
queries.description: Gives the named bone's pivot point as the model file defines it (members `.x`, `.y`, `.z`). It is a rest value: animations never change it.
queries.long:
Looks up the bone by name and returns its pivot point from the geometry, as a struct:

```
v.p = q.bone_origin('head');
return v.p.y;
```

It is the rest position from the model file; animations, scale and bone bindings are not applied. The numbers are in the geometry's units (pixels); whether any axis is mirrored relative to the `pivot` written in the file is not yet verified.

The bone is looked up by name in the entity's model on the client. Because the value never changes, the usual pattern (the one vanilla horses use) is to read it once in the client entity's `scripts.initialize` and keep it in a variable. Where no model is attached - behaviour-pack expressions on the server, and possibly some other client evaluations (not yet verified) - it writes a content-log error and returns the default.

**Arguments.** Exactly one string argument. A wrong count, a non-string argument or an unknown bone writes a content-log error and returns `(0, 0, 0)`.

args.name: bone
args.description: Bone name in the geometry
args.onInvalid: non-string or unknown bone: content-log error, (0, 0, 0)

appliesTo.entities: client entities with geometry

whenUnavailable.when: no model attached to the evaluation (server; other cases not yet verified)
bone name not in the model

pitfalls: It never moves with animation; use `query.bone_orientation_trs` for the animated position.
A failed lookup returns (0, 0, 0), which is also a valid pivot; check the content log.

queries.name: bone_rotation
queries.summary: Rest rotation of a bone from the geometry, in degrees, as {x, y, z}
queries.hover:
`q.bone_rotation('bone')` - struct `.x .y .z`: the bone's rest rotation from the geometry, in degrees.
Animation does not change it. Client only; read it once in `scripts.initialize`.
Unknown bone, wrong argument or no model: content-log error, (0, 0, 0).
queries.description: Gives the angles, in degrees, that the model file assigns to the named bone before any animation (members `.x`, `.y`, `.z`). Animations never change it.
queries.long:
Looks up the bone by name and returns the rotation it has in the geometry file, before any animation, as a struct in degrees:

```
v.r = q.bone_rotation('tail');
return v.r.x;
```

The model keeps this angle in radians internally and the query converts it back to degrees, so tiny rounding differences from the authored value are possible. Whether the sign of any axis differs from the value written in the file is not yet verified.

The bone is looked up by name in the entity's model on the client. Because the value never changes, the usual pattern (the one vanilla horses use) is to read it once in the client entity's `scripts.initialize` and keep it in a variable. Where no model is attached - behaviour-pack expressions on the server, and possibly some other client evaluations (not yet verified) - it writes a content-log error and returns the default.

**Arguments.** Exactly one string argument. A wrong count, a non-string argument or an unknown bone writes a content-log error and returns `(0, 0, 0)`.

args.name: bone
args.description: Bone name in the geometry
args.onInvalid: non-string or unknown bone: content-log error, (0, 0, 0)

queries.formula: `authored rotation (radians) * 180/pi`

appliesTo.entities: client entities with geometry

whenUnavailable.when: no model attached to the evaluation (server; other cases not yet verified)
bone name not in the model

pitfalls: It is the rest rotation only; animated rotation is in `query.bone_orientation_trs(...).r`.
Compare with a tolerance: the value goes through radians and back.

queries.name: camera_distance_range_lerp
queries.summary: 0..1 ramp of the entity's camera distance between two distances
queries.hover:
`q.camera_distance_range_lerp(a, b)` - 0 at distance a or closer, 1 at b or farther, linear between (blocks).
Passing the larger distance first inverts the ramp. Uses the same distance as `q.distance_from_camera`.
Needs exactly two arguments; any other count logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Maps the entity's distance from the camera onto a 0-to-1 ramp between two distances, clamped at both ends. With the larger distance first the ramp runs from 1 down to 0.
queries.long:
Turns the entity's distance from the camera into a 0-to-1 ramp between two distances you give, in blocks:

| camera distance `d` (with `lo = min(a,b)`, `hi = max(a,b)`) | result for `a <= b` |
|---|---|
| `d <= lo` | `0` |
| `d >= hi` | `1` |
| in between | `(d - lo) / (hi - lo)` |

If the first argument is larger than the second, the result is `1 -` the value above, so `(24, 8)` gives `1` near the camera and `0` far away. Two equal distances act as a hard step: `0` up to that distance, `1` beyond it.

The distance is the straight-line distance, in blocks, from the camera to the entity's position, updated by the renderer every frame - the same number `query.distance_from_camera` returns. The camera end is the eye position in first person (an armor stand 12 blocks ahead on flat ground reads about 12.11, not 12). For player targets the position used is the eye position rather than the feet (not yet verified). Where no renderer sets the distance (server, world particles) the stored distance is not meaningful; what it holds there is not yet verified.

Exactly two arguments are required. Any other count returns `0` and writes a content-log error. The message is meant to state the argument count, but in this game version the count is not filled in correctly (it comes out missing or garbled), so read that line simply as 'wrong number of arguments'.

args.name: a
args.description: Distance that maps to 0 (blocks)

args.name: b
args.description: Distance that maps to 1 (blocks)

queries.formula: `clamp((d - min(a,b)) / |b - a|, 0, 1)`, then `1 - x` when `a > b`

appliesTo.entities: entities drawn by the renderer

whenUnavailable.when: no renderer has set a camera distance (server, not yet drawn)

pitfalls: Argument order matters: `(32, 16)` is the inverse of `(16, 32)`.
Server-side evaluation has no camera; do not use it in behaviour packs.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: camera_rotation
queries.summary: Camera pitch (0) or yaw (1) in degrees, from the entity the camera follows
queries.hover:
`q.camera_rotation(axis)` - 0: camera pitch, 1: camera yaw, in degrees, smoothed per frame.
Follows the entity the camera is attached to; front third-person view flips yaw by 180 and negates pitch.
Axis outside 0..1 after dropping the fraction (2, -1) or not exactly one argument: content-log error, 0.
queries.description: Returns the camera's rotation in degrees: `0` selects pitch, `1` selects yaw. The angles come from the entity the camera is attached to, adjusted for the front-facing third-person view.
queries.long:
Returns one angle of the camera, in degrees: `0` = pitch (up/down), `1` = yaw (left/right).

The angles are taken from the entity the camera currently follows (normally the local player), blended between ticks with the frame's partial tick:

| situation | pitch | yaw |
|---|---|---|
| camera entity is not a player | its pitch | its yaw |
| player, first person or rear third person | player's pitch | player's yaw |
| local player, front-facing third person | `-pitch` | `yaw + 180`, wrapped to `[-180, 180)` |
| player sleeping in a bed | `0` | set from the bed's facing |
| player sleeping outside a bed | `0` | `0` |

It does not depend on the entity the expression runs on: every entity reads the same camera angles.

**Argument.** The axis is converted to a whole number by dropping the fractional part, so `1.9` is yaw and `-0.5` is pitch. Whole negative numbers such as `-1` are rejected like `2`: anything outside `0..1`, or a call without exactly one argument, writes a content-log error and returns `0`.

It only has a camera to read while the client is drawing; in other client evaluations it returns `0` without an error.

args.name: axis
args.description: 0 = pitch, 1 = yaw
accepts: number; truncated toward zero (-0.5 acts as 0, 1.9 as 1)
args.onInvalid: 2 or more, or -1 or less: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: any (the value does not depend on the entity)

whenUnavailable.when: axis outside 0..1 after truncation (2 or more, -1 or less)
not evaluated while the client renders

pitfalls: In front-facing third person the yaw is turned by 180 degrees and the pitch is negated.
`q.camera_rotation(-1)` is an error (content log, 0), not the pitch.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: can_climb
queries.summary: 1 if the entity has the minecraft:can_climb component
queries.hover:
1 while the entity has the `minecraft:can_climb` component, else 0.
It reports the component, not whether the entity is on a ladder or climbing right now.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity's definition includes the `minecraft:can_climb` component, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity has the `minecraft:can_climb` component and `0` otherwise.

The flag is switched on when the component is added (directly or through a component group) and switched off when it is removed. Nothing else in the game changes it, so it describes what the entity *may* do, not what it is doing: a player standing in an open field still reads `1`, because the vanilla player definition carries the component.

The flag is part of the entity's synchronised state, so resource packs and behavior packs see the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

To react to actual climbing, use `query.is_wall_climbing` or movement queries instead.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; 1 only while the component is present

pitfalls: It does not mean "is climbing now"; it stays 1 on open ground.
Most vanilla land mobs carry the component too (pig, zombie, camel and even the dolphin read 1); the horse, cod, bee and parrot read 0.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: can_damage_nearby_mobs
queries.summary: 1 while the entity is in a riptide spin attack
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is in a riptide trident spin (the spin that hurts mobs it touches), else 0.
Despite the name it is a state, not a capability: 0 at all other times.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is performing a riptide spin attack, the state in which it damages mobs it runs into. It is 0 the rest of the time.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity is in a spin attack and `0` otherwise.

The name suggests a permanent ability, but the flag behind it is the spin-attack state: it is switched on when a player launches with a Riptide trident and cleared when the spin ends. During that window the spinning entity hurts mobs it collides with, and the renderer uses the same flag to spin the model.

No component or definition field sets it, so for ordinary mobs it is always `0`. The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players using Riptide; 0 for everything else

timing.updates: on change of the spin state

pitfalls: It is not an ability check - it only reads 1 during a riptide spin.
When exactly the flag turns on during the launch is not yet verified in game.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: can_dash
queries.summary: 1 if the entity has the minecraft:dash_action component
queries.hover:
1 while the entity has the `minecraft:dash_action` component (the camel dash), else 0.
Ignores the dash cooldown: use `q.has_dash_cooldown` for that.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity has the `minecraft:dash_action` component, otherwise 0. It does not look at the dash cooldown.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity has the `minecraft:dash_action` component and `0` otherwise. The mark is set when the component is added and cleared when it is removed.

It does not change while a dash is cooling down, so it answers "does this mob have a dash at all". To know whether a dash is ready, combine it with `query.has_dash_cooldown` or `query.dash_cooldown_progress`.

The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; 1 only while the component is present

pitfalls: Stays 1 during the cooldown.
A vanilla camel reads 0 until it is saddled: the dash component lives in its saddled component group.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: can_fly
queries.summary: 1 if the entity has minecraft:can_fly or uses flying/hovering navigation
queries.hover:
1 if the entity has `minecraft:can_fly`, or its navigation is `navigation.fly` / `navigation.hover`; else 0.
Not tied to the player's creative flight ability.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity is marked as a flyer: either it has the `minecraft:can_fly` component or its navigation component is a flying or hovering one.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is marked as able to fly and `0` otherwise.

Two things turn the mark on:

| source | effect |
|---|---|
| `minecraft:can_fly` component | 1 while present, 0 after it is removed |
| `minecraft:navigation.fly` or `minecraft:navigation.hover` | sets 1 when the navigation is set up |

Other navigation types never clear it. The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

It is a property of the definition, not a state: a bee resting on a flower still reads `1`, and a player who can fly in creative mode is not covered by this mark.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; set by the component or by fly/hover navigation

pitfalls: Removing `minecraft:can_fly` clears the mark even if the entity still uses flying navigation.
Creative-mode flight of players is not reported here (not yet verified in game).

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: can_power_jump
queries.summary: 1 if the entity has the minecraft:can_power_jump component
queries.hover:
1 while the entity has the `minecraft:can_power_jump` component, else 0.
Reports the component, not whether a jump is being charged.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity has the `minecraft:can_power_jump` component (the charged jump used by horses), otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity carries the `minecraft:can_power_jump` component and `0` otherwise. The mark is switched on when the component is added and off when it is removed; nothing else changes it.

It tells you the entity *can* charge a jump when ridden, not that it is charging one now. The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; 1 only while the component is present

pitfalls: It stays 1 while the horse is idle; it is not a charge meter.
A vanilla horse reads 0 until it is tamed and saddled: the component lives in its saddled component group.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: can_swim
queries.summary: 1 if the entity's navigation marks it as a swimmer
queries.hover:
1 if the entity's navigation marks it as a swimmer (`navigation.swim`, or `navigation.generic` with `can_swim`), else 0.
Walk-type navigation gives 0 even for mobs that swim fine; players read 0.
0 without an entity; no content-log error.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity's navigation component marks it as a swimmer: `navigation.swim`, or `navigation.generic` with its `can_swim` field set.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is marked as a swimmer and `0` otherwise. Like `query.can_walk`, the mark comes only from the navigation component (see the table there):

- `navigation.swim` sets it to `1`.
- `navigation.generic` copies its `can_swim` field.
- Ground navigation types (`navigation.walk` and similar) set it to `0`, whatever their own `can_swim` field says.
- Entities without navigation, players included, read `0`.

It says nothing about whether the entity is in water; use `query.is_swimming` or `query.is_in_water` for that. The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: mobs with a navigation component; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: entity has no navigation component (e.g. players)

pitfalls: A zombie or pig with `navigation.walk` and `can_swim: true` still reads 0.
It is not "is swimming now".

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: can_walk
queries.summary: 1 if the entity's navigation lets it walk (0 for players and flyers)
queries.hover:
1 if the entity's navigation component marks it as a walker, else 0.
Set by the navigation component: fly, hover and swim navigation give 0; ground types are expected to give 1.
Entities without a navigation component, players included, read 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity's navigation component marks it as a walker. It is decided entirely by which navigation component the entity uses.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is marked as a walker and `0` otherwise. The mark comes only from the entity's navigation component, at the moment the navigation is set up:

| navigation | `can_walk` | `can_swim` |
|---|---|---|
| `navigation.walk`, `navigation.climb`, `navigation.float` and other ground types | 1 | 0 |
| `navigation.swim` | 0 | 1 |
| `navigation.fly`, `navigation.hover` | 0 | unchanged (0) |
| `navigation.generic` | its `can_walk` field | its `can_swim` field |
| no navigation component | 0 | 0 |

The `can_walk` / `can_swim` fields of the other navigation types do not feed this mark; only `navigation.generic` copies them.

Because players have no navigation component, `q.can_walk` is `0` for players. The value is synchronised, so both pack types see it. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: mobs with a navigation component; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: entity has no navigation component (e.g. players)

pitfalls: Players read 0.
Setting `can_walk: false` in `navigation.walk` does not change the result; only `navigation.generic` passes its field through.
Which navigation types count as ground types is partly inferred; walk, climb, fly, hover and generic navigation were checked in game, the others were not.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: cape_flap_amount
queries.summary: How far a player's cape swings out, 0 to 1 (about 0.05 at rest)
queries.hover:
Cape lift of a player, 0 to 1: about 0.048 at rest, rises when moving forward or falling, 0 when rising fast.
Non-player entities always get 0.048. Resource packs only; elsewhere 0.
Content below 1.20.0 aims the swing with head yaw, 1.20.0+ with body yaw.
queries.description: Returns how far a player's cape is lifted, from 0 to 1. It follows a trailing "cape point" that lags behind the player, so it rises while the player moves forward or falls and sits at about 0.048 when standing still.
queries.long:
Returns a value from `0` to `1` describing how far a player's cape swings away from the body. Vanilla uses it as the cape's rotation driver.

**How it works.** Each game tick the player drags a hidden *cape point* towards their position: every axis moves a quarter of the remaining gap (`cape += (position - cape) * 0.25`), and an axis more than 10 blocks behind snaps straight to the player. When the query is read, the cape point and the player's position are both smoothed with the frame's partial tick and compared, giving an offset `(dx, dy, dz)` = cape point minus player position.

- **Vertical lift**: `lift = clamp((40 * dy + 6) / 126, 0, 1)`. At rest `dy = 0`, so the value is `6/126 ≈ 0.048`. Falling leaves the cape point above the player (`dy > 0`) and raises it; jumping or rising pulls it to `0`.
- **Forward swing**: `f` = how well the direction of travel matches the direction the player faces (the dot product of the facing direction with the normalised horizontal offset, reversed; clamped to 0..1). The swing angle is `clamp(50 * (|dx| + |dz|) * f, 0, 90)` and adds `angle / 126`.
- **Result**: `clamp(lift + angle / 126, 0, 1)`.

Measured on a player: about `0.39` walking forward, about `0.49` sprinting, the resting value when walking backwards (`f` is 0), practically `0` while rising from a jump, and up to `1` during a 10-block fall. Sideways movement depends on the version below: in 1.20.0+ content the body turns toward the direction of travel, so strafing still swings the cape (about `0.32`); in older content it stays at rest.

**Version difference.** Content whose Molang version is below 1.20.0 measures the facing direction from the player's head yaw; 1.20.0 and newer use the body yaw. Looking around while standing still therefore moves the cape only in old content.

**Where it works.** Only players have a cape point; any other entity returns the resting value `6/126 ≈ 0.048`. Without an entity the result is `0`. In behavior packs and bound particles it returns the default `0`.
queries.formula: `clamp((40 dy + 6)/126 + clamp(50 (|dx|+|dz|) f, 0, 90)/126, 0, 1)` (lift part clamped to 0..1 first)

appliesTo.entities: players; other entities read 6/126

timing.updates: per tick (cape point), smoothed per frame

pitfalls: It is about 0.048, not 0, when the player stands still.
Walking backwards gives no swing.
Strafing swings the cape in 1.20.0+ content (about 0.32) but not in older content.

behaviourChangesByVersion.change: facing direction taken from head yaw
facing direction taken from body yaw
