queries.name: cardinal_block_face_placed_on
queries.summary: Deprecated: block face from a legacy block trigger (0-5), else 6
queries.hover:
Face number (0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east) filled in only while a legacy block `on_player_placing` or `on_interact` trigger runs.
Anywhere else: content-log error and 6. Deprecated: `q.block_face` returns the same value.
queries.description: Returns the block face number stored by the legacy `on_player_placing` / `on_interact` block triggers. Everywhere else it logs an error and returns 6. Deprecated in favour of `query.block_face`, which reads the same number.
queries.long:
Returns the face number that a legacy block event trigger stores just before it runs its event:

| value | face |
|---|---|
| 0 | down |
| 1 | up |
| 2 | north |
| 3 | south |
| 4 | west |
| 5 | east |
| 6 | not available |

Two triggers fill it in, both on the server: `on_player_placing` (the face the new block was placed against) and `on_interact` (the face the player clicked). The value only exists while that trigger's event runs; it is cleared right after.

In any other expression - entity Molang, render controllers, particles, block permutation conditions - there is nothing to read, so the query writes a content-log error and returns `6`.

The same triggers store the same number for `query.block_face`, which is the supported name; the two queries always agree.

appliesTo.entities: none needed
fields: event run by a legacy on_player_placing or on_interact block trigger

pitfalls: It is not filled in by `minecraft:on_placed` / custom-component placement events - only by the two legacy triggers (not yet verified for every event path).
6 means "no data" and always comes with a content-log error - in a resource-pack entity script, without an entity and in a block expression alike.

queries.name: cardinal_facing
queries.summary: Axis the entity is looking along: 0 down, 1 up, 2-5 north/south/west/east
queries.hover:
Face number of the entity's look direction: 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
Up/down wins once the pitch is steeper than about 45° (less when facing diagonally); exact x/z ties go to north/south.
No entity: content-log error and 6.
queries.description: Returns which of the six axis directions the entity is looking along, including up and down: 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
queries.long:
Returns the face number of the direction the entity is looking in:

| value | face |
|---|---|
| 0 | down |
| 1 | up |
| 2 | north |
| 3 | south |
| 4 | west |
| 5 | east |
| 6 | not available |

The look direction is built from the entity's pitch and yaw and then snapped to the axis with the largest component: vertical wins only when `|y|` is strictly larger than both `|x|` and `|z|`; east/west wins when `|x|` is strictly larger than both others; every remaining case - including exact ties such as a yaw of 45° - resolves to north or south.

In practice: looking more than 45° up or down gives `1` or `0` when facing straight along an axis; when facing diagonally the vertical answer takes over earlier (about 35° of pitch at a 45° yaw). Yaw `0` is south, `90` west, `180` north, `-90` east.

The rotation used is the head's: for players the view direction (the body may lag behind), for mobs the head yaw rather than the body yaw. Without an entity the query writes a content-log error and returns `6`; with an entity it never returns `6`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

pitfalls: On an exact tie between the x and z parts (a yaw of 45° or 135°) the answer is north or south.
Mobs use their head direction: a villager whose head and body point different ways reports the head's axis.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: cardinal_facing_2d
queries.summary: Horizontal axis the entity is looking along: 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east
queries.hover:
Face number of the entity's horizontal look direction: 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
Looking almost straight up or down (steeper than about 84°) gives 2 (north) whatever the yaw.
No entity: content-log error and 6.
queries.description: Returns which horizontal direction the entity is looking toward, ignoring the vertical part: 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
queries.long:
Returns the horizontal face number of the entity's look direction: `2` north, `3` south, `4` west, `5` east.

The look direction is computed as for `query.cardinal_facing`, then its vertical part is dropped and the remaining horizontal vector is snapped to an axis (east/west only when `|x|` is strictly larger than `|z|`, so an exact tie gives north or south). The horizontal vector is **not** normalised first: its length is the cosine of the pitch, and when that falls to 0.1 or below - looking up or down more steeply than about 84° - the direction counts as undefined and the query returns `2` (north).

It never returns `0` or `1`. Without an entity it writes a content-log error and returns `6`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: pitch steeper than about 84° up or down

pitfalls: Looking straight up or down reads north (2), not the direction the body faces.
On an exact x/z tie (45° yaw) the answer is north or south.

queries.name: cardinal_player_facing
queries.summary: Like cardinal_facing, but only for players (0-5); others log an error and get 6
queries.hover:
Face number of a player's look direction: 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east.
Same computation as `q.cardinal_facing`, restricted to players.
Non-player or no entity: content-log error and 6.
queries.description: Returns the axis direction a player is looking along (0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east). On any entity that is not a player it logs an error and returns 6.
queries.long:
Returns the face number of the direction a player is looking in, using exactly the same rule as `query.cardinal_facing`:

| value | face |
|---|---|
| 0 | down |
| 1 | up |
| 2 | north |
| 3 | south |
| 4 | west |
| 5 | east |
| 6 | not available |

The look direction is built from the entity's pitch and yaw and then snapped to the axis with the largest component: vertical wins only when `|y|` is strictly larger than both `|x|` and `|z|`; east/west wins when `|x|` is strictly larger than both others; every remaining case - including exact ties such as a yaw of 45° - resolves to north or south.

The only difference from `query.cardinal_facing` is the entity check: when the entity is not a player - or there is no entity - the query writes a content-log error and returns `6`. On a player the two queries always agree.

appliesTo.entities: players only

pitfalls: Using it in an attachable or particle bound to a non-player floods the content log.

queries.name: client_max_render_distance
queries.summary: Render-distance limit of the local client, in chunks
queries.hover:
A render-distance figure of the local client, in chunks - probably the slider's upper limit, not the current setting (not yet verified).
Same value for every entity. Resource-pack entity rendering only; elsewhere content-log error and 0.
queries.description: Gives a render-distance number, in chunks, taken from the client options of the device the game runs on - most likely the top of the render-distance slider. Every entity on that client reads the same number.
queries.long:
Returns a render-distance number, in chunks, for the client the game runs on. The number is stored with the local player's client options and sent to the server along with them, so it is the same for every entity rendered on that client.

It is expected to be the top of the render-distance slider rather than the distance currently selected; this is not yet verified in game.

It needs an entity that is being rendered on the client: resource-pack entity Molang (render controllers, animations, client entity scripts) and attachables. In behavior packs it writes a content-log error and returns `0`; with no entity it also writes an error and returns `0`. Evaluations that run outside the render pass (for example a particle not bound to an entity) are expected to fail the same way; this is not yet verified in game.

appliesTo.entities: any rendered entity (value is per device)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity or not in a rendering pass

timing.updates: on change of the client options

pitfalls: Whether it follows the current render-distance setting or the device maximum is not yet verified.
Particles emitted into the world cannot use it.

queries.name: client_memory_tier
queries.summary: Memory tier of the device running the client, 0 (lowest) to 4 (highest)
queries.hover:
Memory tier of this device: an integer from 0 (least memory) to 4 (most).
Same value for every entity - it describes the local device, not the entity.
Resource-pack entity rendering only; elsewhere content-log error and 0.
queries.description: Returns the memory class of the device the client runs on, as a whole number from 0 (least memory) to 4 (most). Useful for trimming detail on low-memory devices.
queries.long:
Returns the memory tier of the device running the game client, a whole number from `0` (the lowest class) to `4` (the highest). The tier is derived from the device's memory and kept with the local player's client options, so every entity rendered on that client reads the same number.

It needs an entity that is being rendered on the client: resource-pack entity Molang (render controllers, animations, client entity scripts) and attachables. In behavior packs it writes a content-log error and returns `0`; with no entity it also writes an error and returns `0`. Evaluations that run outside the render pass (for example a particle not bound to an entity) are expected to fail the same way; this is not yet verified in game.

Treat `0` with care: it is both the lowest tier and the fallback value of every failure path.

appliesTo.entities: any rendered entity (value is per device)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity or not in a rendering pass

timing.updates: on change of the client options

pitfalls: 0 is also the error value - check the content log if everything reads 0.
Particles emitted into the world (not bound to an entity) cannot use it.

queries.name: combine_entities
queries.summary: Merge entities and entity arrays into one array without duplicates
queries.hover:
`q.combine_entities(a, b, ...)` - one entity array holding every entity found in the arguments.
Arrays are flattened, duplicates and missing entities dropped, other values ignored silently.
The order of the result is arbitrary.
queries.description: Collects every entity found in its arguments - single entities or arrays of them - into one array, dropping duplicates and entities that no longer exist. Any other kind of argument is ignored.
queries.long:
Builds one entity array from any number of arguments. Each argument is evaluated in turn:

| argument | what happens |
|---|---|
| a single entity | added if it exists |
| an array of entities | each existing entity added |
| a number, string or anything else | ignored, no error |

Entities kept as references to be looked up again (for example ones carried over from an earlier evaluation) are resolved through the world of the entity running the expression and dropped if they no longer exist.

The collected list is then sorted by an internal identity and duplicates are removed, so the result never contains an entity twice but its order has nothing to do with the order of the arguments. When nothing valid is found the result is an empty array, so `q.count(q.combine_entities(5, 'x'))` is `0`.

To call it with no arguments write it without parentheses: `q.combine_entities` is an empty array, while `q.combine_entities()` does not parse at all (empty parentheses are a syntax error for every query).

The result is an array, not a number: pass it to something that takes entity arrays, such as `query.count`, or to `for_each`.

args.name: entities
args.description: Entities or entity arrays to merge
args.onInvalid: ignored, no log

appliesTo.entities: any; looked-up entity references need an entity running the expression

whenUnavailable.when: written without arguments (`q.combine_entities`) or nothing valid found
argument is not an entity or entity array
stored entity reference with no entity running the expression

pitfalls: Do not rely on the order, even for two arguments.
A typo that turns an argument into a number is silently skipped.
`q.combine_entities()` with empty parentheses is a parse error; write `q.combine_entities` for an empty array.

queries.name: cooldown_time
queries.summary: Full cooldown length, in seconds, of the item in an equipment slot
queries.hover:
`q.cooldown_time('slot.weapon.offhand')` - the item's configured cooldown length in seconds, or 0.
Not the time left: it stays the same while the item cools down (use `q.cooldown_time_remaining`).
Hotbar, inventory, ender chest and chest slots need an index as second argument.
queries.description: Returns the total cooldown length, in seconds, of the item in the given equipment slot - the fixed length the item puts on cooldown, not the time remaining. 0 when the slot is empty or the item has no cooldown.
queries.long:
Returns how long the cooldown of the item in a slot lasts, in seconds. This is a fixed property of the item: the value is the same before, during and after use. For the time still left, use `query.cooldown_time_remaining`.

The length comes from the item: the `minecraft:cooldown` item component (its `duration` in seconds, stored as whole ticks, so it is truncated to a multiple of 0.05 s) or a built-in value for some vanilla items - shield 5 s, goat horn 7 s, ender pearl 1 s. Items without a cooldown return `0`.

**Slot.** The first argument is a slot name as used by `/replaceitem` (`'slot.weapon.mainhand'`, `'slot.weapon.offhand'`, `'slot.armor.head'`, …). The slots `'slot.hotbar'`, `'slot.inventory'`, `'slot.enderchest'` and `'slot.chest'` need a second, numeric index (fraction dropped). For every other slot the second argument is not evaluated at all.

An empty slot, an index outside the container (negative ones included), or a slot the entity does not have returns `0` without an error. Three or more arguments, an unknown slot name, a missing or non-numeric index for a slot that needs one, and a missing entity each write a content-log error and return `0`; mobs get the same argument errors as players. Empty parentheses, `q.cooldown_time()`, are rejected when the expression is parsed.

Measured lengths: shield 5, goat horn 7, ender pearl 1, wind charge 0.5, apple 0.

args.name: slot
args.description: Equipment slot name
args.onInvalid: content-log error, returns 0

args.name: index
args.description: Slot index; required for hotbar, inventory, enderchest and chest
args.onInvalid: content-log error, returns 0 (only for slots that need it)

queries.formula: `ticks × 0.05`

appliesTo.entities: entities with the slot (players for hotbar/inventory/ender chest)

whenUnavailable.when: first argument not a string / unknown slot name
indexed slot without exactly two arguments
slot empty, index out of range, or item without cooldown

pitfalls: It does not count down - compare with `q.cooldown_time_remaining` for progress.
`q.cooldown_time('slot.hotbar')` without an index is an error, not slot 0.
A fractional `duration` in `minecraft:cooldown` is truncated to whole ticks.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: cooldown_time_remaining
queries.summary: Seconds left on a player's item cooldown (by category or by slot)
queries.hover:
`q.cooldown_time_remaining(['category' | 'slot', index])` - seconds until the player's cooldown ends; 0 when none.
No argument: the longest running cooldown. A slot name reads the cooldown category of the item in that slot.
Players only: every other entity gets 0 without an error. Steps in 0.05 s (one tick).
queries.description: Seconds remaining on one of the player's item cooldowns: the longest one, a named cooldown category, or the category of the item held or worn in an equipment slot. Returns 0 when nothing is cooling down.
queries.long:
Returns how many seconds are left before a player's item cooldown runs out. Cooldowns are counted in whole ticks and converted to seconds, so the value moves in steps of `0.05` and reaches exactly `0` when the cooldown is over.

There are four call forms:

| call | reads |
|---|---|
| `q.cooldown_time_remaining` | the longest cooldown the player currently has, of any category |
| `q.cooldown_time_remaining('minecraft:goat_horn')` | the cooldown category with that name |
| `q.cooldown_time_remaining('slot.weapon.mainhand')` | the cooldown category of the item in that slot |
| `q.cooldown_time_remaining('slot.hotbar', 3)` | same, for a slot inside a multi-slot container |

**Category or slot.** A string that is one of the `/replaceitem` slot names (`slot.weapon.mainhand`, `slot.weapon.offhand`, `slot.armor.head`, `slot.armor.chest`, `slot.armor.legs`, `slot.armor.feet`, `slot.armor.body`, `slot.hotbar`, `slot.inventory`, `slot.enderchest`, `slot.saddle`, `slot.armor`, `slot.chest`, `slot.equippable`) is treated as a slot; any other string is treated as a cooldown category name. For a slot, the query takes the item there and looks up the cooldown category that item declares; an empty slot, or an item without a cooldown category, gives `0`.

**Category names.** For the vanilla goat horn, `'minecraft:goat_horn'` and plain `'goat_horn'` both match and read the same value. An empty string or an unknown name reads `0` without an error.

**Slot index.** `slot.hotbar`, `slot.inventory`, `slot.enderchest`, `slot.chest` and `slot.equippable` need the index as a second, numeric argument; the fractional part is dropped. Leaving it out, or passing a string, writes an error to the content log and returns `0`. For single slots (hands, armor) a second argument is ignored, and a category name also ignores it.

**Who has cooldowns.** Only players. On any other entity every form returns `0` and nothing is logged. Without an entity, or with three or more arguments, or with a first argument that is not a string, the query logs an error and returns `0`.

**Client and server.** The client counts the cooldown down too, one `0.05` step per tick: a goat horn reads `7` on use and reaches exactly `0` seven seconds later in resource-pack Molang.

Use `query.cooldown_time` for the full length of the same cooldown, e.g. to draw a progress bar.

args.name: category_or_slot
args.description: Cooldown category name, or a /replaceitem slot name
accepts: cooldown category name ('minecraft:goat_horn'; the bare 'goat_horn' also matched in game)
args.onInvalid: not a string: content-log error, returns 0; unknown category: returns 0, no log

args.name: slot_index
args.description: Index inside a multi-slot container; required for those slots
accepts: ignored for single slots and for category names
args.onInvalid: missing or non-numeric for a multi-slot container: content-log error, returns 0

queries.formula: `ticks_left * 0.05`

appliesTo.entities: players; every other entity returns 0

whenUnavailable.when: first argument is not a string
multi-slot container without a numeric index
category not cooling down, or unknown
slot empty, missing, or its item has no cooldown category

pitfalls: Mobs and other non-player entities always return 0, even if they use items with cooldowns.
A misspelt category name silently reads 0; there is no error for unknown names.
`slot.hotbar` and the other container slots need the index; without it the query logs an error.
The value only changes once per tick, so it looks stepped at high frame rates.

queries.name: count
queries.summary: Number of values passed; an entity list counts as its length
queries.hover:
`q.count(a, b, ...)` - how many values you passed; a list of entities adds its length instead of 1.
Numbers, strings and other single values count 1 each. No arguments gives 0.
Every argument is evaluated, even though only its kind matters.
queries.description: Adds up its arguments: an entity list contributes the number of entities in it, every other value contributes 1. With no arguments it returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns a count built from its arguments. Each argument is evaluated in order and adds to the total:

| argument | adds |
|---|---|
| a list of entities (for example the result of `query.combine_entities`) | the number of entities in it |
| anything else - a number, a string, a single entity | `1` |

So `q.count(v.targets)` is the length of the list in `v.targets`, and `q.count(v.a, v.b)` is the combined length of two lists. An empty list adds `0`, so `q.count(q.combine_entities)` is `0`. With no arguments (`q.count`, without parentheses) the result is `0`.

The query works in every context, needs no entity and logs nothing itself. Because every argument is evaluated, expressions with side effects inside the call run - and a variable that was never set still counts `1` (the game logs the unknown variable, not the count).

args.name: value
args.description: Values to count; entity lists count as their length

queries.formula: `sum(len(arg) if arg is an entity list else 1)`

appliesTo.entities: not needed

pitfalls: A plain number counts as 1, not as its value: `q.count(5)` is 1.
Passing a variable that holds a single entity counts 1 even when you meant a list.
An unset variable counts 1, not 0.

queries.name: current_squish_value
queries.summary: Squash-and-stretch amount of a slime, magma cube or sulfur cube
queries.hover:
`q.current_squish_value` - squash (negative) or stretch (positive) of slime-like mobs.
Take-off peaks near 0.55 (magma cube 0.76), landing near -0.27 (magma cube -0.38); then it eases to 0.
Only slimes, magma cubes and sulfur cubes; everything else is 0. Changes once per tick, not smoothed.
queries.description: The current squash-and-stretch value of a slime-like mob: positive after it jumps, negative after it lands, easing back to 0. Other entities return 0.
queries.long:
Returns the squash-and-stretch value that slime-like mobs use for their bounce. It is positive (stretched) just after the mob leaves the ground and negative (squashed) just after it lands, and it eases back toward `0` while nothing happens.

Each tick the game sets a *target* when the mob takes off or lands, moves the value halfway toward the target, then shrinks the target by a per-type decay factor:

1. if the mob has just left the ground, `target = 1`; if it has just landed, `target = -0.5`
2. `value = value + (target - value) * 0.5`
3. `target = target * decay`

So the first tick after take-off reads `0.5` and the first tick after landing about `-0.25`; the value then moves a little further while the shrinking target catches up, and eases back toward `0`.

| mob | decay per tick | take-off peak | landing low |
|---|---|---|---|
| slime | 0.6 | 0.55 (2nd tick) | about -0.27 |
| magma cube | 0.9 | 0.755 (3rd tick) | about -0.38 |
| sulfur cube | 0.6 | 0.55 | about -0.27 |

The landing low depends on where the value was when the mob touched down, so it varies slightly. A sulfur cube holding an item does not hop, and its value just fades toward 0.

At rest the value keeps shrinking toward `0` without landing on it exactly (readings like `-0.00003` or `1e-12` are normal), so test with a threshold rather than `== 0`.

The value is updated once per tick and is not smoothed between frames; `query.previous_squish_value` holds the value from the tick before, so `math.lerp(q.previous_squish_value, q.current_squish_value, q.frame_alpha)` gives a smooth curve.

Every other entity returns `0`, and so does an expression without an entity. Nothing is logged.
queries.formula: per tick: `t = 1` on take-off or `-0.5` on landing; then `s' = s + (t - s) * 0.5`; then `t' = t * decay`

appliesTo.entities: slimes, magma cubes and sulfur cubes; others always 0

whenUnavailable.when: entity is not a slime, magma cube or sulfur cube

pitfalls: A custom entity that looks like a slime returns 0: only the three built-in slime-like mobs have the value.
It is not smoothed between ticks; blend with `query.previous_squish_value` for smooth scaling.
It never gets near 1 or -0.5: a slime peaks around 0.55 and -0.27.
At rest it is tiny but rarely exactly 0; compare with a threshold.

queries.name: dash_cooldown_progress
queries.summary: Removed: camel dash cooldown progress (old files only)
queries.hover:
`q.dash_cooldown_progress` - how far a camel's dash cooldown has run, 0..1 (1 = ready again). Deprecated.
Only resolves in files with a Molang version below 1.20.50; newer files get an unknown-query error.
Resource packs only, camels only; elsewhere it logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Deprecated. For a camel, the fraction of its dash cooldown that has elapsed; 0 when no cooldown is running. Only resolves in content whose Molang version is older than 1.20.50.
queries.long:
Deprecated and only resolvable in older content: in a file whose Molang version is 1.20.50 or newer, the name is not recognised at all. The vanilla camel now tracks its dash cooldown itself with variables in its client entity's `pre_animation` script; new content should do the same.

Where it still resolves, it returns how far the camel's current dash cooldown has run, as a fraction:

`progress = clamp((now - end + length) / length, 0, 1)`

where `now` is the current game tick, `end` is the tick the cooldown finishes and `length` its duration in ticks. For the vanilla camel the cooldown is 55 ticks (2.75 s): the value climbs by 1/55 per tick from about 0 right after the dash to about 0.96, then drops straight to `0` - it never reads `1`. When no cooldown is running, or once it has expired, the result is `0`.

It works only in resource-pack evaluation (on the client) and only on camels. On the server, on any other entity, or without an entity, it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`.
queries.formula: `clamp((now - end + length) / length, 0, 1)` while a cooldown runs, else 0

appliesTo.entities: camels only

whenUnavailable.when: no cooldown running, or it has expired

pitfalls: It drops back to 0 (never 1) the moment the cooldown expires, so `== 1` is never true.
Raising a file's format version past 1.20.40 makes every use of it an unknown-query error.

versionGate.meaning: resolvable only while the file's Molang version is below this SemVersion; unknown-query error at/after it

queries.name: day
queries.summary: World clock in days, as a fraction (not a whole day number)
queries.hover:
`q.day` - the overworld clock expressed in days: (ticks + 6000) / 24000. Fractional, not a whole number.
Wrap it in math.floor for a day counter; the whole part changes at midnight, not at sunrise.
Needs an entity; 0 in world particles and blocks.
queries.description: The world clock converted to days: `(clock + 6000) / 24000`. The result has a fractional part; take `math.floor` of it to get a day number.
queries.long:
Returns the overworld clock converted to days, including the fraction of the current day:

`q.day = (t + 6000) / 24000`, where `t` is the clock in ticks.

It is not rounded. Right after `/time set 0` (sunrise) it reads `0.25`, at noon of the same day `0.5`, and it passes `1.0` at the next midnight. The whole part therefore counts midnights, and `math.floor(q.day)` is the day number. `math.mod(q.day, 1)` is the same fraction that `query.time_of_day` returns.

The clock is the overworld's even when the entity is in the Nether or the End. `/time set` replaces the clock, so it also resets the day count (`/time set 0` after eleven days reads `0.25` again), while `/time add` carries the count forward. The value advances once per tick. For very large clocks the fraction loses precision, because the computation is done in single-precision floats.

The entity is only used to reach the world; without one (world particles, blocks) the result is `0`.
queries.formula: `(t + 6000) / 24000`, `t` = world clock in ticks

appliesTo.entities: any entity (only used to reach the world)

pitfalls: It is fractional: `q.day == 3` is almost never true. Use `math.floor(q.day)`.
The whole part ticks over at midnight, a quarter of a day after sunrise.
It is the overworld clock in every dimension.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22 (client side)

queries.name: death_ticks
queries.summary: Ticks since a mob started dying (0 while alive)
queries.hover:
`q.death_ticks` - how many ticks the mob has been dying, counting up by 1 per tick from the moment it dies.
0 while alive and for every entity that is not a mob. Whole numbers; not smoothed between frames.
queries.description: Counts the ticks since the mob began its death: 0 while alive, then 1, 2, 3 ... once per tick. Entities that are not mobs always return 0.
queries.long:
Returns the mob's death timer in ticks. While the mob is alive it is `0`; from the tick it dies it increases by exactly 1 per tick (20 per second) until the body is removed, about 20 ticks later for an ordinary mob (the last reading seen on a zombie was 19). An armor stand is removed the moment it is destroyed and never shows a count.

The count is a whole number and is not smoothed between frames, so an animation driven directly by it moves in 1/20-second steps. For a smooth death animation add the partial tick: `q.death_ticks + q.frame_alpha` while `q.death_ticks > 0`.

Only mobs (players included) have the timer; other entities and an expression without an entity return `0` without logging.

Resource-pack evaluation sees the count too: the client advances its own copy of the counter.

appliesTo.entities: mobs (players included); others always 0

pitfalls: It counts ticks, not seconds: divide by 20 for seconds.
It is 0 for the whole life of the mob, so `q.death_ticks > 0` is a dying test, not `>= 0`.

queries.name: debug_output
queries.summary: Returns its first argument and writes all arguments to the game's diagnostic log
queries.hover:
`q.debug_output(value, ...)` - returns `value` unchanged and writes the arguments to the game's diagnostic log.
The line goes to the platform/debug log, not the content log, so normally you will not see it.
No arguments: returns 0 and writes nothing.
queries.description: A pass-through for debugging: returns the first argument unchanged and writes every argument, as a decimal number, on one line of the game's diagnostic log.
queries.long:
Returns its first argument unchanged, so it can wrap any sub-expression, e.g. `v.x = q.debug_output(q.ground_speed) * 2;`.

As a side effect it formats every argument as a decimal number (six places), separates them with spaces and writes the line to the game's diagnostic log. That log is the platform's developer output, not the content log shown in game, so in a normal retail game the line is usually not visible anywhere you can read (not yet verified per platform).

All arguments are evaluated. Arguments are read as numbers; pass numbers only - a string argument does not fail, but it returns a meaningless huge number (`q.debug_output('abc')` gives about `4.2e26`). With no arguments the query returns `0` and writes nothing. None of these forms writes to the content log.

It works in every context and needs no entity.

args.name: value
args.description: Returned unchanged and logged

args.name: more
args.description: Extra numbers added to the same log line

queries.formula: returns `value`

appliesTo.entities: not needed

pitfalls: Nothing appears in the content log or chat; do not expect to see the output in a retail game.
It writes a line every time it is evaluated - every frame in an animation - so remove it before shipping.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: delta_time
queries.summary: Game time since the entity's previous animation update, in seconds
queries.hover:
`q.delta_time` - seconds of game time since this entity's animations were last updated (usually one frame).
Counts game ticks plus the partial tick, so it stops while the game is paused and is never negative.
Client entities and attachables only; elsewhere it is 0.
queries.description: Seconds of game time between this entity's previous animation update and the current one - normally the length of one frame. Only client entities and attachables have it; elsewhere it is 0.
queries.long:
Returns how much game time passed since the entity's animations were last updated, in seconds. For an entity on screen that is normally one frame, so it is the value to multiply per-second rates by (`v.spin = v.spin + 90 * q.delta_time;`).

It is measured on the game clock, not the wall clock: the entity's age in ticks plus the frame's partial tick, divided by 20, minus the same value at the previous update. It is clamped at `0`, so it is never negative. As a consequence it is `0` while the game is paused and follows the game's tick rate rather than the wall clock. On a client running at 60-110 frames per second it reads 0.009-0.017 s. While an entity is off screen its animations are not updated and the stored value stays at its last on-screen frame; the first update after it comes back should cover the whole gap (not yet verified in game).

Only client entities and attachables (resource-pack evaluation) fill it in. In behavior packs, block expressions and particle effects the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: `max(0, (age_ticks + partial_tick) / 20 - previous)`

appliesTo.entities: rendered entities and attachables; 0 in other contexts

pitfalls: It is game time: during a pause it is 0, and it does not follow real time when the tick rate changes.
It is 0 in behavior packs and particle effects; do not use it for server-side timers.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: distance_from_camera
queries.summary: Distance in blocks from the camera to the entity (or emitter)
queries.hover:
`q.distance_from_camera` - straight-line distance in blocks from the camera to the entity's position.
Updated by the renderer each frame the entity is considered for drawing; expected 0 on the server (unverified).
For particle emitters the value is not yet verified.
queries.description: The straight-line distance, in blocks, between the camera and the entity's position, as measured by the renderer. Behavior packs and blocks have no camera to measure from.
queries.long:
Returns the straight-line (3D) distance in blocks between the camera and the entity. The renderer measures it while it decides which entities to draw, from the camera position to the entity's current position, and stores it on the entity; the query reads the stored value.

That means:

- It is refreshed per frame for entities the renderer looks at; for an entity the renderer skips, it keeps the last value.
- It uses the entity's position rather than a model point; for players that position is at eye height (not yet verified in game).
- In third-person view it is measured to the camera, not to the player.

In behavior-pack (server) evaluation there is no camera; the result is expected to be `0` there (not yet verified in game). For entity-bound and world particle effects the query is registered as available, but what it returns there is not yet verified.
queries.formula: `|camera_position - entity_position|`

appliesTo.entities: rendered entities

whenUnavailable.when: entity not considered for rendering this frame

pitfalls: It keeps a stale value while the renderer is not processing the entity.
There is no camera in behavior packs (expected 0 there), so a server-side level-of-detail check sees the entity as close.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: effect_emitter_count
queries.summary: Live emitters of the current particle effect, across the whole world
queries.hover:
`q.effect_emitter_count` - how many emitters of this particle effect's identifier are alive right now, world-wide.
Only meaningful inside a particle effect; in entity animations it returns 0.
Client only.
queries.description: Inside a particle effect: the number of emitters currently alive that belong to the same effect identifier, counted over the whole client, not just this emitter.
queries.long:
Evaluated inside a particle effect, returns how many emitters of **that effect identifier** exist right now. The count is kept per identifier by the client's particle system, so it includes emitters from every copy of the effect in the world, not only the emitter evaluating the expression.

Typical use is to thin an effect out when many copies are running, e.g. lowering the spawn rate once the count passes a budget.

The value is read live when the expression is evaluated. Outside a particle effect - in client entity scripts, animations and render controllers - there is no emitter to ask and the result is `0`. It is a client-side value: behavior packs and blocks have no particle system to read (not yet verified for dedicated servers).

For the totals over all effects use `query.total_emitter_count`; for the other count of the same effect use `query.effect_particle_count`.

appliesTo.entities: not needed; the particle emitter is the subject

whenUnavailable.when: not evaluated inside a particle effect

pitfalls: It counts every copy of the effect in the world, not just this emitter.
In an entity's animation or render controller it is always 0.

queries.name: entity_biome_has_all_tags
queries.summary: 1 if the biome at the entity has every listed biome tag
queries.hover:
`q.entity_biome_has_all_tags('tag', ...)` - 1 if the biome at the entity's position has all listed tags.
Resource packs only; in behavior packs it logs an error and returns 0.
Stops at the first missing tag; a non-string argument reached before that logs an error.
queries.description: Looks up the biome at the entity's position and returns 1 when that biome carries every biome tag you list, otherwise 0. Client (resource pack) only.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the biome at the entity's position has **all** of the listed biome tags and `0` otherwise.

The biome is the one at the block containing the entity's position - the same point `query.position` reports: the feet for most entities, but for the player it is at eye height, about 1.62 blocks above the feet. Biomes change with height, so an entity in a cave reports the cave biome, and a player standing just below a cave-biome boundary can already read the biome above.

Tags are compared as written (for example `'forest'`, `'cold'`, `'overworld'`). The arguments are checked in order and the check stops at the first tag the biome lacks, returning `0`. An argument that is not a string writes an error to the content log and returns `0` - but only if the check reaches it.

Only resource-pack (client) evaluation supports it: in a behavior pack it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`. It also needs an entity and world access, so particle effects and block expressions get an error and `0`.

args.name: tag
args.description: Biome tag
accepts: biome tag name, as written in the biome definition
args.onInvalid: non-string reached during the check: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: any entity

pitfalls: It does not work in behavior packs: there it logs an error and returns 0.
Arguments after the first missing tag are never checked, so a typo there goes unreported.

queries.name: entity_biome_has_any_identifier
queries.summary: 1 if the biome at the entity is one of the listed biome identifiers
queries.hover:
`q.entity_biome_has_any_identifier('minecraft:plains', ...)` - 1 if the biome at the entity is one of them.
Exact, case-sensitive match: vanilla biomes need the `minecraft:` prefix ('plains' never matches).
Resource packs only; in behavior packs it logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Looks up the biome at the entity's position and returns 1 when its identifier equals one of the listed identifiers, otherwise 0. Client (resource pack) only.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the identifier of the biome at the entity's position is one of the listed identifiers, and `0` otherwise.

The biome is the one at the block containing the entity's position - the same point `query.position` reports: the feet for most entities, but for the player it is at eye height, about 1.62 blocks above the feet. Biomes change with height, so an entity in a cave reports the cave biome, and a player standing just below a cave-biome boundary can already read the biome above.

The comparison is an exact match of the whole string, so `'minecraft:plains'` and `'plains'` are different values, and only the first matches a vanilla plains biome. Write the identifier with its namespace, in lower case, e.g. `'minecraft:cherry_grove'`.

The arguments are checked in order and the check stops at the first match, returning `1`. An argument that is not a string writes an error to the content log and returns `0` - but only if the check reaches it before a match.

Only resource-pack (client) evaluation supports it: in a behavior pack it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`. It also needs an entity and world access, so particle effects and block expressions get an error and `0`.

args.description: Biome identifier
args.onInvalid: non-string reached during the check: content-log error, returns 0

whenUnavailable.when: a non-string argument is reached before a match

It does not work in behavior packs.

queries.name: equipment_count
queries.summary: Number of occupied armor slots (hands not counted)
queries.hover:
`q.equipment_count` - how many armor slots hold an item: head, chest, legs, feet and body, so 0..5.
Anything in the slot counts, not only armor (a carved pumpkin on the head counts). Hands are not counted.
Needs an entity; 0 otherwise.
queries.description: Counts the entity's armor slots that are not empty - head, chest, legs, feet and the body slot - so the result is 0 to 5. Held items are not counted.
queries.long:
Returns how many of the entity's armor slots currently hold an item. The armor slots are head, chest, legs, feet and the body slot used by wolf armor, horse armor and similar gear, so the result is between `0` and `5`. A tamed wolf in wolf armor and a horse in horse armor each read `1`.

Any non-empty item counts - a carved pumpkin or a mob head on the head slot counts just like a helmet. This is different from `query.has_armor_slot`, which only accepts real armor pieces.

Main hand and off hand are not part of the count; use `query.is_item_name_any` for those. Entities without armor slots return `0`, and so does an expression without an entity. Nothing is logged.

Vanilla uses it to scale experience drops by how much gear a mob wore, and on the happy ghast to tell whether it wears a harness (a body-slot item).

appliesTo.entities: any entity; those without armor slots return 0

pitfalls: Non-armor items in armor slots count too.
The body slot is included, so a wolf in wolf armor or a horse in horse armor counts 1.
A mob with a full armor set and a sword reads 4, not 5: hands never count.

queries.name: equipped_item_all_tags
queries.summary: 1 if the item in a hand or armor slot has every listed item tag
queries.hover:
`q.equipped_item_all_tags('slot.weapon.mainhand', 'minecraft:is_sword', ...)` - 1 if that item has all tags.
Only hands and armor slots are read; other slot names read as empty.
An empty slot returns 0. A non-string tag logs an error and makes the result 0.
queries.description: Takes an equipment slot name followed by item tags and returns 1 when the item in that slot has every tag, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Checks the item in one equipment slot against a list of item tags and returns `1` only if it has **all** of them.

```
q.equipped_item_all_tags('slot.weapon.mainhand', 'minecraft:is_sword', 'minecraft:diamond_tier')
```

**Slot.** The first argument is a `/replaceitem` slot name. Only the hands and armor slots are actually read: `slot.weapon.mainhand`, `slot.weapon.offhand`, `slot.armor.head`, `slot.armor.chest`, `slot.armor.legs`, `slot.armor.feet`, `slot.armor.body`. Other valid names (`slot.hotbar`, `slot.inventory`, ...) take no index and read as an empty slot. An unknown name writes an error to the content log and returns `0`.

**Empty slots.** An empty hand or armor slot has no tags, so the result is `0`; the same goes for every slot name outside the hands and armor.

**Tags.** Item tags as the item declares them, e.g. `'minecraft:is_sword'`. They are checked in order and the check stops at the first missing tag. A non-string tag writes an error to the content log and counts as a tag the item does not have, so the result is `0`.

Fewer than two arguments logs an error and returns `0`. A first argument that is not a string, or no entity, returns `0` without logging.

args.name: slot
args.description: Equipment slot name as used by /replaceitem
accepts: other /replaceitem slot names: read as empty
args.onInvalid: unknown name: content-log error, returns 0; not a string: returns 0, no log

args.name: tag
args.description: Item tag the item must have
args.onInvalid: non-string: content-log error, counts as missing (result 0)

appliesTo.entities: any entity with hand or armor slots

whenUnavailable.when: first argument is not a string
slot is empty, or the slot name is outside the hands and armor
a tag argument is not a string

pitfalls: A bad tag argument (a number) logs an error and the whole check returns 0, even if the other tags match.
`slot.hotbar`, `slot.inventory` and other container slots are not read - there is no index argument.
Some tools list it as taking at most one argument, but it needs at least two; they may warn about a correct call.

queries.name: equipped_item_any_tag
queries.summary: Whether the item in a hand or armor slot has at least one of the given tags
queries.hover:
`q.equipped_item_any_tag('slot.weapon.mainhand', 'minecraft:is_sword', ...)` - 1 if the item has any listed tag, else 0.
Only the two hands and the armor slots are read; any other valid slot name always gives 0.
Needs a slot name plus at least one tag; a non-string slot argument returns 0 without an error.
queries.description: Looks at the item in one hand or armor slot of the entity and returns 1 when it carries at least one of the listed item tags, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Checks the item in one equipment slot for item tags and returns 1 on the first tag it finds.

```
q.equipped_item_any_tag('slot.weapon.mainhand', 'minecraft:is_sword', 'minecraft:is_axe')
```

**Slot.** The first argument is a `/replaceitem` slot name. Only these slots are actually read:

| slot name | item read |
|---|---|
| `slot.weapon.mainhand` | the held item (the selected hotbar slot for players) |
| `slot.weapon.offhand` | the off-hand item |
| `slot.armor.head`, `slot.armor.chest`, `slot.armor.legs`, `slot.armor.feet`, `slot.armor.body` | that armor piece |

Other slot names that the game knows (`slot.hotbar`, `slot.inventory`, `slot.saddle`, ...) are accepted without an error but always read as an empty slot, so the result is 0. A name the game does not know logs an error and returns 0.

**Tags.** Every argument after the slot is a tag name, compared exactly (`'minecraft:is_sword'`). The tags are checked from left to right and the first match returns 1. A tag argument that is not a string writes an error to the content log but the check continues with the next tag, so a later match can still return 1.

An empty slot has no tags, so it always gives 0.

Use `query.equipped_item_all_tags` when every tag must be present.

args.name: slot
args.description: Slot name, e.g. 'slot.weapon.mainhand'
accepts: other known slot names are accepted but always read as empty
args.onInvalid: unknown name: content-log error, returns 0; not a string: returns 0 with no log

args.name: tag
args.description: Item tag to look for; repeat for more tags
accepts: tag name as written in the item definition, e.g. 'minecraft:is_sword'
args.onInvalid: not a string: content-log error, that argument never matches, later tags are still checked

appliesTo.entities: any entity; hands and armor are read through the entity's equipment

whenUnavailable.when: first argument is not a string
slot is known but not a hand or armor slot

pitfalls: `'slot.hotbar'` or `'slot.inventory'` gives 0 even when the item there has the tag - only hands and armor are read.
`q.equipped_item_any_tag('slot.weapon.mainhand')` with no tag logs an error; there is no 'has any tag' form.
A misspelled slot name logs an error, but passing a number as the slot returns 0 silently.

queries.name: equipped_item_is_attachable
queries.summary: Whether the item in a hand is drawn through an attachable definition
queries.hover:
`q.equipped_item_is_attachable(0|1|'main_hand'|'off_hand')` - 1 if the item in that hand has an attachable, else 0.
Resource packs only, and only while the entity is being rendered; elsewhere it logs an error and returns 0.
Exactly one argument; any other hand value logs an error.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the item in the chosen hand is rendered with an attachable (a client-side definition for held or worn items), otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Looks up the item in the chosen hand and returns 1 if the resource packs provide an attachable for it, otherwise 0. An empty hand gives 0.

**Hand.** Exactly one argument:

| argument | hand |
|---|---|
| `0` or `'main_hand'` | main hand |
| `1` or `'off_hand'` | off hand |

Numbers lose their fractional part (`0.7` is the main hand); negative numbers act as `0`. Any other number or string writes an error to the content log and returns 0.

**Where it works.** It is answered by the client while an entity is being drawn - in render controllers, client animations and attachables. With no entity, outside rendering, or with the wrong number of arguments it logs an error and returns 0.

The game declares an unusual result type for this query, although the value it produces is a plain 0 or 1. Whether the pack loader accepts it inside arithmetic is not yet verified.

args.name: hand
args.description: 0/'main_hand' or 1/'off_hand'
accepts: numbers: fractional part dropped, negative acts as 0
args.onInvalid: content-log error, returns 0

queries.name: eye_target_x_rotation
queries.summary: Guardian eye: sideways offset toward its target, -2 to 2
queries.hover:
Guardians and elder guardians only: how far the eye should shift sideways toward the target, -2..2 (0 = straight ahead).
Not an angle. Every other entity returns 0; a guardian also tracks a player it is only watching (no attack needed).
Pairs with `q.eye_target_y_rotation`, which is only 0 or 1.
queries.description: For guardians and elder guardians, a sideways offset for the eye that points it at the current target, from -2 to 2. Every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Despite the name this is not a rotation in degrees. It is the horizontal offset a guardian's eye needs to look at its target, in the range `[-2, 2]`, meant to be used directly as a position offset of the eye bone.

**How it is computed.** The game takes the horizontal direction between the guardian's eyes and its target's eyes (height ignored) and measures how far that direction lies to the side of where the guardian is facing - the sine `s` of the angle between them. The result is `2 * sign(s) * sqrt(|s|)`: `0` when the target is straight ahead (or straight behind), `+-2` when it is exactly to the side. The square root makes the eye move quickly away from the centre. The facing vector is not flattened, so a guardian looking steeply up or down gives smaller values.

**Target.** The guardian's synced attack target is used first; if it has none, the entity it is looking at is used - in game a guardian that was not attacking (the player was in creative) still gave values of about 0.7 to 1.8 in size while it watched the player. Only with neither is the result 0.

**Entities.** Only guardians and elder guardians compute this. Every other entity, including custom entities, returns 0.
queries.formula: `2 * sign(s) * sqrt(|s|)`, `s` = sideways component of the horizontal direction to the target relative to the facing

appliesTo.entities: guardian and elder guardian only; everything else 0

whenUnavailable.when: entity is not a guardian or elder guardian
guardian has no target and is not looking at any entity

pitfalls: It is an offset in `[-2, 2]`, not degrees; feeding it to a rotation channel barely moves the bone.
Custom entities always get 0, even with a guardian-like target behaviour.
The sign follows the side the target is on relative to the guardian's facing; in game it flipped when the player walked to the other side. Test the direction on your model before relying on it.
It is not zero while the guardian is merely watching someone: an idle guardian's eye already follows a nearby player.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22 (client side)

queries.name: eye_target_y_rotation
queries.summary: Guardian eye: 1 if its target's eyes are higher than its own, else 0
queries.hover:
Guardians and elder guardians only: 1 when the target's eye height is above the guardian's, else 0.
Only ever 0 or 1 - not an angle. Other entities return 0; an idle guardian uses the player it watches.
queries.description: For guardians and elder guardians, 1 when the current target's eyes are higher than the guardian's eyes, otherwise 0. Every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
The vertical partner of `query.eye_target_x_rotation`, but much simpler: it compares the eye height of the guardian's target with the guardian's own eye height and returns `1` if the target is higher, `0` otherwise (including when both are at exactly the same height).

The name suggests an angle, but there are only two values, so an eye driven by it jumps between two positions instead of following the target smoothly.

The target is chosen the same way as for `query.eye_target_x_rotation` (attack target first, otherwise the entity the guardian is looking at). With neither, and for any entity that is not a guardian or elder guardian, the result is 0.
queries.formula: `target_eye_y > own_eye_y ? 1 : 0`

appliesTo.entities: guardian and elder guardian only; everything else 0

whenUnavailable.when: entity is not a guardian or elder guardian
guardian has no target and is not looking at any entity

pitfalls: Only 0 or 1: it cannot tell how far above or below the target is.
A target at the same eye height gives 0, the same as a target below.

queries.summary: Whether the entity's ranged-attack behaviour is currently running

queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity's ranged-attack behaviour is running (from the moment the goal starts until it stops), otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Reads a flag that the ranged-attack behaviour (`minecraft:behavior.ranged_attack`) switches on when it starts and off when it stops. While the goal runs the value is 1; before it starts and after it stops, 0.

Nothing else in the game sets this flag, so entities without the ranged-attack goal always return 0. The flag is part of the entity's synced state, so resource-pack Molang sees the same value.

To react to the shot itself, use the goal's own timing (or `query.is_charging` for charged weapons) rather than this flag.

queries.name: frame_alpha
queries.summary: Where the current frame falls between two game ticks, 0 to 1
queries.hover:
Fraction of the way from the last game tick to the next one at the moment this frame is drawn, 0..1.
Use it to smooth per-tick values: `math.lerp(v.prev, v.now, q.frame_alpha)`.
Set while entities and attachables are drawn; server-side it is expected to be 0 (not yet verified).
queries.description: How far the frame being drawn is between the previous and the next game tick, as a value from 0 to 1. It lets you smooth values that only change once per tick.
queries.long:
The game updates entities 20 times a second but draws many more frames. `query.frame_alpha` tells you where the current frame sits between two ticks: `0` right on the last tick, approaching `1` just before the next one.

```
math.lerp(v.last_tick_value, v.this_tick_value, q.frame_alpha)
```

It is set by the client each frame while it prepares an entity or attachable for drawing. In behavior-pack (server) Molang nothing is expected to set it, so it should read `0` there - not yet verified in game. Whether particle and block expressions get a real value has not been verified either; vanilla's own particles do use it.

Several built-in queries already mix this value in (for example `query.modified_distance_moved`), so they need no extra smoothing.

appliesTo.entities: entities and attachables being rendered

pitfalls: Server-side it is expected to be 0 (not yet verified), so a `math.lerp` built on it would just return the first value there.
Queries that are already smoothed should not be lerped again with it.

queries.name: fuse_time
queries.summary: Fuse ticks left before an exploding entity goes off; -1 without minecraft:explode
queries.hover:
Remaining fuse of the entity in ticks (20 per second); counts down only while the fuse is lit.
Entities without `minecraft:explode` report -1.
Reaches 0 one tick before the entity explodes.
queries.description: The entity's fuse in game ticks: while the fuse burns it counts down to 0, at which point the entity explodes. An entity that has no `minecraft:explode` component gives -1 instead.
queries.long:
Returns the fuse value of an entity with the `minecraft:explode` component, in ticks (20 per second).

Every tick the game copies the component's fuse into the entity's synced data. While the fuse is lit, it first subtracts one, so from a fuse of `n` it reads `n-1, n-2, ... 1, 0`; on the next tick after `0` the entity explodes. While the fuse is not lit the value stays at whatever fuse the component holds.

Every other entity has the value `-1`, which is the default the game gives all entities. Nothing was found that sets it back to `-1` when the component is removed, so an entity that loses `minecraft:explode` may keep its last value (not yet verified).

Whether the fuse is lit is available separately as `query.is_ignited`, which the same update keeps in step.

```
q.is_ignited ? (q.fuse_time / 80) : 1
```

appliesTo.entities: entities with minecraft:explode; others -1

pitfalls: The unit is ticks, not seconds: divide by 20 for seconds.
Without an entity the result is 0, not -1.
An unlit fuse does not count down; check `query.is_ignited` before treating the value as time left.
Right after a lit entity appears, resource-pack Molang can briefly still read -1 and `is_ignited` 0 until the first synced update arrives.

queries.name: get_animation_frame
queries.summary: Icon frame of the item a mob holds (bow draw stage, compass, clock...)
queries.hover:
Icon frame number of the item in the mob's main hand; 0 for items without animated icons.
Bow-like items: 0 while not drawing, then 1..frame count as the draw charges.
Only mobs (players and armor stands included); other entities, or none, log an error and return 0.
queries.description: Returns which icon frame the item in the entity's main hand is showing - for example the draw stage of a bow. Items without animated icons return 0.
queries.long:
Takes the item in the entity's main hand (for players, the selected hotbar slot) and asks it which icon frame it would show right now. Most items have a single icon and return `0`.

Items with animated icons compute their own frame:

| item kind | frame |
|---|---|
| bow and other charge-and-release weapons | `0` while not being used; while a player draws it, `floor(0.99 * p * frames) + 1`, where `p = min(1, (t^2 + 2t) / 3)` and `t` is seconds spent drawing - so it climbs from 1 to the last frame over about one second (for mobs such as skeletons this is not yet verified) |
| compass, clock | the frame their icon currently shows (in game a compass read 30, and a clock 52 at `query.time_of_day` 0.29) |
| crossbow, recovery/lodestone compass, fishing rod, wolf armor | their own rules, not documented here yet |

A player drawing a vanilla bow was seen at frame 1 from the start, 2 after about half a second and 3 after about 0.8 seconds, staying at 3 - as the formula gives.

Only mobs have this - players, other living entities and armor stands (an armor stand holding a bow reads 0 without an error). Without an entity the query writes an error to the content log and returns 0.
queries.formula: bow-like items: `floor(0.99 * min(1, (t^2 + 2t)/3) * frames) + 1` while drawing, `t` in seconds; otherwise 0

appliesTo.entities: mobs (players and armor stands included); others log an error

whenUnavailable.when: no entity, or the entity is not a mob
held item has no animated icon (or the hand is empty)

pitfalls: It always reads the main-hand item, so an item carried in the off hand never drives it; in an attachable (as vanilla's bow does) the main hand is expected to be the holder's - not yet verified.
Custom data-driven items return 0 - their icons have no frame logic.
Drawing frames start at 1, so `== 0` means 'not drawing', not 'first frame'.

Resource packs only; needs a rendered entity. A bone name that does not exist returns 0 without an error.

queries.description: Returns the x, y or z coordinate of a bone's pivot as written in the entity's geometry, unaffected by animation.
queries.long:
Looks up a bone of the entity's model by name and returns one coordinate of its pivot point, as defined in the geometry file (model units, 16 per block). Animations do not change it.

```
q.get_default_bone_pivot('head', 'y')
```

**Arguments.** Exactly two: the bone name (a string, compared exactly) and the axis - `0`/`'x'`, `1`/`'y'`, `2`/`'z'`, lower case. A number loses its fractional part (`0.9` reads x). `3` or more, another string, or - on Windows - a negative number logs an error and returns 0; other platforms may instead read a negative axis as x, so never pass one.

queries.long:
Returns the name of the item in one of the entity's hands as a string, **without the namespace**: a bow gives `'bow'`, not `'minecraft:bow'`. An empty hand gives `''`.


queries.name: get_level_seed_based_fraction
queries.summary: Meant as a seed-based 0..1 value; in this version it is 0 for practically every world

queries.description: Intended to give a stable 0-1 value derived from the world seed. In the current game version the result is 0 for practically every world (1 for about one seed in four billion).
queries.long:
The query folds the 64-bit world seed into 32 bits (the high half combined bit-wise with the low half) and then turns that into the result - but the conversion keeps only the whole part, so the result is `1` when the folded value is the largest possible 32-bit number and `0` for every other seed.

In practice: **expect 0**. Do not use it to vary visuals between worlds in this version; a random value stored in an entity property or a script-set variable is a reliable alternative.

It needs access to the world, which it finds through the context: a world context, the block being evaluated, or the entity. With none of those it writes an error to the content log and returns 0.

whenUnavailable.when: no world, block or entity in the context

pitfalls: It is 0 in practically every world; a `> 0.5` test is always false.

queries.name: ground_speed
queries.summary: How fast the entity moved during the last tick, in blocks per second
queries.hover:
Speed of the entity over the last tick in blocks per second: the length of its last movement times 20.
Despite the name, vertical movement counts too - a falling or jumping entity has a non-zero value.
Changes once per tick, not smoothed; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns the distance the entity moved during the last game tick, converted to blocks per second (multiplied by 20). Movement in all three directions counts, including falling and jumping.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's speed over the most recent tick, in blocks per second.

The game takes the change in the entity's position across the last tick, measures its length in all three directions, and multiplies it by 20 (ticks per second). A mob walking one block per second reads about `1`; a mob falling at terminal speed reads a large value even while standing still horizontally.

Because vertical movement is included, the name is misleading. In game a pig falling straight down with no sideways movement read its fall speed (several blocks per second). There is no direct horizontal-only version: `query.position_delta` looks like the building block, but in resource-pack Molang it read `0` for moving mobs in testing, so it cannot stand in for this query there.

The value changes once per tick and is not smoothed between frames. It works on any entity, not only mobs. It takes no arguments (extra arguments are ignored). Without an entity it returns `0`.

Vanilla uses it in resource-pack entities and entity-bound particles, where it follows the smoothed position the client draws. Whether behavior-pack (server) Molang sees the same value is not yet verified.
queries.formula: `20 * |p_now - p_prev|`, the 3D distance moved during the last tick times 20

appliesTo.entities: any entity

queries.side: both (used by vanilla resource packs; server value not yet verified)
pitfalls: Falling, jumping and flying all raise the value - it is not horizontal speed.
It is a per-tick step value; at 60 fps three frames in a row show the same number.

queries.name: had_component_group
queries.summary: Whether a saved entity had a component group active (property defaults only)
queries.hover:
`q.had_component_group('group')` - 1 if the entity's save data lists that component group as active.
Only meaningful in an entity property's `default`, while an entity is being loaded from a save.
Group name exactly as in the entity file (no '+' prefix); new spawns and every other moment give 0.
queries.description: While a saved entity is being loaded, returns 1 if the named component group was active in its saved data. Used to give a new entity property a starting value that matches an older version of the entity.
queries.long:
Lets an entity property pick its first value from the state an entity was saved in, which is useful when an add-on replaces a component group with a property and existing entities must keep their state.

```
"properties": { "my:has_nectar": { "type": "bool", "default": "q.had_component_group('has_nectar')" } }
```

**When it answers.** Only while the game builds an entity from saved data and sets up its properties. The saved list of active groups is attached for exactly that step and removed right afterwards, so the query returns `0` for newly spawned, bred or transformed entities, and at any later time. The property `default` is also the only field that accepts this query - and it is the only query that field accepts.

**The name.** The save records active groups with a `+` in front (`+has_nectar`); the query compares against the name without it, so write the group name exactly as it appears under `component_groups` in the entity file, including any namespace it has. Groups recorded as removed do not count.

accepts: the group name exactly as declared, without a leading '+'
args.onInvalid: not a string: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: entities being loaded from a save

whenUnavailable.when: entity not being loaded from saved data (new spawn, or any later evaluation)

timing.updates: once, while a saved entity is loaded

It cannot be used in animations, events or filters; only the property default accepts it.

queries.name: has_armor_slot
queries.summary: Whether a mob wears an armor piece in the given slot (0 head .. 3 feet)
queries.hover:
`q.has_armor_slot(slot)` - 1 if the mob wears armor in that slot: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet.
Only real armor pieces count; a pumpkin or mob head on the head slot gives 0.
Other slot numbers return 0 without an error. An elytra counts as chest armor.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the mob has an armor piece in the given armor slot, otherwise 0. Slots are 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity wears an armor item in the given slot and `0` otherwise.

| slot | body part |
|---|---|
| `0` | head |
| `1` | chest |
| `2` | legs |
| `3` | feet |

Only items that are humanoid armor count. Something worn in an armor slot that is not armor - a carved pumpkin or a mob head on the head slot - gives `0`. An elytra in the chest slot does count. Horse and wolf armor live in the body slot (`4`), which never counts as humanoid armor, so `q.has_armor_slot(4)` is `0` in practice.

Negative whole numbers are converted differently on different platforms - on Windows `-1` reads no slot and returns `0` - so do not use them. The query does not check the range: numbers above 3 return `0` without logging anything. Calling it with no argument or more than one logs an error.

Entities that are not mobs (minecarts, items, projectiles) always return `0`. Without an entity the query logs an error and returns `0`.

args.description: 0 head, 1 chest, 2 legs, 3 feet
args.onInvalid: 4 or more: returns 0, no log

Negative slots are not portable: on Windows `q.has_armor_slot(-1)` is 0 even when a helmet is worn.

queries.name: has_collision
queries.summary: Whether the entity collides with blocks
queries.hover:
1 if the entity's collision flag is set, else 0. The flag comes from `minecraft:physics` (`has_collision`).
Entities without `minecraft:physics` read 0 unless the game sets the flag for them (not yet verified).

An entity that has no `minecraft:physics` component and is not one of those built-in cases keeps the flag at its initial value, expected to be `0` (not yet verified).

The flag is part of the entity data sent to clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

queries.name: has_dash_cooldown
queries.summary: Whether the entity's dash (or aquatic charge) is cooling down
queries.hover:
1 while the entity's dash-cooldown flag is set, else 0.
Set after a dash of a `minecraft:dash` mount (camel) and during the cooldown of an aquatic charge attack (nautilus).
Synchronised flag; no arguments; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is in its dash cooldown - after a camel-style dash, or after the charge of an aquatic charge attack - otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's dash-cooldown flag.

Two things set it in this version:

| source | set | cleared |
|---|---|---|
| `minecraft:dash` (camel, camel husk) | when the ridden mount dashes | when the dash cooldown runs out - a vanilla camel read `1` for about 2.75 seconds after its dash |
| `minecraft:behavior.aquatic_charge_attack` (nautilus, zombie nautilus) | when the charge ends and the cooldown starts | when the goal resets for the next charge (not yet verified in game) |

The flag is part of the entity data sent to clients, so the value is the same in resource and behavior packs. It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

appliesTo.entities: entities with minecraft:dash or an aquatic charge attack; others 0

pitfalls: It is not camel-only: nautilus-style charge attacks use the same flag.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: has_gravity
queries.summary: Whether gravity pulls the entity down
queries.hover:
1 if the entity's gravity flag is set, else 0. The flag comes from `minecraft:physics` (`has_gravity`).
Entities without `minecraft:physics` read 0 unless the game sets the flag for them (not yet verified).
Synchronised flag: same value in resource and behavior packs; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 if the entity is flagged to be affected by gravity, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's gravity flag: `1` when gravity applies to it, `0` otherwise.

The flag is set from the `has_gravity` field of the entity's `minecraft:physics` component when the component is applied (the field defaults to `true`). Items and falling blocks set the flag from their own built-in behaviour, and hover-style movement control changes it while it runs.

An entity that has no `minecraft:physics` component and is not one of those built-in cases keeps the flag at its initial value, expected to be `0` (not yet verified).

The flag is part of the entity data sent to clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

Seen in game (collision / gravity): players, pigs, zombies, horses and boats `1 / 1`; a dropped item, an experience orb and a falling sand block `1 / 1`; a hovering bee `1 / 0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

pitfalls: Adding or removing `minecraft:physics` in a component group changes the value; toggling it off with a later group needs the field set explicitly.
Not a flight test: some flying mobs (phantom, allay, vex) turn gravity off, others such as the bat keep it on; use `query.can_fly` for flight ability.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: has_head_gear
queries.summary: Whether anything is worn in the entity's head slot
queries.hover:
1 if the entity's head armor slot holds any item - helmet, carved pumpkin, mob head, anything - else 0.
Unlike q.has_armor_slot(0) it does not require real armor. 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 if there is any item in the entity's head armor slot, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the head armor slot is not empty. Any item counts: helmets, carved pumpkins, mob heads, or anything placed there with `/replaceitem ... slot.armor.head`.

Compare `query.has_armor_slot(0)`, which is `1` only for actual armor pieces. Use `has_head_gear` to hide hair or ears whenever something is on the head.

Entities that have no armor slots are expected to return `0` (not yet verified). It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

appliesTo.entities: entities with armor slots (mobs, players, armor stands); others 0

pitfalls: A pumpkin or mob head counts; use `query.has_armor_slot(0)` if only armor should count.

queries.name: has_owner
queries.summary: Whether the entity has an owner recorded (tamed mob, projectile shooter, ...)
queries.hover:
1 if an owner is recorded for the entity, else 0: tamed mobs, and projectiles fired by someone.
The owner does not have to be loaded or online - only the stored owner id is checked.
No arguments; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 if the entity has an owner id recorded - for example a tamed animal, or a projectile fired by an entity - otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when an owner is recorded for the entity.

The owner is looked up in two places, in order:

1. the owner stored in the entity's synchronised data - set by taming, and expected to be set by other kinds of ownership such as summoned mobs (not yet verified);
2. for projectiles, the entity that fired them.

Only the stored id is checked. A tamed wolf whose owner is offline or in another dimension still returns `1`.

It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

pitfalls: An arrow or snowball thrown by a player returns 1 - it is not only about taming.
It stays 1 while the owner is offline; it does not mean the owner is nearby.
Mounting an untamed horse in creative tames it, after which it reads 1.

queries.name: has_player_rider
queries.summary: Whether any of the entity's passengers is a player
queries.hover:
1 if any of the entity's passengers is a player, else 0 - any seat, not only the driver's.
Only direct passengers count (a player riding a mob that rides this entity does not). 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 if at least one of the entity's direct passengers is a player, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Goes through the entity's passengers and returns `1` as soon as one of them is a player. The seat does not matter: a player in the second seat of a boat counts as much as the driver.

Only direct passengers are checked. In a stack (a player on a chicken that rides this entity) the player is a passenger of the chicken, not of this entity, so the result is `0` (in game: a boat carrying a horse ridden by the player read `0`, the horse `1`).

It takes no arguments and returns `0` without an entity.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no passengers, or none of them is a player

pitfalls: A player in a passenger seat counts too; use seat-specific logic if only the driver matters.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22 (client side)

queries.name: has_property
queries.summary: Whether the entity declares an entity property with the given name
queries.hover:
`q.has_property('ns:name')` - 1 if the entity type declares that entity property, else 0.
Checks that the property exists, not its value; the name must include the namespace.
No entity, a non-string argument or a wrong argument count logs an error and returns 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity's type declares an entity property with the given full name (for example `'my:variant'`), otherwise 0. The property's current value does not matter.
queries.long:
Tells you whether the entity has a property called `name` among the entity properties declared in its behavior definition (`description.properties`). The answer is `1` as soon as the property is declared, whatever its current value - even `false` or `0`. Use `query.property` to read the value.

**Argument.** Exactly one string: the property name exactly as declared, namespace included (`'my:variant'`, not `'variant'`). The string is compared as a whole; there is no partial or case-insensitive matching.

**Errors.** Calling it with no argument or more than one, with a number instead of a string, or where there is no entity writes an error to the content log and returns `0`. An entity that declares no properties at all simply returns `0`.

This makes it a guard for shared Molang (an animation or expression reused by several entity types) that should only read a property where it exists.

In resource-pack Molang a vanilla property that is sent to clients is visible (a cow reads `1` for `'minecraft:climate_variant'`). Whether properties that are not sent to clients are visible there is not yet verified.

args.name: property
args.description: Full property name including the namespace, e.g. 'my:variant'
accepts: string literal or string-valued expression, compared exactly
args.onInvalid: number instead of string: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: any entity; 0 for entity types without declared properties

pitfalls: It reports whether the property is declared, not whether it is true: a declared `false` boolean still gives 1.
The name must match exactly, namespace included: `q.has_property('variant')` is 0 for `my:variant`.
