queries.name: is_selected_item
queries.summary: Whether the player's selected hotbar slot holds an item
queries.hover:
1 when the entity is a player and the selected hotbar slot is not empty, else 0.
Every entity that is not a player always reads 0, even when holding something.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity is a player whose selected hotbar slot holds an item, and 0 otherwise. Mobs always return 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is a player and the item in the selected hotbar slot is not empty, and `0` otherwise.

Only players are checked. For every other entity - including mobs holding a weapon, and armor stands - the result is always `0`. Only the main hand counts; the off hand is not looked at.

Which item it is does not matter; for that use `query.get_equipped_item_name` or `query.is_item_name_any`. Any arguments are ignored; without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players only; every other entity 0

pitfalls: For mobs this is always 0 - use `query.is_item_name_any('slot.weapon.mainhand', ...)` or `query.get_equipped_item_name` instead.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_shaking
queries.summary: Whether the entity is shaking (minecraft:is_shaking, or frozen solid)
queries.hover:
1 while the entity shakes: from the `minecraft:is_shaking` component, or while a mob is fully frozen in powder snow.
While a mob is freezing, the freezing state decides the value and overrides the component.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is shaking - set by the `minecraft:is_shaking` component, or while a mob is fully frozen by powder snow - and 0 otherwise.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity is shaking and `0` otherwise.

Two things drive the state:

- **The `minecraft:is_shaking` component.** Adding it turns the state on, removing it turns it off. Vanilla uses it for mobs that shiver in the wrong environment - a strider out of lava, a zombie about to turn into a drowned, a skeleton turning into a stray.
- **Powder snow.** While a mob (players included) is freezing in powder snow, the state is set every tick to whether it is fully frozen: `1` once the freeze has built up completely (about 7 seconds in the snow), `0` before that and from the moment it leaves the snow. Players in creative mode freeze too; leather armor prevents freezing altogether. When the freeze has worn off completely this stops.

Because the freezing update writes the state every tick, it wins over the component while the entity is freezing: an entity with `minecraft:is_shaking` that steps into powder snow drops to `0` at once, and stays at `0` after it leaves the snow, until something re-adds the component.

The flag is kept by the server and copied to clients, so behavior-pack and resource-pack Molang read the same value. Any arguments are ignored; without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with minecraft:is_shaking, and any mob while freezing; others 0

timing.updates: on change of the component; per tick while freezing

pitfalls: Powder snow makes any mob read 1 once fully frozen - a check meant for your own `minecraft:is_shaking` setup will also fire there.
A strider that touched powder snow stops shivering (reads 0) even after it is back on land.
Unrelated to a wolf shaking off water; that is `query.is_shaking_wetness`.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_shaking_wetness
queries.summary: Whether a wolf is shaking itself dry after getting wet
queries.hover:
1 while a wolf plays its shake-off after getting wet, about 2 seconds (40 ticks), else 0.
Only wolves: every other entity type always reads 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 while a wolf is shaking itself dry after leaving water or rain, and 0 otherwise. Only wolves can return 1.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while a wolf is shaking itself dry and `0` otherwise.

**When it shakes.** A wolf that has been in water or rain becomes wet. Once it is out of the water and rain again and standing on the ground, it starts a shake - not always at once: between landing and the start anything from under a second to several seconds can pass. Tamed or wild makes no difference. The shake is timed: a counter goes up by 0.05 each tick and the shake ends once the counter reaches 2, so the query reads `1` for about 40 ticks (2 seconds). It turns `1` on the first tick after the shake starts, not on the starting tick itself. If the wolf gets wet again during the shake, the shake is cancelled and the query drops to `0`.

**Only wolves.** The entity type is checked first; for any other entity - including custom entities that copy the wolf's components - the result is always `0`.

The start and cancel are sent from the server to clients as entity events and both sides run the same counter, so the value is expected to match in behavior-pack and resource-pack Molang (only the client side was measured). Any arguments are ignored; without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: wolves only; every other entity 0

pitfalls: Custom entities never read 1, even with wolf-like components: the check is on the entity type.
Not related to `query.is_shaking`, which is the component / freezing state.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_sheared
queries.summary: Whether the entity currently has the minecraft:is_sheared component
queries.hover:
1 while the entity has the minecraft:is_sheared component, else 0.
Only that component drives it: shearing does nothing unless the entity's events add the component.
Saved with the entity; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity carries the `minecraft:is_sheared` component, otherwise 0. Vanilla sheep, bogged and snow golems add that component in their shear event.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sheared state is on and `0` otherwise.

The state is switched on when the `minecraft:is_sheared` component is added to the entity (usually through a component group added by the entity's shear event) and switched off when the component is removed. Vanilla sheep, bogged and snow golems work this way, and the query drives the fleece, mushroom and pumpkin visibility. The game does not decide by itself whether an entity *can* be sheared: any entity that has the component reads `1`, and a sheared-looking custom mob without it reads `0`.

The state is also written to the entity's saved data and restored on load. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with the minecraft:is_sheared component; everything else 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Using shears on a custom mob does not set the value; the entity's shear event must add `minecraft:is_sheared`, and a regrow event must remove it again.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_shield_powered
queries.summary: Whether a wither is in its armored, projectile-proof phase
queries.hover:
1 while a wither is in its armored (shielded) phase, else 0. Every other entity type always returns 0.
The phase starts on the hit that brings the wither to half health or less, stays on after it heals, and flickers while it dies.
While the value is 1, projectiles cannot hurt the wither.
queries.description: Returns 1 while a wither has its armor up, otherwise 0. Only the wither has this state; any other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while a wither is in its armored phase and `0` otherwise. The query first checks that the entity is a wither; for any other type it returns `0` without looking further.

A wither keeps an "air attack" state that starts on when it spawns or loads. When damage brings it down to half of its maximum health or below, the air attack is turned off and the armor comes on; this query reports that armor state. It reads `0` for the whole spawn charge (while the health fills up) and turns `1` on the same hit that brings health to half or below. Nothing turns it back off: a wither healed back above half keeps reading `1`. During the death animation the value alternates between `1` and `0` every few ticks, which makes the armor flicker.

The same state decides whether projectiles can damage the wither: while the query reads `1`, projectile damage is ignored. The state is saved with the wither and shared with clients.

Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: withers only; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
the entity is not a wither

timing.updates: on change of the wither's armor phase (hurt, load, death animation)

pitfalls: A custom entity that is not a wither always returns 0, even with wither-like components.
The armor does not come off when the wither heals back above half health, so the query is not a health test.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_silent
queries.summary: Whether the entity's silent state is on (no vanilla feature turns it on)
queries.hover:
1 while the entity's silent state is on, else 0; a silent entity plays no sounds.
No component, command or behavior in this game version switches the state on, so in practice it reads 0.
Not saved with the entity; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity's silent state is on, otherwise 0. The state mutes the entity's sounds, but no add-on-facing feature sets it, so the query normally returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's silent state is on and `0` otherwise.

When that state is on, the game refuses to play the entity's sound events. However, no component, entity behavior, command or saved-data field in this game version turns it on, and it is not part of the data saved with an entity. For add-ons this means the query reads `0` for every entity (players, summoned and named mobs alike). To silence a custom entity, leave its sounds out of the resource pack or gate them with your own property or variable instead.

Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity (always 0 in practice)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: There is no `minecraft:is_silent` component; the query cannot be driven from a behavior pack.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_sitting
queries.summary: Whether the entity is sitting
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is sitting, else 0.
Set by sitting behaviors (random sitting, look-around-and-sit, ocelot/cat sitting on blocks) and by tamed pets told to sit.
Saved with the entity; lying down and sleeping are separate queries.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is sitting, otherwise 0. Sitting behaviors (cats, ocelots, foxes, camels, pandas) set it, and so do tamed pets told to sit and (not yet verified in game) the perching ender dragon.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sitting state is on and `0` otherwise.

Several things switch it on and off:

- sitting behaviors: `minecraft:behavior.random_sitting`, `minecraft:behavior.random_look_around_and_sit` and the ocelot/cat "sit on block" behavior turn it on when they start and off when they stop;
- tamed pets that are ordered to sit (the `minecraft:sittable` component): a tamed wolf reads `1` right after the owner tells it to sit and `0` again after it is told to stand;
- the ender dragon, which is expected to report sitting while it is perched and to clear it when it starts charging or strafing a player (not yet verified).

Removing `minecraft:sittable` turns the state off. The state is saved with the entity (only when it was saved at all, so older saves keep their default). The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value.

Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with a sitting behavior or sittable pets; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A mob that is lying down (`query.is_laying_down`) or sleeping (`query.is_sleeping`) reads 0 here.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_sleeping
queries.summary: Whether the entity is sleeping (player in bed, villager, napping fox)
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is sleeping, else 0.
Players in a bed, villagers using minecraft:behavior.sleep and foxes using minecraft:behavior.nap.
Not saved; a bat hanging upside down is query.is_resting instead.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is asleep, otherwise 0. Players in bed, sleeping villagers and napping foxes set it.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sleeping state is on and `0` otherwise.

| who | when it is `1` |
|---|---|
| players | from lying down in a bed until they get up |
| villagers (and any mob with `minecraft:behavior.sleep`) | while the sleep behavior has them in bed |
| foxes (and any mob with `minecraft:behavior.nap`) | while the nap behavior runs |

The state is not written to saved data; a mob that was asleep when the world closed starts awake and its behavior puts it back to sleep. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value.

Resting bats (`query.is_resting`), sitting pets (`query.is_sitting`) and mobs lying down (`query.is_laying_down`) are different states. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players, and mobs with a sleep or nap behavior; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A resting bat reads 0; use `query.is_resting` for it.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_sneaking
queries.summary: Whether a player is sneaking
queries.hover:
1 while a player is sneaking (crouching), else 0.
Follows the player's sneak input; no vanilla mob behavior is known to set it, so mobs read 0.
Not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the player holds sneak, otherwise 0. The state follows the sneak input, so for mobs it is normally 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sneaking state is on and `0` otherwise.

For players the state follows the sneak input: pressing sneak turns it on and releasing it (or toggling it off) turns it off. The local client sets it immediately for its own player, and the server applies the start/stop requests it receives, then shares the state with every other client, so other players see the crouch too.

No entity behavior or component is known to set it for mobs, so a mob reads `0`. The state is not saved.

Vanilla uses it to lower the head and arms of the player model (`- query.is_sneaking * 27.0` style offsets); because it is 0 or 1 it can be multiplied directly. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players; mobs always 0 in vanilla

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

timing.updates: on change of the sneak input

pitfalls: Vanilla mobs are not known to ever sneak; a custom crouching mob needs its own property or variable.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_sneezing
queries.summary: Whether the mob is sneezing through minecraft:behavior.sneeze
queries.hover:

Nothing else sets it; not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the sneeze behavior is running on the mob, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sneezing state is on and `0` otherwise.

The only thing that switches it is `minecraft:behavior.sneeze`: the state turns on when the behavior starts and off when it stops, so it spans the whole sneeze behavior rather than a single frame. The state is not saved. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value.

Vanilla resource packs do not read it (the panda animates its sneeze in other ways), but it is a direct way to drive a custom sneeze animation. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities running minecraft:behavior.sneeze; others 0

1 while minecraft:behavior.sniff is running (the warden's sniff), else 0.
Nothing else sets it; the sniffer mob does not use it. Not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the sniff behavior is running on the mob, otherwise 0. Vanilla uses it for the warden.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sniffing state is on and `0` otherwise.

Only `minecraft:behavior.sniff` switches it: on when the behavior starts, off when it stops. In vanilla that behavior belongs to the warden, whose sniff animation is driven by this query. The sniffer's digging and searching are separate states and do not set it.

The state is not saved. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

queries.name: is_sonic_boom
queries.summary: Whether the mob is using minecraft:behavior.sonic_boom (warden)
queries.hover:
1 while minecraft:behavior.sonic_boom is running (the warden's ranged blast), else 0.
Covers the whole behavior, including the charge-up before the blast. Not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the sonic boom behavior is running on the mob, otherwise 0. Vanilla uses it for the warden's ranged attack animation.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sonic-boom state is on and `0` otherwise.

Only `minecraft:behavior.sonic_boom` switches it: on when the behavior starts and off when it stops, so the value stays `1` for the charge-up as well as the blast itself. Vanilla uses it to play the warden's sonic attack animation.

The state is not saved. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities running minecraft:behavior.sonic_boom; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_spectator
queries.summary: Whether the entity is a player in spectator mode
queries.hover:
1 when the entity is a player whose game mode resolves to spectator, else 0.
A player set to "default" game mode counts when the world's default is spectator. Non-players always 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity is a player in spectator mode, otherwise 0. Mobs and other non-players always return 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is a player in spectator mode and `0` otherwise.

The value is worked out each time it is read: the entity's own game mode is looked up, and if the player uses the "default" game mode, the world's default game mode is used instead. Entities that have no game mode at all - everything that is not a player - return `0`.

Vanilla player rendering uses it to switch to the spectator material and first-person view and to hide the cape. Arguments are ignored: `q.is_spectator(1)` and `q.is_spectator(1, 2)` read the same as the bare form and log nothing. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
the entity is not a player (has no game mode)

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_sprinting
queries.summary: Whether the entity is sprinting
queries.hover:
1 during a sprint, otherwise 0.
Players: follows the sprint state that also grants the sprint speed bonus. Mobs: only in a few movement cases.
Not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is sprinting, otherwise 0. For players this is the normal sprint; mobs rarely set it.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's sprinting state is on and `0` otherwise.

For players the state is switched together with the sprint speed bonus: starting to sprint turns both on, stopping the sprint turns both off. The local client sets it for its own player straight away: walking reads `0`, sprinting `1`, and the value drops back to `0` as soon as the sprint key is released.

Mobs normally read `0`. The engine sets it for a mob only in a few movement situations (for example some pathfinding while in water) and clears it when a player stops controlling a ridden mob. Idle or wandering dolphins, cod, drowned, cows, horses, polar bears and wolves all read `0`; mobs that are chasing a target or being ridden are not yet verified.

The state is not saved. Vanilla resource packs do not read this query; sprinting players are usually animated from their speed instead. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players; mobs only in rare movement cases

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A mob moving fast is not sprinting; use `query.ground_speed` for run animations.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_stackable
queries.summary: Whether the entity has the minecraft:is_stackable component
queries.hover:
1 while the entity has the minecraft:is_stackable component, else 0.
That component lets other entities stand on the entity like a block (boats and minecarts in vanilla).
0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity carries the `minecraft:is_stackable` component, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's stackable state is on and `0` otherwise.

Only the `minecraft:is_stackable` component switches it: on when the component is added, off when it is removed. The component marks entities whose collision box others can rest on (vanilla boats and minecarts use it). The query itself does not change collision; it only reports whether the component is present.

The state follows the component, so it is restored whenever the entity's components are rebuilt on load. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. No vanilla resource pack reads it. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with the minecraft:is_stackable component; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_stalking
queries.summary: Whether a mob is creeping up on prey (stalk-and-pounce behavior)
queries.hover:
1 while minecraft:behavior.stalk_and_pounce_on_target has the mob creeping toward its prey, else 0.
On while creeping and preparing to pounce, off when the behavior ends (exact phases not yet verified). Used by the fox.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the stalk-and-pounce behavior has the mob crouched and creeping toward its target, otherwise 0. Vanilla uses it for the fox.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's stalking state is on and `0` otherwise.

Only `minecraft:behavior.stalk_and_pounce_on_target` switches it. The behavior turns it on when it starts and when it is getting ready to pounce, and turns it off while the mob is closing in by other means and when the behavior ends. In short it marks the crouched, creeping part of the hunt; exactly which phases read `1` is not yet verified. A fox that lands in snow and gets stuck is reported by `query.is_stunned`, not by this query.

The state is not saved. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities running minecraft:behavior.stalk_and_pounce_on_target; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: is_standing
queries.summary: Whether a horse is rearing or a polar bear stands up to stomp
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is rearing up on its hind legs, else 0.
Polar bear (minecraft:behavior.stomp_attack): alternates 1/0 through each attack. Horse family: while rearing (triggers not yet verified).
Not saved; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is reared up on its hind legs, otherwise 0. Horse-family mobs set it while rearing; stomp-attack mobs such as the polar bear set it while rising for the hit.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's standing (rearing) state is on and `0` otherwise.

| who | when it is `1` |
|---|---|
| horse family (horse, donkey, mule, skeleton horse, zombie horse) | while the horse rears (for example when an untamed horse throws off its rider). In a client-side test neither punching an untamed horse nor the horse throwing off a mounted player made it read `1`, so the exact trigger is not yet verified |
| mobs using `minecraft:behavior.stomp_attack` (the polar bear) | from about halfway through the attack cooldown until the stomp lands; the behavior clears it after the hit and when it stops. An angry polar bear attacking a player reads `1` for about 0.6 s, then `0` for about 0.4 s, repeating with every attack |
| anything else | always `0` |

The state is not saved. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value. Vanilla horses use it to stop the grazing animation while rearing. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: horse-family mobs and stomp-attack mobs; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_stunned
queries.summary: Whether the entity is stunned (is_stunned component, or stuck after a pounce)
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is stunned, else 0.
Set by the minecraft:is_stunned component (the ravager after a blocked attack) and by the stalk-and-pounce behavior when the pounce leaves the mob stuck.
Saved with the entity; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is stunned, otherwise 0. The `minecraft:is_stunned` component and the fox's pounce behavior both set it.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's stunned state is on and `0` otherwise. Two things set it:

- the `minecraft:is_stunned` component: on while the component is present. The vanilla ravager adds it through a component group when its attack is blocked by a shield and removes it again after a timer;
- `minecraft:behavior.stalk_and_pounce_on_target`: when the pounce lands the mob in a block it gets stuck in (the fox diving into snow), the behavior turns the state on, and clears it when the mob gets free or the behavior ends (the exact moments are not yet verified in game).

The state is saved with the entity and restored on load. The state is kept on the server and shared with clients, so resource-pack and behavior-pack Molang see the same value.

The query only reports the state; being stunned does not by itself stop the entity from moving - that is up to the components and behaviors in the same component group. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with minecraft:is_stunned, or stuck stalk-and-pounce mobs; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Adding `minecraft:is_stunned` alone does not freeze a mob; disable its movement in the same component group.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: is_swimming
queries.summary: Whether a player is in the swimming pose (sprint-swimming)
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is in the swimming pose - a player sprint-swimming - else 0.
Not a water test: a player floating or sinking in water reads 0; use query.is_in_water for that.
Dolphins and fish read 1 whenever they swim; drowned read 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 while a player is swimming in the horizontal sprint-swim pose, otherwise 0. Being in water alone does not set it.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's swimming state is on and `0` otherwise.

For players the state is the horizontal swimming pose: it turns on when the player starts sprint-swimming (sprinting while underwater) and off when they stop. The server applies the start/stop requests that come from the player's client and shares the state with every other client. A player who is simply in water, bobbing at the surface or walking on the bottom, reads `0`.

Mobs are different: dolphins and fish (cod was measured) read `1` the whole time they are in water, even when simply cruising, while drowned read `0`. So the query tells a swimming mob apart from a walking one, not a sprint. The state is written to the entity's saved data and restored on load.

Vanilla uses it to switch the player and elytra models into the swimming pose, often together with `query.is_crawling`, which uses the same pose on land. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players (sprint-swim pose); dolphins and fish while in water

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Use `query.is_in_water` to test for water; for players `is_swimming` is only the sprint-swim pose.
Dolphins and fish read 1 all the time in water, so a shared player/mob animation keyed on it will fire for them.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_tamed
queries.summary: Whether the entity carries the tamed flag
queries.hover:
1 if the entity is flagged as tamed, else 0.
Taming (minecraft:tameable or minecraft:tamemount) and the minecraft:is_tamed component set it; removing that component clears it.
Having an owner is a separate question (q.has_owner). 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity carries the tamed flag and 0 otherwise. The flag is set when a player tames the entity, when it has the `minecraft:is_tamed` component, or when it is born tamed.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; normally set only on tameable or rideable mobs

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Tamed and owned are separate: a mob given `minecraft:is_tamed` from a component group reads 1 even with no owner.

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; a plain flag or copy with nothing to measure in game

queries.name: is_transforming
queries.summary: Whether the entity has a transformation component (is about to convert)
queries.hover:
1 once the entity has been given minecraft:transformation, else 0.
It turns on as soon as the component is added and stays on until the entity is replaced by its new form.
0 without an entity; no vanilla pack uses it.
queries.description: Returns 1 after the entity has received the `minecraft:transformation` component, which is how conversions such as curing a zombie villager are set up. Otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity is marked as transforming and `0` otherwise.

The mark is placed the moment the entity gains the `minecraft:transformation` component - vanilla adds it through a component group when a conversion starts (a zombie villager being cured, a piglin or hoglin in the Overworld, a husk or zombie drowning). From then on the query reads `1` during the whole delay configured in the component, until the entity is removed and replaced by the new one. There is no gradual value: use your own timer if an animation needs the progress.

Nothing else sets the mark. Whether removing the component group again (cancelling the conversion) turns it back to `0` is not yet verified.

The mark is part of the synchronised entity state, so it can drive client animations such as the shaking of a converting zombie villager. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities that have been given minecraft:transformation; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: It is not a progress value: it is 1 for the whole conversion delay and gives no fraction of it.
Cancelling a conversion by removing the component group may leave it at 1 (not yet verified).

verification.label: Documented for 1.26.60.22; this behaviour cannot be observed from the client in game, so it is not verified there

queries.name: is_using_item
queries.summary: Whether the entity is in the middle of a hold-to-use action
queries.hover:
1 while the entity is using an item (drawing a bow, eating, charging a crossbow...), else 0.
Players: set when a use with a duration starts, cleared when it stops. Mobs: set by the behaviors that use items.
0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity is in the middle of using an item - drawing a bow, eating or drinking, charging a crossbow - and 0 otherwise.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's using-item flag is set and `0` otherwise.

- **Players.** The flag is switched on when the player starts using an item that has a use time (bow, crossbow, trident, food, potions...) and off when the use stops, whether it completed or was released early. A single click on an item without a use time never sets it.
- **Mobs.** The flag is switched on and off by the built-in behaviors that make a mob use its held item: charging a crossbow (pillagers, piglins), using or drinking an item, and item interactions. Mobs that only swing a weapon never set it.

The flag is synchronised, so the value is the same in behavior packs (vanilla's allay checks it in a filter) and resource packs (vanilla zombies use it to time their spear animation). Raising a shield does not count: a sneaking player with a shield in the off hand reads `0` here while `query.blocking` reads `1`. A pillager reads `1` while it charges its crossbow and `0` once the crossbow is loaded.

Without an entity the query returns `0`. For the duration of the current use, see `query.item_remaining_use_duration`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Swinging or attacking is not using an item: only hold-to-use actions set it.
Blocking with a shield reads 0; use `query.blocking` for that.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: is_wall_climbing
queries.summary: Whether a mob with climbing navigation is climbing a wall
queries.hover:
1 while a mob using minecraft:navigation.climb is pressed against a wall on its way to a destination, else 0.
Ladders, vines and minecraft:can_climb do not set it. Refreshed every tick by the navigation.
0 for every entity without climbing navigation.
queries.description: Returns 1 while a mob that navigates with `minecraft:navigation.climb` (spiders, cave spiders) is climbing a wall. Otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's wall-climbing flag is set and `0` otherwise.

Only the climbing navigation (`minecraft:navigation.climb`) writes this flag, and it rewrites it every tick. The flag is `1` when all of these hold during the tick:

1. the mob has a destination to walk to;
2. it is blocked horizontally by a solid obstacle;
3. none of the block columns within 1.2 blocks of it contains a border block.

As soon as one condition fails - the path is finished or dropped, or the mob is no longer pushing against a wall - the flag returns to `0`. A spider sitting still next to a wall therefore reads `0`. Measured on a spider penned in with walls four blocks high below a player: `1` for the whole climb up the wall, `0` again as soon as it stands on top or on the ground.

Climbing a ladder, scaffolding or vines is a different mechanic (`minecraft:can_climb`) and never sets this flag; neither does a player. The flag is synchronised, so resource packs can use it to rotate a model against the wall. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: mobs with minecraft:navigation.climb; all others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Ladder and vine climbing never set it.
A climbing-capable mob standing still next to a wall reads 0: it needs a destination.
A border block close to the mob stops it from counting as climbing.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: item_in_use_duration
queries.summary: Elapsed use of the main-hand item, as ticks x 20 (not seconds)
queries.hover:
Elapsed use of the main-hand item in ticks multiplied by 20: 1 second of use reads 400.
Computed as (item use time - ticks left) x 20, so a player holding a usable item without using it reads the full item use time x 20.
Empty hand or no use time: 0. Armor stands count like mobs; a pillager reads 0 until it starts charging.
queries.description: Reports how far the current use of the main-hand item has progressed, computed as the item's full use time minus the ticks left, and scaled by 20. The scale makes one second of use read as 400, not 1.
queries.long:
Returns how much of the main-hand item's use time has been spent, in a scaled unit: the difference between the item's use time and the ticks left on the current use, **multiplied by 20**. One tick of use adds 20 to the value and one second adds 400; divide by 400 to get seconds or by 20 to get ticks.

| situation | value |
|---|---|
| player drawing a bow for 1 second | `400` |
| player holding a bow but not using it | the bow's full use time x 20 (the ticks-left counter is 0) |
| crossbow-carrying hostile humanoid (pillager-style) | `0` before its first charge, then rises by 20 per tick while charging and stays at the full value (`500`) once loaded |
| other mob holding an item with a use time (skeleton, and also an armor stand) | the item's full use time x 20 |
| empty main hand, or an item without a use time | `0` |
| entities without hands (items, projectiles...) | `0` |

The counter of ticks left is a single value per entity: it counts down by one per tick while an item is being used and is `0` when nothing is being used. Because the query subtracts it from the full use time, the result is only meaningful while `query.is_using_item` is `1`; the rest of the time it jumps to its maximum. The item's use time is read from the item in the main hand, even when the item being used is in the off hand.

No vanilla pack uses this query. `query.item_remaining_use_duration` with a normalization value is usually the better tool, since it gives a clean `0..1` progress.
queries.formula: `(U - r) * 20`, where `U` = main-hand item use time in ticks, `r` = ticks left on the current use
queries.range: [0, U x 20] while the main-hand item is the one in use

appliesTo.entities: mobs, players and armor stands; other entities always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
main-hand item has no use time

pitfalls: The unit is ticks x 20, not seconds: after 1 second of use it reads 400.
When nothing is being used it reads the item's full use time x 20, not 0; guard it with `query.is_using_item`.
Uses the main-hand item's use time even while the off-hand item is being used; if that use is longer, the result can go negative.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: item_is_charged
queries.summary: Whether the item in a hand holds a charged projectile (loaded crossbow)
queries.hover:
`q.item_is_charged(hand?)` - 1 if the item in that hand has a projectile loaded into it (a loaded crossbow), else 0.
Hand: omitted/0/'main_hand' = main hand, 1/'off_hand' = off hand. Numbers are truncated (0.9 -> 0, 1.5 -> 1).
Negative numbers, 2 or more, and other strings log an error and return 0 (Windows).
queries.description: Returns 1 when the item in the chosen hand has a projectile loaded into it - a charged crossbow - and 0 otherwise. With no argument the main hand is checked.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the item in the chosen hand carries a loaded projectile and `0` otherwise. In vanilla the only such item is a charged crossbow; the check is on the loaded projectile, so an uncharged crossbow and every other item read `0`.

**Hand argument.**

| argument | hand |
|---|---|
| omitted | main hand |
| number that truncates to `0` (`0` to `0.99`) | main hand |
| number that truncates to `1` (`1` to `1.99`) | off hand |
| `'main_hand'` | main hand |
| `'off_hand'` | off hand |

Any other number or string writes an error to the content log and returns `0`: `2` or more, and on Windows also negative numbers such as `-3` (the Windows build treats them as out of range; the ARM64 build reads them as `0`, the main hand, so do not rely on either). Only the first argument is looked at; `q.item_is_charged(1, 0)` checks the off hand and ignores the rest without a message.

The entity's own hands are read, so it works for players and for mobs that hold a crossbow. Without an entity the query returns `0` without a message, whatever the argument (even an invalid one is not reported then). Measured with a pillager's loaded crossbow: `1` for the bare form, `0`, `0.9` and `'main_hand'`, `0` for the empty off hand.

queries.name: item_max_use_duration
queries.summary: Full use time of the main-hand item, as ticks x 20 (not seconds)
queries.hover:
The main-hand item's full use time in ticks multiplied by 20 (a crossbow's 25-tick charge reads 500).
0 for an empty hand or an item that has no use time. Works for any entity with a main hand.
Same scale as q.item_in_use_duration, so their ratio is a clean 0..1 progress.
queries.description: Returns the full use time of the item in the main hand - how long a bow can be drawn, how long a crossbow takes to charge - in ticks multiplied by 20. Returns 0 for items without a use time.
queries.long:
Returns the use time of the item in the main hand, in ticks **multiplied by 20**: a use time of one second (20 ticks) reads `400`.

The use time is a property of the item, not of the current action, so the value is the same whether or not the item is being used. For a crossbow it depends on the item's enchantments: the base charge time is 25 ticks (`500`), each Quick Charge level removes 5 ticks (`400`, `300`, `200` for levels I-III). Other measured values: bread `640` (32 ticks), bow `1440000` (72000 ticks, the bow can be held almost indefinitely), iron spear `28800000`.

An empty main hand, or an item that has no use time (blocks, swords, most tools), gives `0`. Only the main hand is read.

Because `query.item_in_use_duration` uses the same scale, `q.item_in_use_duration / q.item_max_use_duration` is the fraction of the use completed (only meaningful while the item is being used).
queries.formula: `U * 20`, where `U` = main-hand item use time in ticks

appliesTo.entities: any entity with a main hand; others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
main-hand item has no use time

pitfalls: The unit is ticks x 20: divide by 400 for seconds.
Only the main hand is read; an off-hand bow is not seen.

queries.name: item_remaining_use_duration
queries.summary: Time left on the current item use: seconds, or a 0..1 fraction times a scale
queries.hover:
`q.item_remaining_use_duration(slot?, scale?)` - time left on the player's current item use.
No argument: seconds. With a scale: (ticks left / item use time) clamped to 0..1, times the scale (the main hand unless a slot is named).
A slot name alone returns ticks x 20, not seconds. Players only; other entities 0.
queries.description: Reports how much of the current item use is left. With no argument the result is in seconds; with a normalization value it is the remaining fraction of the item's use time, times that value.
queries.long:
Returns how much is left of the entity's current item use (drawing a bow, eating, charging a crossbow). The underlying counter holds the ticks left on the use: it starts at the item's use time when the use begins, drops by one per tick, and is `0` when nothing is being used. Only players have this counter; for every other entity it is `0`, so the query returns `0`.

The argument forms change both the unit and the item that is checked:

| call | result |
|---|---|
| `q.item_remaining_use_duration` | ticks left / 20 (**seconds**); `0` if the main hand is empty |
| `q.item_remaining_use_duration('main_hand')` / `('off_hand')` | ticks left x 20 (**not seconds**); `0` if that hand is empty |
| `q.item_remaining_use_duration(s)` with a number `s` | `clamp(ticks left / U, 0, 1) * s` for the main-hand item |
| `q.item_remaining_use_duration('off_hand', s)` | same, with `U` taken from the named hand's item |

`U` is the use time of the item in the checked hand. When that hand is empty or its item has no use time, the normalized forms return `0`. With `s = 1` the value falls from `1` to `0` as the use proceeds, which is how vanilla drives the first-person bow pull.

Note that the counter is not tied to a hand: naming a slot only chooses which item's use time is used and which hand must hold something.

**Older packs.** Content whose Molang version is below 1.17.30 gets a legacy variant: without arguments it returns ticks left x 20, and the normalized forms return the *elapsed* fraction `(1 - clamp(ticks left / U, 0, 1)) * s` instead of the remaining one.

args.onInvalid: a string in second position: content-log error, returns 0

queries.formula: none: `r / 20`; slot only: `r * 20`; with scale `s`: `clamp(r / U, 0, 1) * s` (legacy: `(1 - clamp(r / U, 0, 1)) * s`)
queries.units: seconds (no argument); ticks x 20 (slot only); scale units (normalized)
queries.range: [0, U / 20] seconds with no argument; [0, s] when normalized

The fraction counts down (1 at the start of the use, 0 at the end); in packs older than 1.17.30 it counts up.

queries.name: item_slot_to_bone_name
queries.summary: Bone name for a hand slot: 'main_hand' -> 'rightitem', 'off_hand' -> 'leftitem'
queries.hover:
`q.item_slot_to_bone_name(slot)` - string: 'main_hand' gives 'rightitem', 'off_hand' gives 'leftitem', any other string is returned unchanged.
It does not look at the model; the mapping is fixed.
Needs an owning entity; a missing or non-string argument logs an error and returns ''.
queries.description: Turns a hand slot name into the name of the bone that held items attach to: `'main_hand'` becomes `'rightitem'` and `'off_hand'` becomes `'leftitem'`. Any other string is passed through unchanged.
queries.long:
Returns the bone name that an item held in the given slot is attached to. The mapping is fixed:

| argument | result |
|---|---|
| `'main_hand'` | `'rightitem'` |
| `'off_hand'` | `'leftitem'` |
| any other string | the same string, unchanged |

The entity's model is not consulted, so the result does not tell you whether the bone exists. Vanilla uses the query in attachable geometry, as the `binding` of the root bone together with the `c.item_slot` context variable, so that an item model follows whichever hand holds it.

**Failures.** If the context has no owning entity (an attachable item that nobody is holding), if the argument is missing, or if it is not a string, an error is written to the content log and the result is the empty string `''`. The owning-entity check comes first: without an entity every call, even `q.item_slot_to_bone_name('main_hand')`, logs the missing-owner error and returns `''`. Only the first argument is used: `('main_hand', 'x')` still gives `'rightitem'`. The match is exact: `'MAIN_HAND'` or `'slot.weapon.mainhand'` come back unchanged.

whenUnavailable.when: no owning entity (for example an attachable without a holder)

queries.name: key_frame_lerp_time
queries.summary: Progress between the surrounding keyframes, 0 to 1, inside keyframe values
queries.hover:
Inside a keyframe value: how far the animation time is from the previous keyframe to the next, 0 to 1.
Written while a bone channel is interpolated between two keyframes; anywhere else it returns a leftover value, not 0.
Keyframes closer than 0.000001 s give 1.
queries.description: Gives how far the animation has moved from the previous keyframe toward the next one, as a fraction from 0 to 1. It is meant to be read in the value expressions of those keyframes.
queries.long:
Returns the interpolation fraction of the keyframe segment currently being evaluated:

`(t - t_prev) / (t_next - t_prev)`

where `t` is the animation time and `t_prev`, `t_next` are the times of the keyframes on either side. It is `0` at the previous keyframe and approaches `1` at the next. If the two keyframes are less than 0.000001 seconds apart the value is `1`.

The value is written by the animation system each time it interpolates a bone channel (rotation, position or scale) between two keyframes, just before it evaluates the Molang in those keyframes. It is therefore meaningful only inside keyframe values - vanilla's sheep uses it in the `pre`/`post` values of its grazing head rotation to add a wobble across the segment.

Elsewhere - in a channel with a single keyframe, before the first or after the last keyframe, in animation controllers, render controllers - the query returns a leftover value from an earlier keyframe evaluation, not `0`. The leftover is not tied to the entity being evaluated: outside entity rendering the same value (about 0.88) was read for the player and with no entity at all, and it stayed constant for seconds. Treat any read outside keyframe values as meaningless.
queries.formula: `(t - t_prev) / (t_next - t_prev)`; `1` when `t_next - t_prev < 0.000001`

appliesTo.entities: any entity being animated; only meaningful inside keyframe values

whenUnavailable.when: read outside the interpolation of a keyframe segment (also with no entity, on the client)
whenUnavailable.value: a leftover value from an earlier keyframe evaluation

pitfalls: Read in an animation controller or a render controller it returns a stale value from an earlier keyframe evaluation, possibly of another entity.
It is the progress of the segment, not of the whole animation (use `query.anim_time` for that).

queries.name: last_frame_time
queries.summary: Length of a recent rendered frame in seconds (0 = the latest, up to 29 back)
queries.hover:
`q.last_frame_time(n?)` - seconds between two consecutive entity-render passes, n frames back (default 0 = the latest).
Only 30 frames are kept and n wraps around: 30 reads the same as 0. n is truncated; negatives act as 0.
Needs the renderer: 0 in behavior packs and outside rendering.
queries.description: Gives how long one of the recently drawn frames lasted, in seconds. With no argument (or 0) it is the latest one; a number n looks n frames further back, up to 29.
queries.long:
Returns how long a recent frame took, in seconds. The game keeps a ring of the last 30 frame durations; each one is the real time that passed between two consecutive passes that draw the entities, measured when the next pass starts. So with no argument the query returns the interval that ended at the frame being drawn now - the previous frame's duration.

**Argument.** `n` selects a frame `n` steps further back: `0` (or no argument) is the latest, `1` the one before it, up to `29`. The number is truncated to a whole number and negative numbers act as `0`. The ring has only 30 slots and the index wraps around, so `30` reads the same frame as `0`, `31` the same as `1`, and so on - asking for older frames never returns an error. Extra arguments are ignored.

**Where it works.** The value comes from the renderer, so the query only answers while an entity is being rendered on a client (client entities, attachables, entity particles). In behavior packs, and in any evaluation that happens outside rendering, it returns `0`.

`query.average_frame_time`, `query.minimum_frame_time` and `query.maximum_frame_time` summarise the same 30-frame history.

args.description: How many frames before the latest one
accepts: number; truncated toward zero, negatives act as 0
values of 30 or more wrap around (n mod 30)

queries.formula: `history[(latest - (n mod 30)) mod 30]`

appliesTo.entities: any; the value is shared by everything drawn by the same view

whenUnavailable.when: no render in progress (behavior packs, evaluation outside rendering)

timing.updates: per frame (at the start of entity rendering)

pitfalls: Asking for 30 or more frames back wraps around to recent frames instead of returning the oldest one.

queries.name: last_hit_by_player
queries.summary: Whether a player hurt the entity recently (server side only)
queries.hover:
1 if a player hurt the entity within about the last 20 seconds (400 ticks), else 0.
Server only: every client evaluation returns 0, so it belongs in behavior packs (loot, experience).
0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 when a player has hurt the entity recently, and 0 otherwise. The information is kept on the server only, so client-side evaluation always returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity remembers being hurt by a player, and `0` otherwise.

When a player hurts the entity, a counter on it is set to 400 ticks (20 seconds); the query reads `1` while that counter is above zero. A new hit by a player restarts it. Damage from other sources is not known to clear it, so "last" most likely means "recently", not "most recently" (not yet verified in game).

The counter lives on the server. When the query runs on a client (resource packs) it returns `0` without looking - also right after a player's punch that visibly took health off the mob. Vanilla uses it in behavior packs so that a mob only drops experience on death when a player was involved.

Without an entity it returns `0`. How quickly the counter runs down (one per tick is assumed) is not yet verified.

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Always 0 in resource packs.

queries.name: last_input_mode_is_any
queries.summary: Whether the player's most recent input device is one of the listed kinds
queries.hover:
`q.last_input_mode_is_any('keyboard_and_mouse' | 'touch' | 'gamepad', ...)` - 1 if the local player's last input device is any listed kind, else 0.
Resource packs only: in behavior packs, world particles or without an entity it logs an error and returns 0.
Describes this device's player, not the entity the expression runs on.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the kind of input the local player used most recently (keyboard and mouse, touch or gamepad) is one of the names you pass, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Compares the local player's current input kind with a list of names and returns `1` on the first match, `0` if none match.

| name | input kind |
|---|---|
| `'keyboard_and_mouse'` | keyboard and mouse |
| `'touch'` | touch screen |
| `'gamepad'` | controller |

Names are matched exactly (lower case, with underscores). Any other string simply never matches; there is no name for other input kinds, and when the game reports no known input kind (for example right after start-up) nothing matches.

The answer comes from the player sitting at this device, whatever entity the expression is attached to - every entity in a resource pack sees the same value on a given device, and two players in the same world see their own input kinds.

**Where it works.** Only in client-side entity rendering (client entities, attachables, entity-bound particles). With no arguments, in a world particle, without an entity, or when evaluated by the server (behavior packs), it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`.

Tools that evaluate expressions outside entity rendering hit the same error on every call, even with an entity target.

**Arguments** are read left to right and the first match returns `1` at once. An argument that is not a string logs an error and returns `0` - but only if the names before it did not match. Written without arguments (`q.last_input_mode_is_any`) it logs an error and returns `0`; empty parentheses are a syntax error.

args.description: Input kind to test; repeat to list several
args.onInvalid: non-string argument reached during matching: content-log error, returns 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity or not rendering (world particles, animation evaluated outside rendering)
a non-string argument is reached before any match
the local player's input information is not available yet

queries.name: leashed_entity_count
queries.summary: How many entities are leashed to this entity
queries.hover:
Number of entities currently tied by a lead to this entity (a whole number, 0 or more).
Counts the entities this one holds, not whether this one is leashed.
Clients see the count too (a wandering trader leading its two llamas reads 2); 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns how many entities are currently attached by a lead to this entity as their holder, or 0 if none.
queries.long:
Returns the number of entities whose lead is held by this entity - for a player, the mobs they are leading; for a fence knot, the mobs tied to that post. The result is a whole number, `0` when nothing is attached.

It looks at the holder's side of the lead only. To ask whether the entity itself is on a lead use `query.is_leashed`; to test the types of the attached entities use `query.has_any_leashed_entity_of_type`.

The count is read from the holder's list of leashed entities at the moment of evaluation, so it changes as soon as a lead is attached or breaks. Clients keep that list too: measured in resource-pack context, a player leading one cow reads `1`, a wandering trader with its two llamas reads `2`, and the leashed animals themselves read `0`. A fence knot as the holder has not been measured yet. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity that can hold leads (players, fence knots, mobs)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A leashed mob returns 0 here unless it is itself holding other leads; use q.is_leashed for that.

queries.name: lie_amount
queries.summary: Panda only: how far it has rolled onto its back, 0 to 1, smoothed per frame
queries.hover:
Pandas only: 0 (upright) to 1 (fully on its back), smoothed between ticks with the frame's partial tick.
Rises by 0.15 per tick while the panda is laying down and falls by 0.19 per tick otherwise.
Every other entity - including cats - always returns 0.
queries.description: For pandas, returns how far the lying-on-its-back pose has progressed, from 0 to 1, interpolated between ticks. Every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Works only on pandas. It returns a blend weight from `0` (upright) to `1` (lying fully on its back) that the vanilla panda animations use to roll the body over.

Each game tick the panda's lie amount moves toward its target:

| panda state | change per tick |
|---|---|
| laying down | `+0.15`, up to `1` |
| otherwise | `-0.19`, down to `0` |

So it takes 7 ticks to roll fully onto the back and 6 ticks to get up again. The query blends the previous tick's value into the current one using the frame's partial tick, so the pose moves smoothly each frame:

`lie = prev + (current - prev) * frame_alpha`

Both stored values are clamped to `[0, 1]` before blending.

The "laying down" state is the same one reported by `query.is_laying_down`.

For any entity that is not a panda, and without an entity, the query returns `0`. Outside rendering the frame blend has no partial tick to use and the query reads the plain per-tick values (measured: 0.15, 0.6, 1 while rolling over; 1, 0.62, 0.05, 0 while getting up). What it returns on the server is not yet verified.
queries.formula: `prev + (cur - prev) * frame_alpha`, with `prev` and `cur` the last two per-tick values, each in [0, 1]

appliesTo.entities: pandas; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Only pandas have it: a cat, fox or custom entity always returns 0, even while lying down.
It is not a 0/1 flag; test `> 0` for "started lying down" and `>= 1` for "fully on its back".

queries.name: life_span
queries.summary: Ticks left before a limited-lifetime entity disappears; 0 if unlimited
queries.hover:
Remaining lifetime in ticks for entities created with a limited lifetime (evoker fangs, summoned spell entities); 0 for everything else.
Counts down each tick; when it runs out the entity is removed.
Clients see it count down, but faster (about 2 per tick measured for fangs) - do not time animations on it.
queries.description: For entities that were given a limited lifetime, returns how many ticks they have left before they are removed. Entities with no limit return 0.
queries.long:
Some entities are created with a fixed lifetime and removed automatically when it runs out: evoker fangs (22 ticks) and entities summoned by the summon-entity behavior when it is configured with a lifetime. For those, the query returns the number of ticks remaining.

The counter is decreased by one every tick; when it would drop below one the entity is removed. Entities without a limited lifetime - which is almost all of them - return `0`, and so does the query without an entity.

Because the value counts down, it is not the entity's age: use `query.life_time` for the time since the entity was created (in seconds).

**On the client** (resource packs) the value does change, but not in step with the server: measured on an evoker fang it read `0` before the fang's first tick, then `16` at an age of about 4 ticks, `12` at about 6 and `4` at about 10 - roughly two per tick - and the fang was gone from the client after about 11 ticks. The vanilla evoker fang resource pack computes its own remaining time from the age, which is the safer pattern.

appliesTo.entities: entities with a limited lifetime (evoker fangs, summoned spell entities); all others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: It is the time left, not the total lifetime - it decreases every tick where the entity is simulated.
In resource packs it reads 0 at first and then falls about twice as fast as on the server.
Units are ticks (20 per second), while query.life_time is in seconds.

queries.name: life_time
queries.summary: Seconds since the entity appeared on this client (smooth, per frame)
queries.hover:
How long, in seconds, the entity has existed on this client - a smooth clock that never goes backwards.
Restarts when the entity is loaded again (e.g. re-entering render distance).
Not animation time. Holds its last value while the entity is off screen. Resource-pack Molang only; 0 elsewhere.
queries.description: A per-entity clock in seconds: how long the entity has existed on this client. It advances smoothly from frame to frame and never goes backwards.
queries.long:
A clock that starts when the entity is created on the client and counts up in seconds. It is the usual choice for idle motions that should run continuously, such as the blaze's orbiting rods or a bee's bobbing.

Each rendered frame it catches up with the entity's tick counter: the new value is `(ticks + partial tick) / 20`, and it only ever moves forward. It is only refreshed while the entity is drawn: while the entity is off screen the value holds still, and it jumps to the true count as soon as the entity is in view again. An entity that has not been drawn since it loaded reads `0`.

Because the count starts when the client creates the entity, it restarts from `0` after the entity is reloaded - for example when you walk out of render distance and back, or rejoin the world. It is not the entity's total age and it is not shared between players.

Despite what some references say, it has nothing to do with the current animation: every animation of the entity sees the same value.

Particles, blocks and server-side Molang read `0`.
queries.formula: `max(previous, (entity ticks + frame_alpha) / 20)`
pitfalls: Not animation time - use `query.anim_time` for the animation's own clock.
Restarts when the entity is reloaded; two players can see different values for the same entity.
It is not a continuous clock for entities out of view: it freezes off screen and jumps when seen again.

queries.name: lod_index
queries.summary: Which distance band the entity is in, counted from the camera
queries.hover:
`q.lod_index(d0, d1, ...)` - how many of the listed distances (blocks) the camera distance is beyond, counting from the first until one is not passed.
`q.lod_index(8, 24, 48)` gives 0 up to 8 blocks, 1 up to 24, 2 up to 48, 3 past that. Exactly on a boundary falls in the nearer band.
No arguments returns 0; list the distances from nearest to farthest.
queries.description: Takes a list of distances in blocks and returns the index of the first one that the camera distance does not exceed, or the number of distances when it exceeds them all.
queries.long:
Used to pick a level of detail from how far the entity is from the camera. Pass distances in blocks, nearest first; the result is the index of the band the entity is in:

| camera distance `d` | `q.lod_index(8, 24, 48)` |
|---|---|
| `d <= 8` | `0` |
| `8 < d <= 24` | `1` |
| `24 < d <= 48` | `2` |
| `d > 48` | `3` |

**How it counts.** The distances are checked in order and the count goes up by one for each distance the camera distance is greater than; the first distance that is not exceeded stops the count. The list is not sorted for you: with `q.lod_index(40, 12)` an entity 20 blocks away returns `0`, because the first distance already stops the count.

The camera distance is the same value `query.distance_from_camera` returns, measured by the renderer each frame. Where no camera distance has been measured it is `0`: evaluated outside entity rendering, `q.lod_index(10, 20, 30)` and `q.lod_index(30, 10)` both return `0` and only a negative first distance gives `1` (measured on the client; the server is expected to behave the same).

Written without arguments (`q.lod_index`) the result is `0`; empty parentheses are a syntax error. The query never writes to the content log.

args.name: distance
args.description: Band limit in blocks; repeat, nearest first

queries.formula: count of leading distances `d_i` with `camera_distance > d_i`
queries.range: whole numbers from 0 to the number of distances

appliesTo.entities: any rendered entity

whenUnavailable.when: no camera distance measured (outside entity rendering, server)

pitfalls: The list is not sorted: an out-of-order distance stops the count early.
Exactly on a boundary counts as the nearer band (`d == 8` gives 0 for `q.lod_index(8, 24)`).
Outside entity rendering there is no camera distance; the result is 0 for any non-negative list.

queries.name: log
queries.summary: Debug helper: prints its arguments to the content log and returns the first
queries.hover:
`q.log(value, ...)` - writes every argument as a number to the content log and returns the first one unchanged.
Logs every time it is evaluated - per frame in animations. `q.log` alone returns 0 and logs nothing.
queries.description: A debugging aid: writes the values of its arguments to the content log and passes the first argument through as its result, so it can wrap any sub-expression.
queries.long:
Evaluates its arguments, writes them to the content log as one line, and returns the first argument's value. Because the value passes through, you can wrap part of an expression without changing what it computes:

```
v.speed = q.log(q.ground_speed) * 2;
```

**Output format.** Each argument is converted to a number and printed with six decimals, separated by single spaces - `q.log(1, 2.5)` writes `1.000000 2.500000`. There is no label, so add a constant as a marker when you log from several places (`q.log(101, v.a)`). Strings are not printed as text: a string argument is turned into a meaningless large number derived from the string, and that number is also what `q.log('abc')` returns (the empty string gives `0`).

**Arguments.** Any number of arguments is accepted. Written without arguments (`q.log`) nothing is written and the result is `0`; empty parentheses are a syntax error.

The line is written on every evaluation. In a client entity or animation that is once per frame per entity, which floods the log quickly; remove it once you are done. It works in every context, on both client and server. Whether the line is visible also depends on the content-log level settings (not yet verified).

args.name: value
args.description: Value to print and return; further arguments are printed only
accepts: any number of further arguments (printed, not returned)

appliesTo.entities: none needed

pitfalls: It logs on every evaluation - in a per-frame expression that is a line per frame per entity.
Strings are printed (and returned) as a large number, not as text.
Only the first argument is returned; `q.log(1, 5)` evaluates to 1.

queries.name: main_hand_item_max_duration
queries.summary: How long the held item can be used in one go, in ticks (0 if not usable)
queries.hover:
Maximum use time in ticks of the item in the entity's main hand (players: the selected hotbar slot).
0 for an empty hand or an item that is not used over time; 0 without an entity.
Pairs with q.main_hand_item_use_duration, which counts down from this value.
queries.description: Returns how many ticks the item in the main hand can be used continuously (drawing a bow, eating, blocking). Items that are not used over time, an empty hand and a missing entity give 0.
queries.long:
Returns the item's own maximum use time, in ticks, for the item held in the main hand. For players the main hand is the selected hotbar slot; for other mobs it is their main-hand equipment.

Only items that are "used over time" have a value. Measured vanilla values:

| item | value (ticks) |
|---|---|
| bow, trident, spyglass, wooden sword | `72000` (held as long as you like) |
| crossbow | `25` |
| bread, water bottle | `32` |
| shield, stick, empty hand | `0` |

A shield reads `0` even though it can be raised. The number is a property of the item, not of what the entity is doing: it is the same whether or not the item is being used right now.

Together with `query.main_hand_item_use_duration` it gives use progress: while an item is in use that query counts down from this maximum, so `max - use` is the number of ticks the item has been held in use.

appliesTo.entities: players and mobs with a main-hand item

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
item is not used over time

pitfalls: It does not tell you whether the item is being used; it is non-zero for a bow sitting in the hand.
A shield reads 0, so it cannot be used to detect blocking.
Offhand items are never considered.

queries.name: main_hand_item_use_duration
queries.summary: Players: ticks left in the current item use, counting down to 0
queries.hover:
Players only: ticks remaining in the current item use (eating, drawing a bow, ...), counting down each tick.
Starts near q.main_hand_item_max_duration and falls to 0; 0 when nothing is being used or the main hand is empty.
Every non-player entity always returns 0.
queries.description: For players, returns how many ticks are left in the item use that is in progress. It starts at the item's maximum use time when the use begins and decreases by one per tick. Other entities return 0.
queries.long:
While a player is using an item - eating, drinking, drawing a bow, charging a crossbow or trident, raising a shield - the game keeps a countdown of the ticks left in that use. This query returns that countdown.

- When the use starts the countdown is set to the length of the use (normally the item's maximum use time, see `query.main_hand_item_max_duration`).
- Each tick it goes down by one and stops at `0`.
- When the player stops using the item it disappears and the query returns `0`.

So the number of ticks the item has been in use is `q.main_hand_item_max_duration - q.main_hand_item_use_duration`. Vanilla bow charging is built this way, subtracting the frame's partial tick to smooth it.

Only players have this countdown; every other entity returns `0`, even a skeleton drawing its bow. The query also returns `0` whenever the player's main hand is empty. The countdown belongs to the item use in progress, which is not necessarily the main-hand item (for example a shield raised in the offhand); how that case reads is not yet verified.

Measured while drawing a bow: `72000` before any tick of use, then `71998`, `71995`, ... one less per tick, and `0` again the moment the button is released.

appliesTo.entities: players only; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: It counts down, not up: a freshly drawn bow reads a large number that shrinks.
Mobs using items (skeletons, drowned, piglins) always read 0.
It steps once per tick; subtract q.frame_alpha for smooth per-frame progress.

queries.name: mark_variant
queries.summary: The entity's mark variant number (set by minecraft:mark_variant)
queries.hover:
Whole number from the entity's minecraft:mark_variant component (0 when never set).
Vanilla uses it for horse markings, villager biome skins and bee stingers; its meaning is up to each entity.
Kept by the server and shared with clients; 0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns the whole number stored as the entity's mark variant, normally set by the `minecraft:mark_variant` component in its behavior definition, or 0 when it was never set.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's mark variant: a whole number that the behavior pack sets through the `minecraft:mark_variant` component (usually from a component group chosen at spawn) and that the resource pack reads to pick textures or geometry. It is a companion to `query.variant` and `query.skin_id`; each stores its own independent number.

The number has no fixed meaning - it is whatever the entity's definition assigns. In vanilla, for example, horses use it for their white markings, villagers for their biome outfit, and bees to show that the stinger is gone.

An entity that never had a mark variant set returns `0` (measured: pig, zombie, wandering trader, a baby horse; an adult horse with markings read `4`); the query without an entity returns `0`. The value is synchronised to clients, so it can be read in both behavior and resource packs.

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

queries.name: max_durability
queries.summary: Maximum durability of the item being evaluated (item expressions only)
queries.hover:
Maximum durability of the item the expression is evaluated for, as set by its minecraft:durability component.
Only where an item is the subject (e.g. repair amounts, attachables); elsewhere it logs an error and returns 0.
Items without a durability component return 0 silently.
queries.description: Returns the maximum durability of the item the expression belongs to, such as in an item's repair amount. Items without durability give 0; using it where there is no item logs an error.
queries.long:
Returns how much damage the current item can take before it breaks - the `max_durability` of its `minecraft:durability` component.

It only has an item to look at where the expression is evaluated for an item: the `repair_amount` expressions of `minecraft:repairable` (vanilla spears repair a quarter of it), and attachables, where the item is the one being drawn. In any other place - client entities, particles, animations that are not on an attachable - it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`.

An item that has no durability component (a stick, a block) returns `0` without logging. The same happens for items whose durability is not defined through the data-driven durability component; whether that applies to any current vanilla tool or armour piece is not yet verified.

whenUnavailable.when: item without a data-driven durability component

Returns the maximum value of the entity's health, as set by its `minecraft:health` component (`max`, or `value` when no max is given). A player normally reads `20`, a zombie `20`, an iron golem `100`.

The value is rounded **up** to a whole number, so a maximum of `20.5` reads `21`. Entities that have no health attribute return `0` (in vanilla, those whose definition has no health, such as arrows and minecarts), and so do a maximum of `0` or less and the query without an entity.

Effects that raise the maximum are included: Health Boost II takes a player from `20` to `28` (while `query.health` stays at `20`). Measured: armor stand `6`, dropped item `0`. For the current health use `query.health`.

queries.name: max_trade_tier
queries.summary: Highest trade tier index in a trader's trade table (0 for non-traders)

Index of the last tier in the entity's trade table: a table with 5 tiers gives 4 (tiers counted from 0).
Fixed by the trade table, not by how much the villager has traded - use q.trade_tier for the current level.

queries.description: For trading entities, returns the index of the highest tier in their trade table (number of tiers minus 1). Entities that do not trade return 0.
queries.long:
Traders unlock their trades in tiers (novice, apprentice, journeyman, expert, master for villagers). This query returns the index of the **last** tier in the entity's trade table, counting from `0`:

`max_trade_tier = number of tiers in the trade table - 1`

A standard villager profession with five tiers therefore returns `4` from the moment it gets its profession, no matter how much it has traded. The tier the villager has actually reached is reported by `query.trade_tier`, which never goes above this value.

queries.name: maximum_frame_time
queries.summary: Duration of the slowest recent frame, in seconds
queries.hover:

queries.description: Returns, in seconds, how long the slowest of the most recent frames took. With no argument only the latest frame is considered; with `n` the latest `n + 1` frames.

Looks at the times of recent frames and returns the slowest one, in seconds:

- `q.maximum_frame_time` or `q.maximum_frame_time(0)`: the most recent frame's time on its own.
- `q.maximum_frame_time(n)`: the slowest of the latest `n + 1` frames.

The game remembers the last 30 frames, so `n` is limited to `29`; larger numbers behave as `29`. The argument is truncated to a whole number and negative numbers act as `0`. Only the first argument is used.

Frame times are measured once per rendered frame on this device and are the same for every entity. The value is only available while the client is rendering: evaluated by the server or outside rendering it returns `0` without an error. Right after the game starts, fewer than 30 frames have been recorded and the missing ones may count as 0 (not yet verified).

Compare `query.last_frame_time`, `query.average_frame_time` and `query.minimum_frame_time`, which read the same history.
