queries.name: modified_distance_moved
queries.summary: Walk-cycle counter: grows with horizontal movement, about 4 per block at walking pace
queries.hover:
Walk-cycle phase of a mob: grows by about 4 per block walked, never more than 1 per tick.
Faster when burning or hurt (x1.5), slower while jumping (x0.35), frozen while riding.
Not a distance in blocks. Smoothed between ticks; 0 for non-mob entities.
queries.description: A running counter that drives walk and run cycles. It grows with the mob's horizontal movement - about 4 units per block at walking pace, capped at 1 unit per tick - and is adjusted by the mob's condition.
queries.long:
A counter that advances as a mob moves, used as the phase of leg and arm swing animations (`math.cos(q.modified_distance_moved * 38.17)` is the classic leg swing).

It is **not** a distance in blocks. Every tick the game computes a *swing speed* and adds it to the counter:

1. `d` = horizontal distance moved this tick (blocks).
2. target = `min(0.4, 1.6 * d)` while moving (a rule for turning in place, `min(0.2, 0.02 * |body yaw change in degrees|)`, is not yet verified: turning in place did not advance the counter in our tests).
3. multiplier `k` = `1`, times `1.5` if the mob is on fire or was just hurt, times `0.35` while it jumps.
4. swing speed = `0.6 * previous swing speed + k * target`, and the counter grows by the new swing speed.

At a steady pace the swing speed settles at `k * min(1, 4 * d)`, so walking adds about **4 units per block** and anything faster than 5 blocks per second is capped at **1 unit per tick** (20 per second).

While the mob rides another entity the swing speed is reset to 0 and the counter stops.

Babies advance the counter at the same rate as adults for the same ground speed (their `query.modified_move_speed` reads 1.5 times higher, though). A hit makes the swing speed jump even when the mob stands still, so the limbs kick briefly, and in that tick the smoothed value can step back slightly.

The value you read is smoothed between the last two ticks using the frame's partial tick, so it moves continuously from frame to frame. `query.modified_move_speed` returns the swing speed itself.

The counter starts at 0 whenever the entity is created or loaded, and it only advances for mobs; other entities stay at 0.
queries.formula: per tick: `s' = 0.6 s + k * (d > 0 ? min(0.4, 1.6 d) : min(0.2, 0.02 |Δyaw°|))`, `D' = D + s'`; read value `D' - s' * (1 - frame_alpha)`
queries.range: 0 and up, increases by at most 1 per tick at k = 1

appliesTo.entities: mobs; other entities stay at 0

pitfalls: Do not use it as an odometer: the scale is about 4 per block and it saturates at 1 per tick.
It can briefly decrease by a small amount in the tick a mob is hit; do not assume it is monotonic.
It restarts from 0 when the entity is reloaded.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: modified_move_speed
queries.summary: Mob walk-cycle speed, 0 to 1 (1.5 for babies), smoothed per frame
queries.hover:
Walk-animation speed of a mob, smoothed per frame: 0 standing, 1 at about 5 blocks/s and faster.
Capped at 1, then multiplied by 1.5 for babies (so 0..1.5). Burning or recent hurt only shows below the cap.
Non-mobs and riders read 0.
queries.description: Returns the per-tick amount by which the mob's walk cycle advances, blended between the last two ticks, capped at 1 and scaled by 1.5 for babies. It is the usual driver for the strength of leg-swing animations.
queries.long:
Returns how fast the mob's walk cycle is advancing - the per-tick step that `query.modified_distance_moved` adds up. It is roughly proportional to horizontal speed: about `4 x` the blocks moved per tick while walking, reaching `1` at about 5 blocks per second.

The value is computed each frame as:

1. `s = prev + (cur - prev) * frame_alpha` - the last two per-tick speeds blended with the frame's partial tick, so it changes smoothly.
2. `s = min(s, 1)`.
3. Babies: `s * 1.5`.

So adults stay within `[0, 1]` and babies within `[0, 1.5]`, which makes baby legs swing faster.

The per-tick speed itself (see `query.modified_distance_moved` for the full rule) moves toward `min(1, 4 x blocks per tick)`; it is multiplied by 1.5 while the mob is on fire or was just hurt and by 0.35 while it is jumping. The cap in step 2 is applied after those factors, so the on-fire boost is only visible while the mob moves slowly.

While the mob rides another entity the speed is reset to `0`. Only mobs have a walk cycle; other entities and the query without an entity return `0`.
queries.formula: `min(1, lerp(prev, cur, frame_alpha)) * (baby ? 1.5 : 1)`

appliesTo.entities: mobs; other entities always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Babies go up to 1.5, not 1 - clamp if an animation assumes [0, 1].
It is not a speed in blocks per second; it saturates at about 5 blocks per second.
A mob riding another entity reads 0 even while its mount moves.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: modified_swing_duration
queries.summary: Seconds one arm swing takes for this mob, after item and effects
queries.hover:
`q.modified_swing_duration` - length of one arm swing in seconds (6 ticks = 0.3 by default).
Haste or Conduit Power shorten it by 1 tick per level; Mining Fatigue lengthens it by 2 ticks per level.
Mobs and players only; other entities 0. Strong Haste can make it 0 or negative.
queries.description: Length of one arm swing in seconds: 0.3 by default, set by a swing_duration item, shortened by Haste or Conduit Power and lengthened by Mining Fatigue. Non-mobs read 0.
queries.long:
Returns the length of one arm swing in **seconds**. The engine works in ticks and the query divides by 20 at the end, so the result is always a multiple of `0.05`.

**Base length** comes from the item in the main hand:

| held item | base swing |
|---|---|
| nothing, or an item without a swing setting | 6 ticks (0.3 s) |
| an item with the `minecraft:swing_duration` component | the component's value in seconds, converted to ticks by dropping any fraction of a tick |

**Effects** then adjust the tick count:

- **Haste** or **Conduit Power**: subtract the effect level (amplifier + 1). If both are active, only the higher level counts. When either is present, Mining Fatigue is ignored.
- **Mining Fatigue** (only without Haste/Conduit Power): add `2 × level`.

There is no lower limit: Haste VI on a default 6-tick swing gives `0`, and higher levels give negative values. Clamp the result if you use it as a divisor or animation length.

Only mobs (including players) have a swing; any other entity, or no entity, returns `0`.
queries.formula: (base_ticks - max(haste_level, conduit_level)) / 20, or (base_ticks + 2 x fatigue_level) / 20 when neither is active
queries.range: multiples of 0.05; 0.3 by default; no lower bound

appliesTo.entities: mobs and players; other entities 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity is not a mob (items, projectiles, boats...)

timing.updates: on read (reads held item and effects)

pitfalls: The value is in seconds, not ticks: the default is 0.3.
Haste VI or higher makes it 0 or negative - clamp before dividing by it.
With both Haste and Mining Fatigue active, Mining Fatigue has no effect on the result.

queries.name: moon_brightness
queries.summary: Moon brightness for the current phase: 1 at full moon down to 0 at new moon
queries.hover:
`q.moon_brightness` - 1.0 full, 0.75 gibbous, 0.5 quarter, 0.25 crescent, 0.0 new moon.
Follows the overworld day counter, so it gives the same value in the Nether and the End.
Needs an entity; 0 without one.
queries.description: A 0-to-1 light level looked up from the moon phase: 1 at full moon, 0 at new moon, in steps of 0.25.
queries.long:
Returns the moon's brightness as a number between `0` and `1`, looked up from the current moon phase (see `query.moon_phase`):

| phase | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| brightness | 1.0 | 0.75 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 0.0 | 0.25 | 0.5 | 0.75 |

The phase comes from the world's overworld day counter, not from the dimension the entity is in, so an entity in the Nether or the End reads the same value as one in the overworld. The value changes only when a new day starts; it is not blended between phases.

The query needs an entity to find the world through; without one it returns `0`, which is the same as a new moon - check for an entity first if the difference matters.
queries.formula: table[moon_phase]

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

timing.updates: on change of the day counter

pitfalls: Without an entity it returns 0, the same value as a new moon.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.name: moon_phase
queries.summary: Moon phase index 0-7 (0 = full moon, 4 = new moon)
queries.hover:
`q.moon_phase` - whole number 0..7: 0 is the full moon, 4 the new moon, the others the phases between.
Advances by one each in-game day from the overworld clock; same value in every dimension.
Needs an entity; 0 (full moon) without one.
queries.description: Whole number 0-7 that advances once per in-game day on the overworld clock; 0 is a full moon, 4 a new moon.
queries.long:
Returns the moon phase as an integer in `0..7`. It is the number of whole days the overworld clock has counted, modulo 8:

`phase = floor(clock / 24000) mod 8`

`0` is the full moon and `4` the new moon; the moon thins over phases 1-3 and fills again over 5-7 (`query.moon_brightness` gives the matching light level).

The phase advances when the clock passes a multiple of 24000 ticks, which is time `0` of each day as `/time set` counts it - sunrise, not midnight. `/time set` takes the full clock including the day count, so `/time set 0` gives phase `0`, `/time set 95999` phase `3` and `/time set 96000` phase `4`; `/time add 24000` advances the phase by one, and after phase `7` it wraps to `0` (measured).

The clock is always the overworld's, so entities in the Nether and the End read the same phase. The query needs an entity to reach the world; without one it returns `0`, indistinguishable from a full moon.
queries.formula: floor(clock / 24000) mod 8

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

timing.updates: on change of the day counter

pitfalls: Without an entity it returns 0, the same value as a full moon.
The phase changes at sunrise (time 0 of the day), not at midnight.

queries.name: movement_direction
queries.summary: One axis of the direction the entity moved last tick (unit vector)
queries.hover:
`q.movement_direction(axis)` - x (0), y (1) or z (2) of the entity's last movement as a unit vector, -1..1.
Includes vertical movement. 0 on every axis when the entity barely moved.
Axis is truncated to a whole number; 3 or more logs an error. Client side, only the local player has a movement.
queries.description: Returns one component of the direction the entity moved during the last tick, as a vector of length 1. Vertical movement is part of the vector, so it is a 3D direction.
queries.long:
Takes the change in the entity's position over the last tick, scales it to length 1, and returns the component you ask for: `0` for x, `1` for y, `2` for z. Each component is in `[-1, 1]`, and the three components together always describe a unit vector - so climbing or falling reduces the horizontal components.

When the entity moved less than 0.0001 blocks during the tick, every component is `0` instead of an unstable direction.

**Argument.** The axis is converted to a whole number by dropping the fractional part (`1.9` selects y). Values between -1 and 0 select x. Do not pass negative whole numbers: their conversion differs between platforms, and on Windows `-1` is rejected like an out-of-range axis. `3` or more writes an error to the content log and returns `0`; so does calling the query with no argument or with more than one.

**What counts as movement.** For the local player the movement includes the small downward step gravity adds every tick, even on the ground: standing still reads `y = -1`, and walking on flat ground tilts the vector down (about `y = -0.55` at walking pace). In resource-pack Molang other entities - mobs, for example - have no per-tick movement on the client, so every axis reads `0` even while they walk or fall.

The value changes once per tick and is not smoothed between frames. To get the speed rather than the direction, use `query.position_delta` or `query.ground_speed`.

args.name: axis
accepts: negative whole numbers: platform-dependent (Windows: content-log error, 0)
args.onInvalid: 3 or more: content-log error, returns 0

queries.formula: `normalize(p_now - p_prev)[axis]`; `0` when `|p_now - p_prev| < 0.0001`

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: any entity other than the local player, in resource-pack Molang

pitfalls: It is a 3D direction: horizontal components shrink while the entity climbs or falls.
Negative axes are not portable: on Windows `q.movement_direction(-1)` logs an out-of-range error.
A grounded local player never reads `y = 0`: standing still gives -1 because gravity is part of the movement.
Client side, mobs always read 0 on every axis; only the local player has a movement there.
It gives direction only; a slow and a fast entity moving the same way return the same values.

queries.name: noise
queries.summary: 2D simplex noise at (x, z), fixed seed, about -1..1 (world generation only)
queries.hover:
`q.noise(x, z)` - smooth 2D simplex noise, roughly -1..1; features are about 1 input unit wide.
The pattern is fixed: it does not depend on the world seed, so every world gets the same noise.
Exactly two arguments, otherwise 0 with no error. World-generation expressions only.
queries.description: Samples a smooth 2D simplex noise field at the given x and z and returns a value of about -1 to 1. The field is the same in every world.
queries.long:
Returns a smooth pseudo-random value for the point `(x, z)`, taken from a single layer of 2D simplex noise. Nearby points give similar values; the bumps of the field are about one unit across, so multiply the coordinates by a small factor (for example `q.noise(v.x * 0.05, v.z * 0.05)`) for broad patches and by a larger one for fine detail.

**Range.** The result stays within about `[-1, 1]`; values near the extremes are rare.

**Seed.** The noise generator is created once with a fixed seed built into the game. It is not derived from the world seed, so the same coordinates give the same value in every world. Offset or scale the coordinates yourself if you need variety between features.

**Arguments.** Both arguments are read as plain numbers; fractions are used as-is. Any argument count other than exactly two returns `0` without writing to the content log.

Available only in world-generation Molang (feature and feature-rule expressions).

args.name: x
args.description: X coordinate of the sample point

args.name: z
args.description: Z coordinate of the sample point

queries.formula: simplex2D(x, z) with a fixed seed

appliesTo.entities: not entity-based

pitfalls: Every world gets the same noise pattern; it ignores the world seed.
A wrong argument count returns 0 silently, which looks like a valid noise value.

queries.name: on_fire_time
queries.summary: Ticks since the entity caught fire (or stopped burning, for 5 ticks), else 0
queries.hover:
`q.on_fire_time` - ticks since the entity's burning state last changed.
While burning: ticks since it caught fire. After it goes out: restarts and counts for about 5 ticks, then 0.
Unit is ticks (20 per second), not seconds.
queries.description: Returns how many ticks have passed since the entity's burning state last changed: since it caught fire while it burns, and briefly after it goes out. Otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns an elapsed time in **ticks** (20 per second), measured from the last moment the entity's burning state changed:

- When the entity **catches fire**, the counter starts at `0` and rises by 1 per tick while it burns. It can restart while the entity keeps burning: a zombie burning in sunlight went back to about `0` after roughly 160 ticks, when the sun set it alight again.
- When the fire **goes out**, the counter restarts from `0` and keeps rising for a few ticks; once it reaches 5 the tracking is dropped and the query returns `0` again.
- An entity that has not burned recently returns `0`.

Because the counter restarts on extinguishing, a small non-zero value does not by itself mean the entity is burning - combine it with `query.is_on_fire` if you need both facts, for example to fade a burning overlay in over the first second: `q.is_on_fire ? math.min(q.on_fire_time / 20, 1) : 0`.

One projectile type - believed to be the thrown trident, not yet verified - always returns `0`; an arrow falling through lava counts normally. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: current_tick - tick_of_last_burning_change

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity has not caught fire or stopped burning in the last 5 ticks
one excluded projectile type (thrown trident, unverified)

pitfalls: The unit is ticks: divide by 20 for seconds.
It is briefly non-zero (a few ticks) after the fire goes out; test q.is_on_fire for the burning state.
It does not grow without bound: re-ignition (for example by sunlight) restarts it.

queries.name: out_of_control
queries.summary: Whether the entity has the minecraft:out_of_control component
queries.hover:
`q.out_of_control` - 1 while the entity has the minecraft:out_of_control component, else 0.
Vanilla boats get it over bubble columns; any entity can use it.
0 without an entity.
queries.description: 1 for as long as the `minecraft:out_of_control` component is on the entity, which vanilla boats get over bubble columns; 0 otherwise.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity carries the out-of-control flag and `0` otherwise.

The flag is switched on when the `minecraft:out_of_control` component is added to the entity and off when it is removed. Vanilla uses it for boats: the component groups a boat receives above a bubble column (pulling up or dragging down) include it, so `q.out_of_control` is `1` while a boat is being thrown around by a bubble column. Any custom entity can add and remove the component the same way, typically from a component group.

The flag is part of the entity's synchronised state, so behavior-pack and resource-pack Molang read the same value. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

queries.name: overlay_alpha
queries.summary: Deprecated: wither death-animation fade (0 for everything else)
queries.hover:
`q.overlay_alpha` - deprecated. Only the wither has it, on the client: it fades down while the wither is spawning and rises by 0.005 per tick while it dies.
Every other entity returns 0.
queries.description: A deprecated query. It only has a value for the wither, while it spawns and while it dies; every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Deprecated - do not use it in new content.

The only entity that has an overlay value is the **wither**, in two phases (measured on the client):

- **Spawning.** While a freshly summoned wither charges up, the value falls by `0.0075` per tick (for example `0.27` shortly after the summon, `0.085` about 25 ticks later).
- **Dying.** Each death tick adds `0.005` to whatever the value was, so it keeps climbing through the ten-second death sequence and is not capped at `1` - a wither killed during its spawn phase reached `1.075` at death tick 198.

Every other entity returns `0`.

The value is maintained by the client, so it is meant for resource-pack Molang; in behavior-pack Molang it is `0` (not yet verified). To fade something of your own, drive it from `query.death_ticks` or a variable instead.
queries.formula: spawning: -0.0075 per tick; dying: +0.005 per death tick from the current value (wither only)

appliesTo.entities: wither while spawning or dying; all others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

queries.name: owner_identifier
queries.summary: Full identifier of the entity, e.g. 'minecraft:player' (deprecated)
queries.hover:
`q.owner_identifier` - the entity's full identifier as a string, e.g. 'minecraft:player'.
Deprecated: prefer q.is_owner_identifier_any('minecraft:player').

queries.description: Returns the full identifier of the entity, namespace included, as a string. Deprecated in favour of `query.is_owner_identifier_any`.
queries.long:
Returns the identifier of the entity in scope as a string, including the namespace - `'minecraft:player'`, `'minecraft:zombie'`, `'my_pack:golem'`. In an attachable this is the entity holding or wearing the item, which is how vanilla attachables pick the player-only variant.

The query is deprecated. `query.is_owner_identifier_any('minecraft:player', ...)` does the same test, accepts several names at once and is the form the game wants you to use.

whenUnavailable.value: an empty name that is not equal to ''

queries.summary: How far the entity moved on one axis during the last tick, in blocks

`q.position_delta(axis)` - movement on x (0), y (1) or z (2) during the last tick, in blocks (signed).

queries.name: previous_squish_value
queries.summary: Last tick's squish amount of a slime, magma cube or sulfur cube
queries.hover:
`q.previous_squish_value` - the squish amount of a slime, magma cube or sulfur cube one tick ago.
Positive after a jump (stretched), negative after landing (flattened), easing back to 0; within -0.5..1.
Every other entity returns 0. Blend with q.current_squish_value and q.frame_alpha for smooth motion.
queries.description: Returns the squish amount a slime-type mob (slime, magma cube, sulfur cube) had on the previous tick. Other entities return 0.
queries.long:
Slimes, magma cubes and sulfur cubes stretch when they jump and flatten when they land. The game tracks this as a *squish amount* and this query returns its value from the **previous tick**; `query.current_squish_value` returns the current one.

Each tick the amount moves halfway toward a target, and the target itself shrinks toward `0`:

- jumping sets the target to `1` (stretched),
- landing sets the target to `-0.5` (flattened),
- `squish = squish + (target - squish) x 0.5`, and the previous value is saved before the update,
- for a slime the target is then multiplied by `0.6`.

Measured on a slime, a jump gives `0.5, 0.55, 0.455, 0.336, 0.233, ...` and a landing about `-0.24, -0.27, -0.17, ...`. A magma cube eases back more slowly (the value shrinks by about 0.9 per tick near the end) and peaks higher, about `0.74` after a jump and `-0.35` after landing. Whether behavior-pack Molang sees the same values as the client is not yet verified.

Because both values change only once per tick, vanilla blends them with the frame's partial tick for a smooth animation: `q.previous_squish_value + (q.current_squish_value - q.previous_squish_value) * q.frame_alpha`.

Only these three mob types have a squish amount. Any other entity, including a custom entity that uses slime-like behaviours, returns `0`, as does a context without an entity.

entity is not a slime, magma cube or sulfur cube

queries.name: property
queries.summary: Current value of one of the entity's declared properties
queries.hover:
`q.property('ns:name')` - value of an entity property: number for int/float, 0/1 for bool, string for enum.
Missing property, entity without properties, non-string argument or no entity: content-log error, returns 0.
Test q.has_property first when the property may not exist.
queries.description: Returns the current value of the named entity property declared in the entity's `description.properties`. Enum properties come back as strings, booleans as 0 or 1.
queries.long:
Returns the current value of an entity property, looked up by its full name (for example `'minecraft:armadillo_state'` or `'my_pack:mood'`). The result type depends on how the property is declared:

| property type | result |
|---|---|
| `int` | the integer as a number |
| `float` | the number |
| `bool` | `1` or `0` |
| `enum` | the value as a string - compare with `==`, e.g. `q.property('my_pack:mood') == 'angry'` |

**Errors.** Each of the following writes an error to the content log and returns `0`: an argument count other than one, no entity in the context, an argument that is not a string, an entity that declares no properties at all, and a name the entity does not declare. The name must match exactly, namespace included. When a property only exists on some entities (a shared animation, an attachable), guard the read with `query.has_property`.

Properties are synchronised from the server when declared with `client_sync: true`; resource-pack Molang should only read synced properties. On the client an entity whose properties are all unsynced has no properties at all: `q.property` logs the no-properties error and `q.has_property` returns `0` (measured on a vanilla zombie). A vanilla pig's enum property reads as its string value, e.g. `'warm'`, and the name is case-sensitive.

args.description: Full property name, e.g. 'my_pack:mood'
accepts: string literal or string-valued expression; exact full name
args.onInvalid: not a string, or unknown name: content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: entities that declare properties

whenUnavailable.when: entity does not have a property with that name

pitfalls: An unknown name logs an error on every evaluation; guard with q.has_property.
Enum values are strings: compare with 'value', not with an index number.

queries.name: relative_block_has_all_tags
queries.summary: Whether the block at an offset from the entity has every listed tag
queries.hover:
`q.relative_block_has_all_tags(x, y, z, 'tag', ...)` - 1 if the block at the entity's block + (x, y, z) has all the tags.
Offsets truncated toward zero (-0.5 -> 0). Stops at the first missing tag.
Fewer than 4 args or a non-string tag: content-log error, returns 0.
queries.description: Looks at the block at a whole-block offset from the entity and returns 1 if it carries every listed block tag, otherwise 0.
queries.long:
Returns `1` if the block at the given offset from the entity has **all** of the listed block tags, and `0` as soon as one tag is missing (later tags are not looked at).

**Which block.** The entity's position is rounded down to the block it is in, then the offsets are added. Offsets are whole blocks: fractions are dropped toward zero, so `-0.5` means `0`, not `-1`. `(0, -1, 0)` is the block under the entity's position. For players the position is at eye height, so the block under a standing player's feet is `(0, -2, 0)` (measured).

**Arguments.** At least four: `x, y, z` and one or more tag strings. Fewer than four writes an error to the content log and returns `0`. Tags are only checked as far as they are needed: a non-string tag logs an error when the scan reaches it, and is never noticed if the answer is already decided earlier.

The query needs an entity in a world; where there is none it logs an error and returns `0`.

args.description: Z offset from the entity, in blocks
accepts: number; fractional part dropped toward zero

args.description: Block tag name; repeat for more tags
args.onInvalid: non-string (when reached): content-log error, returns 0

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no world access (contexts without an entity in a world)
a tag argument that is reached is not a string

For players the offsets start at eye height: use (0, -2, 0) for the block under the feet.

queries.name: remaining_durability
queries.summary: Durability points left on the item in scope (max durability minus damage)
queries.hover:
`q.remaining_durability` - durability points left on the item: its maximum durability minus its damage.
Needs an item in scope (attachables, item repair expressions); without one: content-log error, 0.
Items without the minecraft:durability component return 0 silently.
queries.description: Maximum durability minus damage taken, for the item in scope; 0 for items without a durability component.
queries.long:
Returns the item's remaining durability in points: `max_durability - damage`. An undamaged item returns its full durability, and the value drops by one for every point of damage.

**Where it works.** It needs an item in the context - an attachable, or item expressions such as a repair amount (vanilla spears repair by `context.other->query.remaining_durability`, the durability of the item used for the repair). Without an item it writes an error to the content log and returns `0`.

**Which items.** The value is read from the item's durability component. Items defined with the `minecraft:durability` component return real values. Items without it - and built-in items that are not defined through item components - return `0` with no error, which is also what a fully broken item would read. Which built-in tools and armor fall in the second group is not yet verified.
queries.formula: max_durability - damage

appliesTo.entities: items with the minecraft:durability component

whenUnavailable.when: item has no durability component (or is not component-based)

pitfalls: 0 can mean "no durability component" as well as "about to break".

|---|---|

| other entities (boats, minecarts...) | the entity's own yaw |

queries.name: ride_head_y_rotation
queries.summary: Mount's yaw in degrees; head turn vs. body for horse-family mounts (clamped)
queries.hover:
`q.ride_head_y_rotation` / `q.ride_head_y_rotation(limit)` - yaw of the mount this entity rides, in degrees.
Horse-family mount: needs exactly one argument and returns the head turn relative to the body, clamped to +-limit.
Other mounts: must be called with no argument and return the mount's world yaw.
0 when not riding (no error, whatever the arguments).
queries.description: Returns the yaw of the entity this one is riding. For a horse, donkey, mule, skeleton horse or zombie horse it takes a limit and returns the head turn relative to the body, clamped to that limit; for other mounts it takes no argument and returns the mount's world yaw.
queries.long:
What this returns depends on the mount:

| mount | call | returns |
|---|---|---|
| horse, donkey, mule, skeleton horse, zombie horse | exactly one argument `limit` | `clamp(wrap(head_yaw - body_yaw), -limit, limit)` |
| any other mount | no argument | the mount's own yaw in world space |

For the horse family the head and body yaws are both blended between ticks, their difference is wrapped into `[-180, 180)` and then clamped. The limit is used exactly as written (no rounding); give a positive number - a negative limit makes the clamp return only its end values. For other mounts the yaw is the mount's facing, blended between ticks and not wrapped - for mobs that is the direction it is looking, not the body yaw (use `query.ride_body_y_rotation` for that). A boat keeps counting past 360 degrees as it turns. A ridden, unsteered pig read `0` in game while its body turned - not yet explained.

Using the wrong form writes a content-log error and returns `0`: no argument for a horse-family mount, or an argument for any other mount. When the entity is not riding, the query returns `0` silently, whatever you pass - the mount is checked before the arguments.

args.description: Horse-family mounts only: clamp in degrees. Must be omitted for other mounts.
accepts: horse-family mount: any number, used as is (positive expected)
args.onInvalid: missing on a horse-family mount, or present on another mount: content-log error, returns 0

queries.formula: horse family: `clamp(wrapDegrees(head_yaw - body_yaw), -limit, limit)`; others: mount yaw
queries.range: horse family: [-limit, limit]; others: unbounded yaw

appliesTo.entities: any entity that is riding; the clamp form applies when the mount is horse-family

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
the entity is not riding anything
mount is horse-family and the call does not have exactly one argument
mount is not horse-family and an argument is given

pitfalls: One expression cannot serve both horse and non-horse mounts: the argument is required for one and an error for the other.
For non-horse mounts the result is a world-space yaw, not the head turn relative to the body.

queries.description: Returns the up/down angle (pitch) of one of the entity's passengers, in degrees. The passenger is chosen by index; an index with no rider logs an error and returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns the pitch of the passenger at `rider_index`, in degrees, blended between its last two ticks. Entities have a single pitch, so this is the same number as `query.rider_head_x_rotation`.

**Index.** The argument picks a passenger from the entity's rider list, starting at `0`. It is converted by dropping the fractional part (`1.9` reads rider `1`). Not passing exactly one argument, or passing a string, also logs an error and returns `0`.

accepts: any number, used as is (positive expected)
args.onInvalid: missing when the rider is horse-family: content-log error, returns 0

queries.formula: horse-family rider: `clamp(wrapDegrees(head_yaw - body_yaw), -limit, limit)`; others: rider yaw
queries.range: horse-family rider: [-limit, limit]; others: unbounded yaw

appliesTo.entities: entities that carry riders; the clamp form applies when the rider is horse-family

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
no argument, or more than two
the index is not a number
index is negative (Windows) or not below the number of riders (including no riders at all)
the listed rider cannot be found in the world
the rider is horse-family and no limit is given

pitfalls: The horse-family test looks at the rider, not at the vehicle: on a horse carrying a player the one-argument form is the right one.
Calling it on an entity without riders logs an error every evaluation; check `q.has_rider` first.

queries.name: roll_counter
queries.summary: Ticks a panda has been rolling in its current roll; 0 when not rolling
queries.hover:
`q.roll_counter` - number of ticks the panda has spent in its current roll; 0 when it is not rolling.
Only pandas keep this counter; every other entity always returns 0, even with the roll behavior.
Counts up by 1 per tick to about 32 (where the roll ends), then drops back to 0.
queries.description: Returns how many ticks a panda has been rolling in its current roll, or 0 when it is not rolling. Other entities always return 0.
queries.long:
Returns a whole number of ticks: how long the panda has been in its current roll.

Every tick the panda checks its rolling state. While it is rolling the counter goes up by `1`; the moment it stops rolling the counter is reset to `0`. The roll behavior ends a roll once the counter reaches `32`, so during a normal roll the value climbs from `1` to about `32` (1.6 seconds) and then returns to `0`.

The counter exists only on pandas. Other entities - including custom ones given `minecraft:behavior.roll` - have no counter and always read `0`. Without an entity the query also returns `0`. Arguments are ignored.

Because the value advances once per tick, dividing it by the roll length gives a progress fraction for animations.
queries.formula: rolling ? previous + 1 : 0 (evaluated once per tick)

appliesTo.entities: pandas; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A custom mob with `minecraft:behavior.roll` still reads 0: only pandas keep the counter.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: rotation_to_camera
queries.summary: Pitch or yaw, in degrees, that would turn the entity to face the camera
queries.hover:
`q.rotation_to_camera(axis)` - 0: pitch, 1: yaw (degrees) from the entity's position toward the camera.
Yaw is in the game's convention, in (-270, 90] - not wrapped. Camera exactly at the entity: pitch 0, yaw -90.
Axis above 1 returns 0 silently; not exactly one argument logs an error. Resource packs only.
queries.description: Returns the angle, in degrees, that would make the entity face the camera: `0` for pitch (up/down) and `1` for yaw (left/right).
queries.long:
Returns an angle in degrees for the direction from the entity to the camera:

| axis | value |
|---|---|
| `0` | pitch: `-atan2(dy, sqrt(dx^2 + dz^2))` - negative when the camera is above the entity |
| `1` | yaw: `atan2(dz, dx) - 90`, in degrees |

Here `(dx, dy, dz)` is the camera position minus the entity's position. The yaw uses the same convention as entity yaw (`0` = facing south, `90` = west); how that maps onto a bone's rotation is not yet verified. It is not wrapped: results lie in `(-270, 90]`, so subtract the entity's own yaw and wrap if you need a relative turn.

The entity's position is its current tick position, while the camera position is taken for the frame being drawn. When the two coincide the direction is treated as zero: pitch `0`, yaw `-90`.

**Argument.** Exactly one number. It is converted by dropping the fractional part (`0.9` is pitch, `1.9` is yaw). On Windows a negative axis returns `0` without an error (the Android ARM64 build is expected to read it as pitch); an axis of `2` or more also returns `0` **without** an error; the bare name without an argument writes a content-log error and returns `0`.

Only the client knows where the camera is, so this is for resource-pack files and only meaningful while entities are being drawn. Read at any other moment it returns angles left over from earlier drawing that do not follow the camera (seen on Windows), silently. When there is no entity (world particles) the entity is taken to be at the world origin. What behavior-pack Molang returns is not yet verified.

args.name: axis
args.description: 0 = pitch, 1 = yaw
args.onInvalid: 2 or more, or negative (Windows): returns 0 with no log

queries.formula: d = camera - entity; axis 0: `-atan2(d.y, sqrt(d.x^2 + d.z^2))`; axis 1: `atan2(d.z, d.x) - 90` (degrees)

appliesTo.entities: any; the value uses only the entity's position

whenUnavailable.when: axis 2 or more, or a negative axis (Windows)

whenUnavailable.value: stale angles that do not follow the camera
angle from the world origin to the camera

whenUnavailable.when: camera exactly at the entity position

pitfalls: The yaw is not wrapped to [-180, 180): values below -180 are normal.
In world particles there is no entity, so the angle is measured from the world origin, not from the particle.
An axis of 2 or more (or a negative one on Windows) returns 0 without any error message.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: scoreboard
queries.summary: The entity's score on a named scoreboard objective (behavior packs only)
queries.hover:
`q.scoreboard('objective')` - the entity's score on that objective, as a number.
Behavior packs only: on the client it writes a content-log error and returns 0.
Missing objective or no score for this entity: 0 with no error. Scores above 16777216 lose precision.
queries.description: Returns the entity's score on the named scoreboard objective. It works in behavior packs only; a missing objective or an entity without a score gives 0.
queries.long:
Returns the score the entity holds on the objective named by the argument, converted to a number.

**Where it works.** Only on the server, that is in behavior-pack Molang. Evaluated on the client (resource packs) it writes a content-log error and returns `0`.

**Argument.** Exactly one string, the objective's name, matched as written (whether the match ignores case is not yet verified). A number or a wrong argument count writes a content-log error and returns `0`.

**Silent zeros.** If the objective does not exist, or the entity has no score on it, the result is `0` without any error - you cannot tell "no score" from a real score of `0`. Scores are whole numbers stored exactly, but they are returned as a Molang number, so values beyond about +-16.7 million lose their last digits.

Without an entity it writes a content-log error and returns `0`.

args.name: objective
args.description: Name of the scoreboard objective, e.g. 'kills'
accepts: a string with the objective name
args.onInvalid: not a string or wrong argument count: content-log error, returns 0; unknown objective: 0, no log

appliesTo.entities: any entity that can hold scores (players and other entities)

whenUnavailable.when: not exactly one argument, or the argument is not a string
the entity has no score on the objective

pitfalls: An unknown objective or a missing score reads 0 with no error; a typo in the name fails silently.
It does not work in resource packs: client-side evaluation logs an error and returns 0.

queries.name: server_memory_tier
queries.summary: Memory tier (0-4) of the device running the world's server; behavior packs only
queries.hover:
`q.server_memory_tier` - 0 to 4 from the total memory of the device hosting the world (<=1.5, <=2, <=4, <=8, >8 GiB).
Same for every entity; it describes the host machine, not the players' devices.
Behavior packs only: on the client it logs an error and returns 0. Needs an entity.
queries.description: Returns a number from 0 to 4 describing how much memory the device that runs the world's server has. It works in behavior packs only.
queries.long:
Returns a memory tier for the machine that hosts the world (for a local world, the host player's device; for a dedicated server, the server machine). The tier is read from the device's total memory (not yet verified in game):

| tier | total memory |
|---|---|
| `0` | up to 1.5 GiB |
| `1` | up to 2 GiB |
| `2` | up to 4 GiB |
| `3` | up to 8 GiB |
| `4` | more than 8 GiB |

The tier is worked out once and then reused, so it is the same for every entity and does not change while the game runs. Use it to scale down expensive behavior-pack work on weak hosts; for the tier of the device that draws the game, see `query.client_memory_tier`.

It must run on the server: evaluated on the client it writes a content-log error and returns `0`. It also needs an entity in the context - without one it logs an error and returns `0`. Arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: tier from total device memory (see table)

appliesTo.entities: any (the value does not depend on the entity)

timing.updates: on read (computed once per game session)

pitfalls: It describes the host machine: on a dedicated server all players get the server's tier, not their own.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: shake_angle
queries.summary: Progress (0 to about 2) of a wolf shaking itself dry; other entities 0
queries.hover:
`q.shake_angle` - progress of a wolf's shake-dry, 0 to about 2, rising 0.05 per tick; 0 when not shaking.
Wolves only; every other entity returns 0.
Not smoothed between ticks: add 0.05 * q.frame_alpha for a smooth value.
queries.description: Returns how far a wolf is through shaking off water, rising from 0 to about 2 over roughly two seconds, and 0 when it is not shaking. Only wolves have this value.
queries.long:
Returns the progress of a wolf's shake after getting wet, as a number that grows by `0.05` every tick:

| moment | value |
|---|---|
| not shaking | `0` |
| first tick of the shake | `0` |
| each further tick | previous + `0.05` |
| tick 41 | `2` (readable for that tick) |
| the tick after | back to `0` |

Roughly, a wolf starts a shake when it has been wet (in water or rain), is standing on the ground, is out of the water and rain, and has finished its current path. Getting wet again during the shake cancels it and the value returns to `0` at once.

The value is the one reached at the last tick; it is not smoothed between ticks. For a smooth animation add `0.05 * query.frame_alpha` yourself. Every entity other than a wolf returns `0`, as does a call without an entity; arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: 0.05 x (ticks since the shake started - 1), reset to 0 on the tick after it reaches 2

appliesTo.entities: wolves; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: The value steps once per tick; without adding `0.05 * q.frame_alpha` the shake looks jerky at high frame rates.
Only wolves report it; a custom entity always reads 0.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: shake_time
queries.summary: Ticks left in a stuck projectile's wobble (arrows); 0 otherwise
queries.hover:
`q.shake_time` - ticks left in the wobble of a projectile that just stuck into a block; counts down by 1 per tick to 0.
Started from the projectile's stick_in_ground shake_time; entities without it always return 0.
Whole ticks, not smoothed: subtract q.frame_alpha for a smooth value.
queries.description: Returns how many ticks of wobble a projectile that just hit a block has left, counting down to 0. Vanilla uses it to make stuck arrows quiver.
queries.long:
Returns a whole number of ticks. When a projectile with the `stick_in_ground` projectile setting lands in a block, a countdown is started from that setting's `shake_time`; afterwards it drops by `1` every tick and stops at `0`. The client is sent the starting value with the hit and counts down too; whether behavior packs see exactly the same numbers is not yet verified.

For vanilla arrows (`shake_time` `0.35` seconds) the countdown starts at `7`: in game an arrow read `6` one tick after landing and `3` three ticks later, then `0`.

The value only changes once per tick. To animate smoothly, subtract `query.frame_alpha`, which turns the steps into a continuous ramp. Entities that are not stuck projectiles, and calls without an entity, return `0`. Arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: starts at the projectile's shake_time on hitting a block, then -1 per tick down to 0
queries.range: 0 up to the starting value, whole numbers

appliesTo.entities: projectiles with stick_in_ground (arrows); others always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity has not stuck into a block recently

pitfalls: It counts ticks, not seconds, even though `shake_time` in the projectile component is written in seconds.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: shield_blocking_bob
queries.summary: Shield dip for a blocking player (0-4); drops after a damaged-shield block
queries.hover:
`q.shield_blocking_bob` - 0 to 4 for a player holding up a shield; 0 when not blocking.
4 while blocking; drops to 0 when a hit is blocked with a damaged shield and climbs back over 2 ticks.
Players only: other entities or no entity write a content-log error and return 0.
queries.description: Returns a value from 0 to 4 for animating a raised shield: 4 while a player is blocking, briefly dropping toward 0 right after the player blocks a hit with a damaged shield.
queries.long:
Returns a number between `0` and `4` meant to drive the small dip of a raised shield.

| situation | value |
|---|---|
| player not blocking | `0` |
| blocking | `4` |
| the tick a hit is blocked with a damaged shield | starts near `0`, then rises by `2` per tick back to `4` |

The recovery is smoothed with the frame's partial tick:

`clamp((ticks since the damaged-shield block + frame_alpha) / 2, 0, 1) * 4`

Only a block made with a damaged shield starts the dip; an ordinary block keeps the value at `4`. Lowering the shield resets the timing.

The query needs a player: on any other entity, or without an entity, it writes a content-log error and returns `0`. In item attachables the player should be the one holding the item (not yet verified).
queries.formula: blocking ? clamp((t + frame_alpha) / 2, 0, 1) * 4 : 0, t = ticks since the last damaged-shield block

appliesTo.entities: players only; other entities log an error

whenUnavailable.when: no entity, or the entity is not a player

pitfalls: It is 4, not 0, during normal blocking; the dip only appears after blocking with a damaged shield.
Used in a mob's animation it floods the content log: only players are accepted.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: show_bottom
queries.summary: Whether an end crystal should draw its bedrock base
queries.hover:
`q.show_bottom` - 1 if the entity's show-bottom flag is set (end crystals generated on End pillars), else 0.
Crystals placed by players or summoned have it off. The flag is saved with the entity.
0 without an entity.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the entity's show-bottom flag is set, otherwise 0. The game sets it on the end crystals it places on top of the End pillars, which draw a bedrock base.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the entity has its show-bottom flag and `0` otherwise. Vanilla uses it to show the bedrock base under end crystals.

The flag is turned on for the end crystals the game puts on the End pillars when it generates them (including when the pillars are rebuilt for a dragon respawn - not yet verified). A crystal placed from the item or made with `/summon` has the flag off. The flag is saved with the entity and shared with clients, so it reads the same in behavior and resource packs.

No component or command is known to set it, so for other entities it is `0`. Without an entity it returns `0`; arguments are ignored.

appliesTo.entities: end crystals generated on End pillars; everything else 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A crystal summoned with `/summon` has no base; the flag cannot be turned on from a pack.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: sit_amount
queries.summary: Panda only: how far it has moved into its sitting pose, 0 to 1, smoothed
queries.hover:
Panda only: 0 (standing) to 1 (fully sat down), blended between the last two ticks with the frame fraction.
Sitting down adds 0.15 per tick (about 7 ticks), getting up removes 0.19 per tick (about 6 ticks).
Every other entity - including sitting cats, wolves and parrots - returns 0; use q.is_sitting for those.
queries.description: Returns how far a panda is through its sit-down movement, from 0 (standing) to 1 (sitting), smoothed between ticks. Only pandas have this value; everything else returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns a number from `0` to `1` describing how far a **panda** has lowered itself into its sitting pose. Any other entity type returns `0`, even when it is sitting.

**How it moves.** The panda keeps two numbers, the amount at the previous tick and the amount now, both shared with clients. While the panda is sitting down the amount grows by `0.15` per tick until it reaches `1`; while it is getting up it shrinks by `0.19` per tick until it reaches `0`. The sitting flag does not follow the movement exactly: in game it still read `0` early in the sit-down (amounts up to about `0.3`) but already `1` at `0.87`, and while getting up it was still `1` at `0.86`. Animate with `sit_amount`, not with `query.is_sitting`.

**What you read.** Both stored numbers are first clamped to `0..1`, then blended with the frame's partial tick:

`previous + (current - previous) * query.frame_alpha`

so the value moves smoothly every frame even though it only changes once per tick. Where no frame fraction exists (behavior-pack Molang) the blend is expected to use 0, i.e. the previous tick's amount - not yet verified.

Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: lerp(clamp(previous, 0, 1), clamp(current, 0, 1), frame_alpha)

appliesTo.entities: pandas; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

queries.side: both (the amount is shared with clients; server value not yet verified)
pitfalls: Cats, wolves, parrots and custom sitting mobs always return 0: only pandas track this amount.
`query.is_sitting` flips partway through the movement, so it misses the start of the sit-down and the end of getting up.

queries.name: skin_id
queries.summary: The entity's skin index, as set by its minecraft:skin_id component
queries.hover:
Whole number stored with the entity as its skin index (set by the minecraft:skin_id component), else 0.
Shared with clients, so render controllers can index a texture array with it.
0 without an entity; arguments are ignored.
queries.description: Returns the entity's skin index, a whole number that the `minecraft:skin_id` component sets and that is shared with clients. Entities that never set one read 0.
queries.long:
Returns the skin index stored with the entity, as a whole number. The value is part of the entity's synchronised data: behavior packs set it through the `minecraft:skin_id` component (usually from a component group, so different spawn variants pick different skins), and resource packs read it to choose a texture, most often as an array index in a render controller.

Entities that never set a skin index read `0` (cows and players do). There is no range check: whatever integer the component stores is returned, so keep your texture array at least that long.

Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity (non-zero only when minecraft:skin_id sets it)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

timing.updates: on change of the skin index

pitfalls: An index past the end of a render-controller array is not caught by the query; size the array for every skin id your entity can get.

queries.name: sleep_rotation
queries.summary: Players in a bed: the bed's facing as 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees; else 0
queries.hover:
Players only: the facing of the bed they sleep in, as 90 / 0 / 270 / 180 degrees for bed direction 0 / 1 / 2 / 3.
0 when the player is not sleeping or the bed block has no facing - which is also the value of a direction-1 bed.
Sleeping villagers, foxes and other mobs always return 0.
queries.description: Returns the facing of the bed a sleeping player lies in, in degrees (0, 90, 180 or 270). Awake players and every non-player entity return 0.
queries.long:
Returns, for a **player** who is currently sleeping, the facing of the bed block at the player's stored bed position, as an angle in degrees. The angle comes from the bed's `direction` block state (or `minecraft:cardinal_direction` on blocks that use that state instead):

| bed `direction` | compass | value |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | south | `90` |
| 1 | west | `0` |
| 2 | north | `270` |
| 3 | east | `180` |

It returns `0` when:

- the entity is not a player (sleeping villagers, foxes, cats - the check is on the player type only);
- the player is not sleeping;
- the block at the stored bed position has neither facing state (for example the bed was broken).

Because a west-facing bed also gives `0`, `0` alone does not tell you whether the player is in a bed; combine it with `query.is_sleeping`.

Vanilla uses it together with the body yaw to lay the player model along the bed. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: players only; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
block at the bed position has no facing state

pitfalls: A value of 0 is both 'not sleeping' and 'bed facing west'; test `query.is_sleeping` first.
Only players are recognised: a sleeping villager or fox returns 0.

queries.name: sneeze_counter
queries.summary: Ticks the entity has spent in its current sneeze (pandas), else 0
queries.hover:
Whole number of ticks since the entity's sneezing flag was set; 0 while it is not sneezing.
Only pandas advance this counter; every other entity returns 0.
Resets to 0 on the first tick the flag is clear.
queries.description: Counts, in ticks, how long a panda has been in its current sneeze. It is 0 whenever the panda is not sneezing, and 0 for every other entity.
queries.long:
Returns a whole number of **ticks** that grows by one on every tick the entity's sneezing flag (`query.is_sneezing`) is set, and drops back to `0` on the first tick the flag is clear. It is meant for timing a sneeze animation: vanilla lowers the panda's head for the first 15 ticks and then raises it back over the next 5.

Only the panda runs this counter, so every other entity - including custom entities with a sneeze behavior - returns `0`. The counter is advanced by the panda's own tick; whether the client advances its own copy (from the shared sneezing flag) or only the server does is not yet verified, so expect the resource-pack value to follow the flag within a tick.

Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: count of consecutive ticks with the sneezing flag set

appliesTo.entities: pandas; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity has no sneeze counter (anything but a panda)

pitfalls: Custom entities with `minecraft:behavior.sneeze` still read 0: the counter only runs for pandas; use `query.is_sneezing` instead.

queries.name: spellcolor
queries.summary: The entity's spell colour as a struct with .r .g .b .a, each 0 to 1
queries.hover:
Struct with .r .g .b .a (each 0..1): the colour stored with the entity for its spell particles.
Read one member (q.spellcolor.r) - the struct itself is not a number.
All four members are 0 without an entity, and for entities that never set a colour.
queries.description: Returns the entity's spell colour as a struct with `.r`, `.g`, `.b` and `.a` members from 0 to 1. Every member is 0 when there is no entity or no colour has been set.
queries.long:
Returns a struct with four members, `.r`, `.g`, `.b` and `.a`, each from `0` to `1`. They come from a single colour value stored with the entity and shared with clients; each channel is one byte of that value divided by `255`, so the members move in steps of `1/255`.

Vanilla uses it to tint the evoker's spell particles while it casts. The evoker sets the colour when it casts and keeps the last one afterwards (in game two colours appeared, about `0.40, 0.30, 0.35` and `0.70, 0.70, 0.80`, both with `.a` = `1`); other vanilla users are not verified. An entity that never sets it reads `0` in all four members - note that this includes `.a`, so a particle tinted with an unset colour becomes fully transparent.

Without an entity every member is `0` and nothing is logged. Arguments are ignored. Read a member before doing arithmetic; the struct as a whole is not a number.

appliesTo.entities: any entity; non-zero only while something has set its spell colour

whenUnavailable.when: entity has never had a spell colour set

timing.updates: on change of the stored colour

pitfalls: Using the whole struct in arithmetic does not give a number; read `.r`, `.g`, `.b` or `.a`.
An unset colour has `.a` = 0, so it is invisible when used as a tint alpha.

queries.name: standing_scale
queries.summary: Polar bear only: how far it has reared up, 0 to 1, eased and smoothed
queries.hover:
Polar bear only: 0 (on all fours) to 1 (fully reared up), smoothed with the frame fraction and squared (eases in).
Takes 6 ticks to go up or down fully; follows the same standing flag as q.is_standing.
Every other entity - horses included - returns 0.
queries.description: Returns how far a polar bear has reared up on its hind legs, from 0 to 1. The value is smoothed between ticks and eased. Every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns a number from `0` to `1` for a **polar bear** rearing up, and `0` for every other entity type (horses rear too, but this query does not report them).

**How it moves.** The bear keeps a counter from `0` to `6` that goes up by one each tick while its standing flag (`query.is_standing`) is set and down by one each tick otherwise, clamped to that range. So a full rise or fall takes 6 ticks (0.3 s).

**What you read.** The counter's previous and current values are blended with the frame's partial tick, divided by 6, and then **squared**:

`s = (previous + (current - previous) * query.frame_alpha) / 6` → `s * s`

Squaring makes the pose start slowly and speed up; half-way through the rise the query reads `0.25`, not `0.5`.

The counter is updated by a per-tick system that only runs for polar bears; which side runs it, and so what behavior-pack Molang reads, is not yet verified. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: (lerp(previous, current, frame_alpha) / 6)^2

appliesTo.entities: polar bears; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity is not a polar bear

pitfalls: The curve is squared: 0.25 at the half-way point. Take `math.sqrt` if you need a linear ramp.
Horses and custom mobs with a standing flag return 0; only polar bears are recognised.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: state_time
queries.summary: Seconds since the animation controller entered its current state
queries.hover:
Seconds the running animation controller has spent in its current state; restarts at 0 on every state change.
Grows by the frame's delta time each time the controller runs, so it is only meaningful inside a controller.
Outside a controller, and without an entity: 0 without a log.
queries.description: Returns how many seconds the animation controller being evaluated has been in its current state. It restarts from 0 whenever the controller changes state.
queries.long:
Returns the time, in **seconds**, that the animation controller currently being evaluated has spent in its current state. The clock starts at `0` when the state is entered and, each time the controller runs, grows by that frame's `query.delta_time`. A state that is re-entered starts again from `0`.

Use it in a state's transitions (`"q.state_time > 2"`) or in the state's own animations and scripts. Elsewhere it has nothing to report:

- evaluated outside an animation controller (for example in a client entity's `pre_animation` script or in an animation that no controller is playing) it returns `0` silently;
- evaluated on an entity that has no animation data at all it is expected to write a content-log error and return `0` (not yet verified); without an entity (tested in a block context) it returns `0` without a log.

Because the clock advances by frame time, it only moves while the controller is being run; whether it pauses while a client entity is off screen is not yet verified. Behaviour in behavior-pack animation controllers is not yet verified. Arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: sum of delta_time since the state was entered

appliesTo.entities: entities with animations, inside an animation controller

whenUnavailable.when: entity has no animation data (animation-less entities; not yet verified)
no entity (for example a block context)
not inside an animation controller state

timing.updates: per frame (each time the controller runs)

pitfalls: Use it inside an animation controller state; elsewhere (e.g. `pre_animation`) expect 0 rather than a time.

queries.name: structural_integrity
queries.summary: Boats and minecarts: remaining damage buffer, 40 when unhurt; others 1
queries.hover:
Whole number: a boat's or minecart's damage buffer - 40 when unhurt, lowered by hits, recovering 1 per tick.
Boats lose 10 per point of damage, minecarts 8; every other entity reads 1.
Vanilla shakes minecarts with (40 - q.structural_integrity).
queries.description: Returns the damage buffer of a boat or minecart as a whole number: 40 when unhurt, lower after being hit, recovering by 1 each tick. Other entities return 1.
queries.long:
Returns a whole number that only **boats** and **minecarts** use. Both start at `40`. Each hit lowers it:

| entity | per point of damage | recovers by |
|---|---|---|
| boat | `-10` | `+1` per tick while the value is between 1 and 39 |
| minecart | `-8` | `+1` per tick while the value is 19 or less, so it stops at `20` |

So after a hit the value dips and then climbs back, which is what vanilla uses to shake a minecart: `(40 - query.structural_integrity)` is the amount of recent damage still showing. The value is stored with the entity and shared with clients; damage is applied on the server.

A minecart hit down to `32` stays at `32`; one hit down to `16` climbs back to `20` and stays there. Every other entity (mobs, players, armor stands...) reads `1`. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.range: integers, 40 at rest for boats and minecarts; 1 for others

appliesTo.entities: boats and minecarts; everything else 1

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

queries.side: both (changed on the server, shared with clients)
pitfalls: It counts down on damage, not up: an unhurt boat or minecart reads 40, not 0.
Only boats and minecarts use it; every other entity reads 1, not 0. For mob health use `query.health`.
A minecart does not heal back to 40: damage that leaves it at 20 or more stays until the next hit.

queries.name: surface_particle_color
queries.summary: Resource packs: particle tint of the first solid block under the entity
queries.hover:
Struct .r .g .b .a (0..1): the particle tint of the first block with a supporting top, from the entity's feet down 10 blocks.
All zeros if nothing is found in those 10 blocks (no log); no entity or server side: content-log error and zeros.
Files at Molang 1.20.70+ use a slightly wider block test than older files.
queries.description: Returns the colour the game would tint particles of the block under the entity with, as a struct with `.r`, `.g`, `.b` and `.a` from 0 to 1. Resource-pack only; zeros when no block is found.
queries.long:
Returns a struct with `.r`, `.g`, `.b` and `.a` members, each from `0` to `1`: the tint colour the client uses for particles of the block under the entity. This is what lets dust kicked up by a mob take the colour of the ground, for example leaves tinted by their biome (a grass block gives its untinted dirt particle, white). Use it together with `query.surface_particle_texture_coordinate` and `query.surface_particle_texture_size` to build a block-textured particle.

**Which block.** The game looks at the block at the entity's feet and then at up to 9 blocks below it (10 blocks in all), skipping air, and takes the first block whose **top face can support something**. In files whose Molang version is 1.20.70 or newer, blocks with one extra block-type flag also count even when their top is not a supporting face - leaves are such blocks; older files use the supporting-face test only. In game, bottom slabs, carpet and farmland counted in neither version, while fences and glass panes counted in both. If none of the 10 blocks qualifies, the result is all zeros and nothing is logged.

**Where it works.** It is a client feature. Evaluated for a server-side entity (behavior packs) it writes a content-log error and returns zeros; without an entity (for example in a particle not bound to one) it also logs and returns zeros. How the tint itself is computed for each block (biome-dependent blocks, fixed colours) is up to the client's block colour rules and is not documented here.

Arguments are ignored. Read a member before doing arithmetic.

appliesTo.entities: any entity rendered on the client

whenUnavailable.when: no qualifying block in the 10 blocks from the feet down

pitfalls: Only 10 blocks are searched, starting at the feet: a flying entity higher than that gets zeros.
A zero struct also means 'nothing found' - `.a` is 0; but leaves found through the 1.20.70 rule also come back with `.a` = 0 and a real colour, so `.a` alone is not a found/not-found test.
Which blocks count changed at Molang version 1.20.70 (leaves count only from then on); set your file's version deliberately.

behaviourChangesByVersion.change: A block counts only if its top face can support something.
A block also counts when it carries one extra block-type flag, even without a supporting top face.

queries.name: surface_particle_texture_coordinate
queries.summary: Resource packs: atlas UV (.u .v) of the particle texture of the block below
queries.hover:
Struct .u .v: top-left atlas coordinate of the break-particle texture of the first solid block under the entity (10 blocks searched).
Blocks with several texture variants may give a different variant on each read.
Zeros if nothing is found (no log); no entity or server side: content-log error and zeros.
queries.description: Returns where, in the block texture atlas, the break-particle texture of the block under the entity starts, as a struct with `.u` and `.v`. Resource-pack only; zeros when no block is found.
queries.long:
Returns a struct with `.u` and `.v`: the top-left corner, in texture-atlas coordinates, of the texture the client uses for the **break particles** of the block under the entity. Pair it with `query.surface_particle_texture_size` (the width and height of the same texture) to point a particle's UV at the ground block, and with `query.surface_particle_color` for its tint.

**Which block.** The game looks at the block at the entity's feet and then at up to 9 blocks below it (10 blocks in all), skipping air, and takes the first block whose **top face can support something**. In files whose Molang version is 1.20.70 or newer, blocks with one extra block-type flag also count even when their top is not a supporting face - leaves are such blocks; older files use the supporting-face test only. In game, bottom slabs, carpet and farmland counted in neither version, while fences and glass panes counted in both. If none of the 10 blocks qualifies, the result is all zeros and nothing is logged.

**Texture choice.** The texture is the block's own break-particle texture if it defines one, otherwise one of the block's default textures. When a block has several texture variants, one is picked at random on every read, using the entity's own random source - so two reads in the same frame can land on different variants.

**Where it works.** Client only: for a server-side entity it writes a content-log error and returns zeros, and without an entity it also logs and returns zeros.

Arguments are ignored. Read a member before doing arithmetic.

whenUnavailable.when: no qualifying block in the 10 blocks from the feet down

queries.name: swell_amount
queries.summary: Creeper fuse / wither death swelling; can exceed 1, clamp before use
queries.hover:
Creepers: fuse progress, normally 0..1 but up to about 1.07 (30/28); wither: grows during its death animation to about 7.
Every other entity returns 0. Smoothed between ticks except while a creeper's explode fuse is running.
Clamp it (vanilla uses math.clamp(q.swell_amount, 0, 1)) before driving a scale with it.
queries.description: Returns how far a creeper has swollen towards exploding, or how far a dying wither has swollen. Only creepers and withers report a value, and it can go above 1.
queries.long:
Returns a swelling amount for **creepers** and **withers**; every other entity type returns `0`.

**Creeper.** A creeper keeps a swell counter in ticks: each tick it goes up by one while the creeper is ignited (`query.is_ignited`) and down by one otherwise, clamped to `0..30`. The query reads

`(previous + (current - previous) * query.frame_alpha) / 28`

with both counter values cut to whole numbers first. That reaches `1` after 28 ticks and tops out at `30/28 ≈ 1.07`. While the creeper carries a running explode fuse (the `minecraft:explode` component that a behavior pack adds when the fuse is lit), it reads the fuse's progress instead: `1 - remaining fuse ticks / initial fuse ticks`, with no smoothing between ticks. On the client the value kept following the counter (steps of `1/28`) while a creeper's fuse ran.

**Wither.** The same counter is used, but it only grows during the death animation (one per tick for up to 200 ticks), so a dying wither's value rises from `0` to about `7`. A living wither reads `0`.

Values above `1` are normal for both, which is why vanilla clamps the result. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: creeper/wither: lerp(trunc(previous), trunc(current), frame_alpha) / 28; creeper with a running explode fuse: 1 - remaining / initial

appliesTo.entities: creepers and withers; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity is neither a creeper nor a wither

queries.side: both (fuse path server-side; the client reads the counter)
pitfalls: It can exceed 1 (creeper up to 30/28, dying wither up to about 7); clamp before using it as a scale.
A living wither always reads 0: its swelling only runs during the death animation.
Custom entities with an explode behavior read 0; only the creeper and wither types are recognised.

queries.name: swelling_dir
queries.summary: Creepers: +1 while the fuse is building, -1 otherwise (also when idle)
queries.hover:
Creepers: 1 while ignited (swelling up), -1 otherwise - an idle creeper reads -1, not 0.
Every entity without a swell counter returns 0; a wither reads 0 as well.
Refreshed every tick from the creeper's ignited state.
queries.description: Returns which way a creeper's swelling is going: 1 while it is ignited and swelling up, -1 otherwise. Entities without a swell counter return 0.
queries.long:
Returns the direction a creeper's swell counter (see `query.swell_amount`) is moving:

| state | value |
|---|---|
| creeper ignited, swelling up | `1` |
| creeper not ignited (shrinking back, or simply idle) | `-1` |
| entity with no swell counter | `0` |

The creeper sets the direction every tick from its ignited state, and its attack behavior also sets it (to `1` only when ignited, close enough and able to see its target), so an ordinary creeper that has never started a fuse reads `-1`, not `0`. Withers keep a swell counter for their death animation but never set a direction, so they read `0`, alive or dying.

Vanilla uses `query.swelling_dir < 0` to stop the white flash as soon as a creeper starts to defuse. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: creepers (-1 or 1); every other entity 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: An idle creeper reads -1: test `> 0` for 'swelling up' rather than `!= 0`.

queries.name: swim_amount
queries.summary: Blend 0 to 1 into the swimming/crawling pose, one tick behind, not smoothed
queries.hover:
0..1 blend into the swim pose: +0.1 per tick while swimming or crawling, -0.1 per tick otherwise (10 ticks end to end).
Reports the previous tick's value (one tick late) and is not smoothed between ticks.
Updated only where the client animates the entity; behavior-pack value not yet verified.
queries.description: Returns how far the entity has blended into its swimming pose, from 0 to 1. It rises while the entity is swimming or crawling and falls otherwise, 0.1 per tick.
queries.long:
Returns a number from `0` to `1` that fades the entity into and out of its swimming pose. Each tick it moves by `0.1` - up while the entity's swimming flag (`query.is_swimming`) **or** crawling flag (`query.is_crawling`) is set, down otherwise - clamped to `0..1`. A full blend therefore takes 10 ticks (0.5 s). Vanilla uses it for the elytra's swimming pose and to switch the warden's swim animation.

Two details matter when you animate with it:

- it returns the value from the **previous** tick, so it trails the flags by one tick;
- it is **not** blended with the frame's partial tick, so at high frame rates it steps in `0.1` increments. Smooth it yourself if needed.

The blend is kept for any entity and is advanced by a per-tick system that runs where the entity's movement is animated on the client; in behavior-pack Molang it is expected to stay `0` (not yet verified). Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: previous tick's value of: v += 0.1 if swimming or crawling else -0.1, clamped to [0, 1]

appliesTo.entities: any entity (non-zero while swimming or crawling)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Crawling counts as swimming for this blend: a player crawling under a trapdoor reads 1.
It is one tick late and steps in 0.1 increments; it is not smoothed per frame.

queries.name: tail_angle
queries.summary: Wolves only: tail angle in radians (angry, tame by health, or untamed)
queries.hover:
Wolves only, in radians (vanilla multiplies by 57.3): angry 0.49π, tame (0.15 + 0.4 × health / default health)π, else 0.2π.
Tame: 0.55π (about 99 degrees) at full health, 0.35π at half, 0.15π at 0.
Every other entity returns 0.
queries.description: Returns the angle of a wolf's tail in radians: raised when angry, following health when tame, and a fixed angle when untamed. Every other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns an angle in **radians** for **wolves** only (vanilla converts it with `* 57.3`). The first matching row wins:

| wolf state | value | about |
|---|---|---|
| angry | `0.49 × π` | 1.54 rad, 88° |
| tame | `(0.15 + 0.4 × health / default health) × π` | 0.47 rad (27°) at 0 health to 1.73 rad (99°) at full |
| untamed and calm | `0.2 × π` | 0.63 rad, 36° |

"Default health" is the wolf's full health (40 for a tame wolf in game: 1.73 rad at 40 health, 1.10 rad at 20). The value is computed on read from the angry and tame flags and the current health, and is not smoothed between ticks.

Every other entity type returns `0`. Arguments are ignored. Without an entity the query returns `0`.
queries.formula: angry: 0.49π; tame: (0.15 + 0.4·health/default_health)·π; otherwise 0.2π

appliesTo.entities: wolves; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: The result is in radians, while bone rotations are in degrees - multiply by 57.3.
Anger wins over tameness: an angry tame wolf reads 0.49π regardless of health.
