queries.name: target_x_rotation
queries.summary: The entity's own pitch (x rotation) in degrees, smoothed; not an aim angle
queries.hover:
The entity's own x rotation (pitch) in degrees, blended between ticks with the frame fraction.
Despite the name it does not look at any target: projectiles and mobs use it to tilt with their own heading.
Client feature; with no entity it falls back to the emitter's rotation for particles (not yet verified), else 0.
queries.description: Returns the entity's own pitch - its x rotation - in degrees, smoothed between ticks. Despite its name it is not the angle towards the entity's target.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's **own** x rotation (pitch) in degrees, blended between the previous and the current tick with the frame's partial tick (the blend takes the short way round, so it does not jump at the wrap-around). It does not look at the entity's attack target at all - the name is historical (in game a skeleton aiming up at a player read its own head pitch, not the angle to the player). That is why vanilla uses it to tilt arrows, firework rockets and bats along their flight direction, and to pitch mob heads.

Without an entity (for example in a particle emitted into the world) it falls back to a rotation stored with the particle emitter; what that value holds is not yet verified. With neither it returns `0` without a log.

It is provided by the client, so use it in resource packs; what a behavior pack gets is not yet verified. Arguments are ignored.
queries.formula: lerp_rotation(previous pitch, current pitch, frame_alpha)
queries.range: pitch range of the entity, typically [-90, 90]

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity and no particle emitter

pitfalls: It is the entity's own pitch, not the pitch towards its target; for aiming at something compute the angle yourself.
It is already smoothed per frame; do not blend it with `query.frame_alpha` again.

queries.name: target_y_rotation
queries.summary: Head yaw relative to the body (mobs) or own yaw (projectiles), degrees
queries.hover:
Mobs: how far the head is turned left/right from the body, degrees, clamped to -85..85.
Arrows, fireworks and wither skulls: the entity's own yaw instead. Not the direction to an attack target.
Smoothed between ticks. Resource packs only; behavior packs are expected to get 0 (not yet verified).
queries.description: Despite the name, this does not aim at a target. For mobs it is the head's yaw relative to the body, in degrees and clamped to [-85, 85]; for arrows, firework rockets and wither skulls it is the entity's own yaw.
queries.long:
Returns a yaw angle in degrees. What angle depends on the kind of entity:

| entity | value |
|---|---|
| arrow, firework rocket, wither skull (both kinds) | the entity's own yaw (its heading), not clamped |
| any mob, including players | head yaw minus body yaw, wrapped to [-180, 180) and then clamped to [-85, 85] |
| anything else being drawn | a yaw kept by the renderer for that entity - only meaningful while the entity is being drawn |

For mobs this is the angle vanilla feeds into a head bone so the head turns while the body lags behind: positive and negative mean the two sides, and `0` means the head points where the body points. Nothing about attack targets is involved - a mob with no target still turns its head, and the value follows it (in game a villager with no target swung to 75 while watching a player walk past; a player whose camera turned 60 degrees read 50, because the body turned the other 10).

Both the head and the body angle are smoothed with the frame's partial tick, so the value moves every frame. The query only has an answer in resource-pack (client) Molang; in behavior-pack Molang it returns `0` (not yet verified in game).

For the last row, and when there is no entity at all, the number comes from renderer data rather than from the entity. Read outside entity rendering it held leftovers: a boat gave `0`, a minecart gave meaningless numbers that changed between reads (from about 1e-26 to -1.7e18), and with no entity a fixed tiny non-zero number, never with a content-log line. Do not rely on `0` in those cases.

`query.target_x_rotation` is the pitch counterpart and is normally used alongside it.
queries.formula: mobs: `clamp(wrap(head_yaw - body_yaw), -85, 85)`; listed projectiles: `yaw`
queries.range: [-85, 85] for mobs; otherwise the entity's own yaw, not limited by the query

appliesTo.entities: mobs (head relative to body); arrows, fireworks, wither skulls (own yaw); others see text

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
whenUnavailable.value: not reliably 0: a leftover renderer value (outside entity rendering a fixed tiny non-zero number)

whenUnavailable.when: entity is neither a mob nor one of the listed projectiles, read outside its own rendering
whenUnavailable.value: leftover renderer value (boat 0; minecart changing meaningless numbers)

whenUnavailable.when: evaluated in a behavior pack (the server has no answer for this query)

pitfalls: It is not the angle towards an attack target: a mob without a target still returns its head turn.
For mobs the value never leaves [-85, 85], even when the head is turned further.
On boats, minecarts and other non-mob, non-projectile entities, and with no entity, the value is renderer data, not the entity's facing; use `query.body_y_rotation` there.
In behavior-pack Molang it is expected to be 0 (not yet verified in game).

queries.name: ticks_since_last_kinetic_weapon_hit
queries.summary: Ticks since the latest hit during the current kinetic-weapon use; -1 otherwise
queries.hover:
Ticks since the entity's most recent hit during its current kinetic-weapon (spear-style) use.
-1 when it is not using one, has hit nothing in this use, or is not a mob. Resets when a new use starts.
queries.description: While a mob is using a kinetic weapon, returns how many ticks ago it last hit something during that use. Returns -1 when it is not using one, has not hit anything since the use began, or is not a mob.
queries.long:
Returns a tick count, or `-1`.

A kinetic weapon (the spear-style charge attack) keeps a small record for the duration of one use: a tick counter that starts at `0` when the use begins and counts up each tick, plus the counter value at which each entity was hit. The query returns

`counter now - counter at the most recent hit`

so it is about `0` right after a hit and climbs by one per tick afterwards (the exact tick alignment is not yet verified in game). When the use ends, the record is removed and the query goes back to `-1`; a new use starts again from nothing, so hits from an earlier use are not remembered. In game, a spear-carrying zombie charging a villager read `-1` at the start of each charge, dropped back to a small number on every hit, climbed about one per tick in between (up to 191 in one long charge) and returned to `-1` as the charge ended.

It returns `-1` when the entity is not a mob, is not currently using a kinetic weapon, or has not hit anything yet in the current use. Vanilla reads it through the owning entity of an attachable to play a short hit reaction for a few ticks after each hit. Whether a resource-pack client sees the hits at the same tick as the server is not yet verified.
queries.formula: `use_ticks - use_ticks_at_latest_hit`, or `-1`

appliesTo.entities: mobs (players included) during a kinetic-weapon use; everything else -1

whenUnavailable.when: not currently using a kinetic weapon, or nothing hit yet in this use

pitfalls: Test for `>= 0` first: -1 means "no hit to report", not "just hit".
It only covers the current use; after the use ends it is -1 even if the last hit was a tick ago.
Unlike most -1 queries, no entity at all also gives -1, not 0.

queries.name: time_of_day
queries.summary: Position in the day cycle, 0 to 1 (0.25 sunrise, 0.5 noon)
queries.hover:
Position in the day cycle as a fraction: 0 midnight, 0.25 sunrise, 0.5 noon, 0.75 sunset.
Always follows the overworld clock, even in the Nether and the End.
Steps once per tick; needs an entity, otherwise 0.
queries.description: Where the world is in its 24000-tick day, as a fraction from 0 up to (but not including) 1. `/time set 0` (sunrise) reads 0.25, noon 0.5, sunset 0.75 and midnight 0.
queries.long:
Returns how far the world is through its day, as a fraction in the range `[0, 1)`.

The value is derived from the world clock (the number you set with `/time set`), shifted by a quarter day so that `0` falls on midnight rather than on sunrise:

| `/time set` | result |
|---|---|
| `0` (sunrise) | `0.25` |
| `6000` (noon) | `0.5` |
| `12000` (sunset) | `0.75` |
| `18000` (midnight) | `0.0` |

The clock is read once per game tick, so the value moves in steps of `1/24000` and is not smoothed between frames. When the daylight cycle is stopped, the value stops too. The underlying clock keeps counting up past 24000 (it is not reset each day).

The calculation uses single-precision floating point, so very large clock values lose precision: once the clock passes about 16.7 million ticks (roughly 700 in-game days) the result moves in steps of 2 ticks or more, and near 2.1 billion ticks it can be off by more than ten ticks.

Although the query runs on an entity, the entity only provides access to the world: the result is the overworld's time of day wherever the entity is, including the Nether and the End.
queries.formula: `((t + 6000) mod 24000) / 24000`, where `t` is the world clock in ticks

appliesTo.entities: any entity (the entity is only used to reach the world)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: It follows the overworld clock in every dimension; it does not describe a dimension's own sky.
`0` is midnight, not sunrise: `/time set 0` gives `0.25`.
A result of `0` can also mean the expression ran without an entity.
After very long play (clock above ~16.7 million ticks) the value is only accurate to a few ticks.

verification.label: Verified in game on 1.26.60.22

queries.hover:

-1 before any detection, for entities that do not listen for vibrations, and in behavior packs (with a log line).
No entity: -1 and a content-log error.
queries.description: Returns how long ago, in seconds, the entity last detected a vibration. Returns -1 when it never has, when it is not a vibration listener, and when evaluated on the server.
queries.formula: `(current_tick - detection_tick) / 20`
queries.range: -1, or 0 and up in steps of 0.05

appliesTo.entities: entities that listen for vibrations on the client (the warden); others -1

whenUnavailable.when: entity does not track vibrations, or has not detected one yet

Compare against 0 before using the value as a duration.

queries.name: time_stamp
queries.summary: The world's running tick counter (not the time of day)
queries.hover:
The world's running tick counter: +1 every game tick (20 per second), never wraps at a day.
Not the /time clock. Large values lose precision (whole-number steps only up to about 16.7 million).
Needs an entity, otherwise 0.
queries.description: Returns the level's tick counter, which increases by one every game tick. It is not the time of day that `/time set` changes.
queries.long:
Returns the number of game ticks the world has run, as counted by the level (20 per second). It keeps increasing and does not wrap at the end of a day; it is a separate counter from the day-cycle clock, so `/time set` and `/time add` do not move it (checked in game: after `/time set 0` and `/time add 24000` it simply kept counting while `query.time_of_day` jumped).

The counter is a large whole number converted to a Molang number, so above 16,777,216 ticks (about 9.7 days of play) not every tick can be represented and the value moves in steps of 2, then 4, and so on. Vanilla feeds it into `math.sin` for continuous wobbles, which is fine for short sessions but becomes jerky on very old worlds; `query.life_time` or `query.anim_time` avoid that.

The entity only gives access to the world; the value is the same for every entity. Without an entity it returns `0`. Whether the client's counter equals the server's is not yet verified.

appliesTo.entities: any entity (the entity is only used to reach the world)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: It is not the time of day: use `query.time_of_day` for the day cycle.
On worlds that have run for many days the value no longer changes smoothly every tick.

queries.name: timer_flag_1
queries.summary: 1 while the entity's minecraft:behavior.timer_flag_1 goal is running
queries.hover:
1 while the entity's `minecraft:behavior.timer_flag_1` goal is running, else 0.
The goal sets the flag when it starts and clears it when it stops (its duration ran out or it was interrupted).
The flag is synchronised, so behavior and resource packs agree.
queries.description: Returns 1 while the entity's `minecraft:behavior.timer_flag_1` goal is active and 0 otherwise.
queries.long:
Returns `1` while the entity's `minecraft:behavior.timer_flag_1` goal is running and `0` otherwise.

The goal raises a dedicated entity flag when it starts and lowers it when it stops. It runs for a random time taken from its duration range, and after stopping it cannot start again until its cooldown range has passed, so the flag produces on/off windows you can hang animations on (vanilla uses the three timer flags for the sniffer's long sniff, standing up and happy animations). The goal's start and end events fire at the same moments the flag changes.

Only this goal writes the flag: `timer_flag_2` and `timer_flag_3` belong to the other two timer goals and are independent. The flag is part of the entity's synchronised state, so behavior packs and resource packs read the same value. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with minecraft:behavior.timer_flag_1; others always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: A goal that cannot run (lower priority goal running, in cooldown) leaves the flag at 0 even though the component is present.

queries.name: total_emitter_count
queries.summary: All particle emitters alive on the client; meant for particle effects
queries.hover:
Number of particle emitters currently alive on this client, across all effects.
Meant for particle effects; in entity scripts, animations and render controllers it is 0.
Client only.
queries.description: Inside a particle effect, returns how many particle emitters of any kind are alive on the client right now. Everywhere else it returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns the client's total count of live particle emitters, summed over every effect.

The count is only reachable from a particle effect's own expressions (emitter and particle curves, rates, lifetimes and so on). In client entity scripts, animations and render controllers there is no emitter to ask and the result is `0`, even when the world is full of particles (checked in game with particles alive: the player, a pig and no entity all read 0). Behavior packs have no particle system and are expected to get `0` as well.

A typical use is a budget: stop spawning, or spawn less, when the total is already high. For the count of one effect only use `query.effect_emitter_count`; for particles rather than emitters use `query.total_particle_count`.

appliesTo.entities: not needed; the particle emitter is the subject

whenUnavailable.when: not evaluated inside a particle effect (entity animations, render controllers)
evaluated in a behavior pack (the server has no answer for this query)

pitfalls: In an entity's animation or render controller it is 0, however many particles are alive.
It counts every effect on the client, not only this one.

queries.summary: All particles alive on the client; meant for particle effects

Client only.
queries.description: Inside a particle effect, returns how many particles of any effect are alive on the client right now. Everywhere else it returns 0.

Use it to scale an effect down when the client is already busy - for example lowering a spawn rate once the total passes a few thousand. `query.effect_particle_count` gives the count for one effect identifier.

queries.name: touch_only_affects_hotbar
queries.summary: Whether the local player's touch input is limited to the hotbar
queries.hover:
1 if the local player's touch setting "only affect the hotbar" is on, else 0. Same answer for every entity.
Needs an entity being rendered; otherwise 0 with a content-log error. Behavior packs: 0 with an error.
Before the client has the player's input info: 0.
queries.description: Returns 1 when the local player's touch controls are set so that touch only affects the hotbar, and 0 otherwise. It describes the viewing player's settings, not the entity it runs on.
queries.long:
Returns `1` when the player on this client has touch input restricted to the hotbar, and `0` otherwise.

The entity the expression runs on only provides the context: the value always comes from the local player's input settings, so every entity on the client gets the same answer. The query needs an entity that is being drawn; without one (or outside rendering) it returns `0` and writes an error to the content log. In behavior-pack Molang it also returns `0` with an error, because the setting only exists on the client.

If the player's input information has not reached the client yet it returns `0` without a content-log line.

appliesTo.entities: any rendered entity (the value is the local player's setting)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity, or not evaluated while rendering
the local player's input information is not available yet

pitfalls: It never describes the entity it runs on - a mob and the player read the same value.

queries.name: trade_tier
queries.summary: The entity's trade tier (villager career level, 0 = novice)
queries.hover:
The entity's current trade tier from its synchronised data: 0 for the first tier, +1 per unlocked tier.
0 for entities that do not trade. Same value in behavior and resource packs.
queries.description: Returns the entity's current trade tier as stored in its synchronised data. The first tier is 0; each tier the entity unlocks adds 1. Non-trading entities return 0.
queries.long:
Returns the trade tier the entity has reached, counted from `0` (the first tier of its trade table). For a vanilla villager that is its career level minus one: novice `0`, apprentice `1`, journeyman `2`, expert `3`, master `4` (not yet verified in game).

The tier is written by the trading components - both the classic trade-table trading and the economy-based trading that villagers use - into the entity's synchronised data whenever it changes, so behavior packs and resource packs read the same number. Entities without trading never have the value set and return `0`, the same as a novice, so check that the entity trades before treating `0` as a tier.

Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: entities with trading (villagers, wandering trader, custom traders); others 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: 0 means both "first tier" and "does not trade".

queries.name: unhappy_counter
queries.summary: Does nothing: always 0
queries.hover: Always 0, on every entity and in every context. Do not build logic on it.
queries.description: Always returns 0. The query is registered but has no data behind it.
queries.long:
Always returns `0`, whatever the entity, the pack side or the context - even without an entity. There is no state behind it; the name refers to panda moods, but pandas never feed it.

Vanilla still references it in the panda's animation controller, where the transition it guards can therefore never fire. For panda moods use the entity's own properties or variants instead.

appliesTo.entities: none - constant

pitfalls: A transition or condition that depends on it being non-zero never fires.

queries.name: variant
queries.summary: The entity's variant number (minecraft:variant); potions report their look
queries.hover:
The entity's variant number, as set by `minecraft:variant`; 0 when nothing set it.
Thrown splash and lingering potions instead return their potion's visual variant.
Synchronised, so behavior and resource packs agree. No entity: 0.
queries.description: Returns the entity's variant number - the value `minecraft:variant` stores. Thrown splash and lingering potions are the exception: they report the visual variant of the potion they carry.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's variant number, a whole number stored in the entity's synchronised data. For data-driven entities it is the `value` of the active `minecraft:variant` component; entities that never set one read `0`. Vanilla uses it for things such as slime and magma cube sizes (in game a small slime read 1, a medium one 2 and a large one 4) and the piglin's weapon kind.

Thrown **splash potions** and **lingering potions** are handled differently: the query looks up the potion the projectile carries and returns that potion's visual variant, which decides the colour and look of the bottle. If the potion id is not known, it returns `0` (no content-log line).

Because the value is synchronised, behavior packs (filters, loot conditions, Molang in components) and resource packs see the same number. For the second variant number use `query.mark_variant`; for the skin index use `query.skin_id`. Without an entity it returns `0`.

appliesTo.entities: any entity (0 unless something set a variant); splash and lingering potions report the potion's look

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
thrown potion with an unknown potion id

pitfalls: `minecraft:variant` and `minecraft:mark_variant` are separate numbers; this query only reads the first.
On a thrown potion the number is the potion's look, not a `minecraft:variant` value.

queries.name: vertical_speed
queries.summary: Vertical speed over the last tick in blocks per second (up is positive)
queries.hover:
Vertical speed in blocks per second: the height change during the last tick x 20. Up is positive.
Changes once per tick, not smoothed between frames.
No entity: 0.
queries.description: Returns the entity's rate of height change over the last tick in blocks per second: rising gives positive values, falling negative ones.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's vertical speed in blocks per second: its change in height over the last tick, multiplied by 20 (ticks per second). Positive values mean it moved up, negative values that it moved down, and `0` means its height did not change in that tick.

The value is updated once per tick from the movement the entity actually made, so it includes jumps, knockback and being carried (not yet verified for every case), and it is not smoothed between frames. Because it reports the move that already happened, it trails `query.position_delta(1) * 20` (the motion planned for the coming tick) by one tick: in game a falling player read -4.61 while the other read -6.09, the next tick's value. Standing still it reads exactly `0`, while `query.position_delta(1) * 20` keeps showing the pull of gravity (-1.568). Because it is a per-second rate, falling speeds are large numbers, so compare with thresholds rather than small constants.

Without an entity it returns `0`. For horizontal speed use `query.ground_speed`; for the direction of movement use `query.movement_direction`.
queries.formula: `20 * (y_now - y_previous_tick)`

appliesTo.entities: any entity

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: Standing on the ground usually gives exactly 0, but slabs, stairs and step-ups give short spikes.
It moves once per tick; an animation driven directly by it steps at 20 Hz.
It is one tick behind `query.position_delta(1) * 20` and reads 0 on the ground where that one shows gravity; the two are not interchangeable.

queries.name: walk_distance
queries.summary: Horizontal distance walked on the ground, x 0.6 (not plain blocks)
queries.hover:
Running total of horizontal distance moved while on the ground, multiplied by 0.6 (1 block = 0.6).
Only ground ticks add to it; air time and sneaking add (almost) nothing. Other mobs read 0 on the client.
Projected ahead by the frame's partial tick, so it moves every frame; resets when the entity is loaded again (not yet verified).
queries.description: Returns a running total of the horizontal distance the entity has covered while standing on the ground, scaled by 0.6 - so one block walked adds 0.6.
queries.long:
Returns an ever-growing total that increases while the entity moves on the ground. Each tick in which the entity is on the ground, the horizontal distance it moved that tick (vertical movement is ignored) is added to the total; ticks spent in the air add nothing. The query returns that total multiplied by `0.6`, so walking one block adds `0.6`.

Between ticks the value is projected forward: the last tick's increase is added again, scaled by the frame's partial tick (0 to 1). That keeps it moving every frame and makes it suitable for continuous walk cycles such as vanilla's first-person hand bob (`math.sin(-query.walk_distance * 180)`): with the 0.6 scale, one full sine cycle of that form corresponds to about 3.3 blocks.

Measured in game on the player: walking 8.63 blocks added 5.18 and sprinting 8.42 blocks added 5.05 (both 0.600 per block); moving 6.8 blocks while floating off the ground added nothing; and **sneaking** 5.2 blocks added only 0.025, so a sneaking player's walk cycle nearly stops.

Only the player was seen to accumulate: a pig that had been wandering around, and a minecart, both read `0` in resource-pack Molang. Treat the query as a player one; for mobs use `query.modified_distance_moved`. The total is not saved with the entity (not yet verified), and without an entity the query returns `0`. `query.modified_distance_moved` is a different accumulator used by limb swings.
queries.formula: `0.6 * (total + (total - total_prev_tick) * partial_tick)`

appliesTo.entities: players (other mobs and non-mobs read 0 on the client)

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity is not a player (measured: a wandering pig and a minecart)

pitfalls: It is not measured in blocks: divide by 0.6 to get blocks walked.
Movement in the air (jumping, falling, flying, swimming off the ground) adds nothing.
Sneaking adds almost nothing, so a walk cycle built on it freezes while the player sneaks.
Mobs read 0 even while walking; drive mob walk cycles from `query.modified_distance_moved`.

queries.name: wing_flap_position
queries.summary: Accumulated wing-flap phase of a chicken, parrot or ender dragon
queries.hover:
Wing-flap phase counter; only chickens, parrots and the ender dragon have one, everything else returns 0.
Chicken/parrot: grows by 1.8 per tick in the air, so feed it to a sine as radians. Dragon: counts whole flaps (x360 for degrees).
Never wraps; updated once per tick, not smoothed between ticks.
queries.description: Returns the wing-flap phase of a chicken, parrot or ender dragon: a counter that keeps growing while the wings beat. Any other entity returns 0.
queries.long:
Returns an ever-growing phase value that drives a wing-beat animation. Only three built-in entity kinds keep this state - chickens, parrots and the ender dragon - and they advance it in different units. Every other entity, including custom flying mobs, returns `0`. (Whether a custom entity that borrows one of these entities' runtime identifier also gets the state is not yet verified.)

**Chicken and parrot.** Each tick a "flap strength" value is updated and then added, doubled, to the phase:

| situation | flap strength | phase gain per tick |
|---|---|---|
| in the air, not riding | reset to 1, then multiplied by 0.9 | 1.8 |
| on the ground, or riding something (a parrot on a shoulder) | only multiplied by 0.9 | 2 x the decaying strength; about 16 in total after landing, then flat |

Because an airborne bird gains a fixed 1.8 per tick, the value is meant as an angle in **radians**: `math.sin` takes degrees, so multiply by about 57.3 first. A freshly spawned bird starts at `0` with full strength, so it creeps forward for a second even when it spawns on the ground.

**Ender dragon.** The phase counts whole wing beats: multiply by 360 to get degrees. Each tick it grows by `0.2 / (10 x h + 1) x 2^d`, where `h` is the horizontal distance the dragon moved in that tick and `d` how far it dropped (negative when climbing), both in blocks. Diving makes it beat faster, climbing and fast straight flight slower (in game a dragon climbing steadily gained about 0.019 per tick). While the dragon sits (expected to be its perched phase, not yet verified) the gain is a fixed 0.1, and in one further state it is halved (not yet identified). During the death animation the resource-pack value is reset to `0` every tick (checked in game).

In all cases the counter never wraps (a parrot flying around for a few minutes was past 7000), and it changes once per game tick with no smoothing between ticks. The client runs the counter itself - in resource-pack Molang a falling chicken gained exactly 1.8 per tick and, after landing, the gains shrank by a factor of about 0.9 per tick, so the phase kept creeping for about two seconds after `query.wing_flap_speed` had already reached 0. The value is not synchronised as entity data, so whether behavior-pack and resource-pack values agree is not yet verified.
queries.formula: chicken/parrot: p += 2 x s each tick, with s = 0.9 x (airborne ? 1 : s); dragon: p += 0.2 / (10h + 1) x 2^d
queries.units: radians-like phase (chicken, parrot); wing beats (ender dragon)

appliesTo.entities: chickens, parrots and the ender dragon; every other entity always 0

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)
entity is not a chicken, parrot or ender dragon (no wing-flap state)

queries.side: both (each side keeps its own counter; agreement not yet verified)
pitfalls: A custom flying mob returns 0 regardless of its movement components; only chickens, parrots and the ender dragon keep this counter.
`math.sin(q.wing_flap_position)` treats the value as degrees and flaps about 57 times too slowly for chickens and parrots; multiply by 57.3.
The dragon's value is in whole beats, not radians: multiply by 360 for degrees.
The value steps once per tick, so a fast sine of it looks jerky at high frame rates.
After landing the phase keeps advancing for about two seconds while `query.wing_flap_speed` is already 0; multiply by the speed if the wings must stop at once.

verification.label: Partly verified in game on 1.26.60.22; some cases are not measured yet

queries.name: wing_flap_speed
queries.summary: How far a chicken's or parrot's wings are spread, 0 (folded) to 1 (flying)
queries.hover:
0..1 wing-spread amount of a chicken or parrot: jumps to 1 as soon as it is airborne, eases to 0 at 0.3 per tick on the ground or while riding.
Every other entity returns 0, the ender dragon included.
Per tick, not smoothed; usually multiplied with a sine of q.wing_flap_position.
queries.description: Returns how far a chicken's or parrot's wings are open, from 0 when folded to 1 while it is in the air. Other entities, the ender dragon included, return 0.
queries.long:
Returns a value from `0` to `1` saying how much a chicken's or parrot's wings are spread - an amplitude to multiply with a wing-beat sine built from `query.wing_flap_position`.

Each game tick the value moves by a fixed step and is clamped to `[0, 1]`:

| situation | change per tick | result |
|---|---|---|
| in the air and not riding anything | +1.2 | reaches `1` on the first airborne tick |
| on the ground | -0.3 | from `1` to `0` in 4 ticks (0.7, 0.4, 0.1, 0) |
| riding something (a parrot on a player's shoulder) | -0.3 | as on the ground |

Being on the ground takes precedence over riding. A newly spawned bird starts at `0`.

Only chickens and parrots update this value. The ender dragon keeps a wing-flap phase for `query.wing_flap_position` but never sets a speed, so it reads `0` here (checked in game, in flight and while dying); every other entity (bats and phantoms included) has no flap state at all and also returns `0`. The value is not smoothed between ticks. The client computes it itself (in game a falling chicken read 1 and went 0.7, then 0 on landing); whether it matches the server value is not yet verified.

queries.name: yaw_speed
queries.summary: How fast the entity turned during the last tick, in degrees per second
queries.hover:
Turn rate over the last tick in degrees per second: (yaw now - yaw a tick ago), wrapped to [-180, 180), x 20.
Mobs and players use the body yaw, not where the head or camera points; other entities use their own facing.
Positive = yaw increasing (clockwise seen from above). Client-side boats and minecarts ease their yaw, spreading a snap over ticks.
queries.description: Returns how fast the entity is turning left or right, in degrees per second, measured over the last game tick. For mobs and players it is the turn rate of the body.
queries.long:
Returns the entity's turn rate around the vertical axis, in **degrees per second**. It takes the change in yaw since the previous game tick, wraps it into `[-180, 180)` degrees and multiplies it by 20 (ticks per second):

`yaw_speed = wrap(yaw - previous_yaw) x 20`

Which yaw is used depends on the entity:

| entity | yaw measured |
|---|---|
| mobs and players | body yaw - the direction the torso faces, which trails behind the head |
| other entities (boats, minecarts, projectiles, ...) | the entity's own facing |

A positive value should mean the yaw is increasing, which is a clockwise turn when seen from above; negative is counter-clockwise (checked in game). The wrap makes a turn through north, where yaw jumps between 180 and -180, read as a small step, not a jump of nearly 360 degrees. The largest possible magnitude is 3600 (a half turn in one tick).

For players this is the body, so looking around quickly with the camera shows up only after the body follows, and a player standing still while only moving the head reads `0` for as long as the body does not turn. The value is recomputed each tick and not smoothed, so it holds the same number for every frame of a tick. Without an entity it returns `0`.

In game (resource-pack Molang) a player whose camera snapped 60 degrees read a burst from the body turning 10 degrees, not from the head. A boat teleported 10 degrees at a time did not read one +200 tick: the client eases such entities' yaw over several ticks, so the value came out as about 50, 15, 4, 1 per step - including across the 180/-180 seam, with no spike.
queries.formula: wrap(yaw - previous_yaw) x 20, with wrap into [-180, 180)

appliesTo.entities: any entity; mobs and players report body yaw

whenUnavailable.when: no entity in the context (world particles, blocks)

pitfalls: For players and mobs it follows the body, not the head or camera: turning only the head gives 0.
The result is already per second; do not multiply by 20 again.
On the client, a boat's or minecart's turn that the server makes in one tick is spread over several ticks, so peaks are lower than 20 x the turn.
